data.title: Britain must maintain its lead to unlock energy’s holy grail
data.description:
It’s long been the “somewhere over the rainbow” promise of economic transformation that never seems to arrive. No, I’m not talking about AI, which, though already with us, has yet to prove the grandiose claims made of it.

Rather, I’m referring to nuclear fusion. This is the holy grail of energy production – the promise of limitless quantities of low-cost, carbon-free, baseload electricity.

Like the grail itself, commercialisation has thus far eluded even the world’s finest scientific minds and entrepreneurs.

But that doesn’t mean it’s still just science fiction. Lab-made fusion has already been successfully demonstrated on multiple occasions, and the science behind it is now relatively well advanced.

Yet until a few years ago, all such experimentation consumed more power than it generated, rendering it useless as an energy source.

As the old joke goes, economically viable fusion is about 30 years away, and will always be 30 years away. Harnessing the same power as the sun has proved much more difficult in practice than in theory.

In the past several years, however, there have been some very definite signs of the required breakthroughs.

And perhaps surprisingly, some of them are happening in Britain. With its history of academic excellence, the UK has always been good at this sort of stuff, but it has also been notably poor at commercialising it.

Innovative success has not translated well into economic exploitation. Rather, it is the US, and increasingly China, that tend to capitalise on what comes out of British brainpower.

Is fusion likely to suffer the same fate?

Dennis Whyte, who was this month appointed the chief executive of the UK Atomic Energy Authority – the Government body responsible for the nation’s “fusion strategy” – is determined that it should not. Formerly director of the fusion centre at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Whyte believes the UK has a unique set of capabilities that will allow it to excel in fusion’s development and commercialisation.

But first let’s talk about the potential, which to economic nerds like me is the really interesting bit.

Move over AI, the truly transformational technology coming down the road at us is not fully conscious humanoid robots but fusion.

Most economic progress is at root about energy and our ability to harness it to human purposes. At the heart of the industrial revolution, for instance, was not so much the machines themselves as the transformative power of coal.

The so-called Kardashev scale, though in some respects quack science, provides one way of charting economic advancement according to energy consumption.

Named after Nikolai Kardashev, the Soviet era astronomer, it seeks to measure progress in civilisation based entirely on the amount of energy that can be harnessed and deployed.

According to Kardashev, it’s only when humans manage to access unlimited quantities of it beyond mere Earth-bound sources that civilisation achieves its true potential.

This may or may not be an endorsement, but Elon Musk is particularly keen on the Kardashev way of thinking.

Only for him it’s about accessing the power of the sun via solar panels, battery storage and infrastructure in space. Indeed, he has dismissed pursuit of Earth-bound fusion reactors as “super dumb and farcical”.

Musk is the undisputed master of tech commercialisation, so he has to be taken seriously. Nonetheless, he should know better than anyone that progress involves, through a process of trial and error, testing the frontiers of science to virtual destruction and eventually finding a way through.

Think about it; if manmade fusion can be achieved at scale, it is likely to be a far bigger driver of productivity growth than anything AI can offer, as well as being a potential solution to any existential threat posed by climate change.

As Whyte points out, AI is a technology with unproven potential, despite the hundreds of billions of dollars being invested in it.

A lot of questions remain about its supposedly transformational powers, as last week’s wobble in AI-related stocks and shares seemed to confirm.

Nobody knows what its effect on jobs and growth might be, still less whether it is capable of generating the returns needed to justify the vast amounts being invested in it.

With energy, on the other hand, we already know what cheap power can do; fusion is moreover not just a further time-limited energy source, in the same way as a new gas field might be.

It is a forever, unlimited resource that promises to power hitherto undreamt levels of technological advancement and human progress. If it can be achieved, it truly would be a game changer, and as an economic leap forward, perhaps bigger than even the Industrial Revolution.

Interestingly, it is also complementary to the development of AI, which both has an insatiable appetite for power and whose computational skills are already helping to turbo-charge the pursuit of commercially viable fusion.

There is a developing symbiosis between the two, a mutually beneficial co-dependency which ought to help both technologies achieve their potential.

I’m no expert, so I cannot tell you if in 30 years’ time we’ll still be saying fusion is 30 years away and will always be 30 years away.

But Whyte knows as much as there is to know about fusion, and he’s never been more optimistic.

A growing number of labs and companies are successfully achieving it, including recently General Fusion Group, which has announced that its magnetised target fusion (MTF) technology has reached electron temperatures exceeding 12 million degrees Celsius, well in advance of what’s needed for fusion to take place.

The results were confirmed using the UK Atomic Energy Authority measurement techniques.

What’s more, around £10bn of private capital globally has been invested in fusion in a clear signal that commercialisation is beginning to be seen as eminently possible and even likely.

Not to be outdone, China is also chasing hard, having elevated fusion to a core strategic frontier and national infrastructure priority.

Some readers may be familiar with an Apple TV science fiction series called For All Mankind, which is based around the idea that the space race never ended.

The consequent superpower rivalry drives rapid technological progress, such that by the year 2000 space exploration and colonisation are far in advance of anything we see today.

The same rivalry already apparent between the West and China in AI is beginning to take hold in nuclear fusion, where China has a significant advantage in terms of the supply chains and manufacturing capacity needed to make fusion reactors a reality.

Still, Britain is for now very much part of the race. The UK was the first country in the world to produce nuclear power at scale for civilian use. It would be nice to think it is still capable of doing the same with fusion.

data.title: Amazon orders coders to rein in AI use as costs mount
data.description:
Amazon has ordered its coders to rein in their AI use amid concerns that tech workers are blowing through company budgets on chatbots.

The online retailer told staff that technology giants’ efforts to track AI usage by their software engineers were “deeply flawed” and risked driving up costs.

Some technology businesses have started ranking staff by how many AI tokens, the building blocks of AI bots, they use.

It has driven a trend of “tokenmaxxing” among workers as they compete to maximise their AI use.

However, bosses have since had to curb usage and limit AI spending after engineers burned through budgets on coding projects.

In a note to the company’s coders, Terk Terkowitz, an Amazon vice president, said companies that tried to track AI adoption by ranking staff on token use risked driving up costs.

He said: “We know that using these metrics could, if used as a target instead of a measure, drive negative outcomes, increasing costs (tokenmaxxing is at odds with frugality) and increasing complexity.”

The warning comes as technology giants grapple with surging AI costs while employees race to incorporate the new technology into their work.

Earlier this year, Amazon shut down an internal leaderboard tracking the most prolific AI users, measured by how much they spent on AI.

The trend has raised concerns that staff have been doing needless tasks to boost their rankings while racking up substantial computing costs.

Disney and Meta have adopted similar leaderboards, prompting the Facebook owner to implement AI token caps for some employees to keep costs under control.

While Amazon has not implemented a cap on AI tokens, it has urged software engineers to consider the benefits the technology brings.

It said: “Judgment and care are key ... we believe that it is best to measure and be measured by long-term outcomes.”

Amazon insisted that AI would be at the centre of software engineering. However, it told staff not to use the technology if they did not need it.

The company said: “If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing.”

Under Andy Jassy, Amazon’s chief executive, the company has been ramping up its internal use of AI.

Mr Jassy has previously said the company would need fewer employees in the future as more work became automated.

Amazon is a major backer of Anthropic, the developer of Claude. Amazon has invested $13bn (£10bn) in the AI company, which is now valued at $190bn, putting it in line for a major windfall when Anthropic goes public next month.

data.title: Reform urges Labour to block Poundland break-up
data.description:
Reform UK is urging the Government to prevent the owner of Poundland breaking up the business.

In a letter to Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, the party accused Gordon Brothers of confecting Poundland’s insolvency by cutting funding from the business earlier this week.

Directors filed a notice to appoint administrators on Thursday, putting 12,000 jobs across Britain at risk.

In the letter, Robert Jenrick, Reform’s Treasury spokesman, and Richard Tice, the party’s deputy leader, blamed Gordon Brothers for the retailer’s cash crisis. They also questioned why Gordon Brothers rejected a solvent bid for the business that could have kept it afloat, echoing concerns raised by Andy Burnham last night.

“We are writing to you to express our shock at the way the sale of Poundland is being handled,” they said.

“If it is allowed to collapse into administration as many as 12,000 jobs, and over 600 high street stores, are at risk.

“However, its current cashflow issues appear to be the result of Gordon Brothers restricting lines of credit it had extended to the business, forcing it into a liquidity crisis.”

The Telegraph revealed on Thursday that Poundland’s directors had filed a notice to appoint Alix Partners as administrators.

This will now trigger a 10-day moratorium that will prevent creditors from calling in their debts, giving Poundland time to consider bids to carve up the business.

Rival retailers have expressed interest in snapping up some of the estate, but it is unclear how many of its 600 stores would be sold.

Mr Jenrick and Mr Tice said ministers must take immediate action to ensure that Poundland “is not stripped for parts by its American owners”.

Ireland’s Martin Property Group reiterated its interest on Friday in acquiring thousands of Poundland’s stores after its original offer was rejected by Gordon Brothers.

The refusal related to Martin Property Group’s unwillingness to meet Gordon Brothers’ demands for up-front repayment of a £30m shareholder loan. Gordon Brothers acquired Poundland last year for £1.

Reform said Gordon Brothers’ financial interests could not come before those of workers and the high street, especially after Poundland posted a strong run of recent sales growth.

Mr Jenrick and Mr Tice said: “This is clearly a business that is in recovery, and it would be a travesty for the hardworking employees that keep it going day to day to have it carved up, with significant job losses in the process.

“Poundland is a mainstay of the British high street, and its disappearance would do irreparable harm to what remains of high street footfall in huge swathes of Britain.

“We are calling on the government to take urgent action to ensure that Poundland is not stripped for parts by its current American owners, and that full consideration is given to bids that ensure its continuing operation as a going concern.

“An American asset fund’s desire to get full repayment of a £30m loan it paid only £1 for cannot come before the interests of the thousands of British workers that are working hard to help Poundland recover from its issues.”

A separate letter was also sent to Mr Reynolds by a group of Labour MPs whose constituencies contain Poundland shops. They also urged the Government “explore every available option to safeguard jobs”.

Gordon Brothers first put Poundland up for sale in September, although industry sources suggested that the firm may have favoured selling the business piecemeal.

Turnaround firm Modella Capital, retailer B&M, Poundstretcher owner Fortress and The Range’s CDS Superstores have all expressed interest in buying at least some stores.

Amdy Burnham, the Prime Minister, told The Telegraph last night that he was demanding answers over the Poundland’s anticipated collapse.

Mr Reynolds also said he was “keeping a close eye on the situation”, which threatens to become the biggest retail collapse since BHS went bust in 2016.

He said: “If it is true that it was not necessary to put the business into administration then the present owners will have to account for that.”

As well as pointing the finger at Gordon Brothers, Reform also blamed the Government for fuelling Poundland’s struggles.

In particular, they criticised Rachel Reeves’ employers’ National Insurance tax raid for piling pressure on retailers, reiterating calls for Labour to reverse the policy.

Gordon Brothers was contacted for comment.

data.title: ‘China Shock 2.0’ is crushing the West
data.description:
Robot vacuum cleaners are typically less noisy than their older, hand-operated cousins. But the volume of the Chinese-made versions is not the only quiet thing. They are also stealthily taking over the world.

Dreame, a company founded in Suzhou less than a decade ago, is now said to be the world’s biggest seller of robot vacuums. Its founder, 39-year-old Yu Hao, claims to be building a $100tn (£75tn) ecosystem of smart appliances and frontier tech.

After just two years in Britain, Dreame is still a relatively small player here. Euromonitor International put the company’s UK market share at 4pc last year.

But four Chinese companies control almost half the UK market. And their cheapest products are all priced below those of SharkNinja and Dyson, which manufacture in Asia but do at least some of the brain-work in the US and Britain, respectively.

When it comes to Chinese imports, most people think first of electric vehicles (EVs), which are swarming into markets worldwide, such as Jaecoo, a brand that has become the go-to for British consumers. It is certainly the prime battlefront, with Britain under growing pressure to mimic the EU’s tariffs of up to 45pc on EVs.

Beneath these headlines, however, cut-price Chinese imports of just about any manufactured product are now sweeping into the West and challenging local businesses.

Consumers love the low prices. But companies and governments across Europe now fear that the Chinese juggernaut will hoover up Western industries and jobs, and leave the Continent utterly dependent on the whims and will of Beijing.

The timing of this “China Shock 2.0” – the first shock was the flood of low-priced toys, clothes and other manufactured goods that hit in the early 2000s – is not a coincidence. In the past few years, Beijing has unmuzzled its most potent weapon to win the export war.

Chinese factories have long enjoyed advantages such as cheap workers and raw materials, generous subsidies and massive economies of scale. But now a new wave of cheap credit – that is, loans made on concessional or non-commercial terms – has swept through the Chinese manufacturing sector, unlocking the export tsunami.

“This is probably the single biggest component of China’s industrial policy,” says Camille Boullenois, a China expert at the Rhodium Group consultancy.

“It has been the most powerful and the most influential factor shaping the economic system in China, because the entire economic system is based on credit.”

‘Everything in China is political’

Ever since China’s banks pulled back from lending to households after the spectacular property crash of 2021, they have been scrambling to find enough borrowers.

And with the Chinese government ever more focused on ramping up high-tech and advanced manufacturing, that’s where the banks have been pouring all that surplus cash.

“There’s a natural herding in the way the Chinese private sector operates. Once everybody realised that manufacturing is where the political light was shining, then capital and human talent moved into manufacturing,” says David Lubin, of the think tank Chatham House.

The banks have become the pivotal enabler of Beijing’s ambition to ensure companies, such as Dreame, dominate global markets and supply chains.

“Lending is political, because everything in China is political. And credit is a political tool,” says Leo Austin, a businessman who advises multinationals on working in China.

These dirt-cheap loans mean that, unlike their Western rivals, many Chinese companies can receive capital on tap.

“There is always cash flow available to you, and you have no short-term fear around the viability of the business, so you can afford to be incredibly aggressive,” Austin says.

This has wrought a transformation in China that is little appreciated outside its borders.

Once there were private firms and state-owned enterprises. But now most companies are a hybrid: they have a private-sector management culture, but are almost entirely funded by government-sourced equity and state-backed lending.

Austin calls this model “state-capitalised private enterprises”. The emerging Chinese high-tech giants are almost all cut from this cloth.

Chinese banks are bound by law to lend money “in accordance with the needs of the national economic and social development, and under the guidance of the industrial policies of the state”.

And they do. Beijing’s corporate debt totals about 138pc of GDP, almost double the ratio in the US. But Chinese companies’ interest costs amount to less than 1pc of turnover, compared with 5pc for their American peers.

The effect of this fresh wave of cheap credit has been immediate.

China’s domination

Between 2021 and 2024, the number of products where China accounts for more than half of global exports nearly doubled, from 192 to 315.

China’s trade surplus will again surpass $1tn this year. The surplus with both Germany and France has doubled in the past year. For the EU as a whole, it amounts to more than €1bn (£840m) a day.

Although this export surge makes China appear like a rising economic superpower, the boom in cheap credit and factory exports has a dark side.

Companies are exporting their credit-fuelled output because Chinese households, burnt by the property crash, are not spending. At home, Chinese companies are forced into painful discounting wars just to move stock.

Profitability has plummeted and one in three companies is loss-making. Without the exports, which often provide more than 40pc of revenue, many businesses would be unviable.

Yet the banks keep lending and lending. Often, they have to discount the interest rate simply because otherwise the borrower would go bust.

Instead, it is European competitors who are absorbing the blow. In Britain, some have complained to the Trade Remedies Authority (TRA), which can impose quotas or tariffs.

The TRA has sought to protect local manufacturers from cut-price Chinese imports of everything from ceramics to ironing boards, tyres and cherry-pickers.

One recent TRA ruling noted that Chinese companies “have access to preferential financing, and access to financing from institutions which implement public policy objectives or otherwise do not act independently of the state”.

The TRA added: “They have more flexibility and can adjust their business and pricing strategies to maximise their export sales and gain market share in the UK, even if they would have otherwise made negative profit margins.”

No easy answers

Given that the Government is aware of the problem, many businesses want to see it push back harder. “There are probably plenty of stones that could be unturned,” one industry veteran says.

Rhodium’s Boullenois says the same is true in Europe, where Brussels’s trade directorate is overwhelmed with business requests for protection.

“We’re protecting too few products. Our defences need to be much broader, and work much faster,” she says.

But if the EU and US protect their own markets, more of the ultra-cheap Chinese exports will simply shift to Asia, Africa and Latin America – displacing European and American rivals in those countries’ markets.

“We normally look at how much is China selling to the EU. A lot less time is spent thinking about how many EU products the Chinese manufacturers are displacing in foreign markets – and it’s huge,” says Joe Peissel, of the consultancy Trivium China.

The battle against China’s factories is on in earnest. But as long as the Chinese are backed up by the bazooka of the country’s banking system, it will be a war that the West will struggle to win.

data.title: Britain ‘risks becoming uninvestable’ after TalkTalk rescue deal
data.description:
Government backing for BT’s TalkTalk rescue has undermined confidence in Britain and risks making the country “uninvestable”, a major French fund has warned.

Bruno Candès, a partner at French infrastructure investment fund InfraVia, said recent interventions in the UK broadband market had fuelled uncertainty and risked deterring foreign investment.

Mr Candès pointed to the Government’s support for BT’s takeover of TalkTalk, which serves 2.5 million customers and had been teetering on the brink of collapse.

Ministers reserved the right to override competition concerns to drive the merger through, citing fears about the risk to vulnerable customers should TalkTalk have gone under.

However, the deal triggered a furious response from rivals, who warned it would cement the former monopoly’s dominant position in the market.

Writing in The Telegraph, Mr Candès said: “Investors judge countries by what governments and regulators do, not simply what they say. Confidence takes years to build, can be lost quickly and, once lost, is difficult to win back.

“An unpredictable market becomes an uninvestable market. The UK is in danger of becoming one.”

The Government’s support for BT’s takeover of TalkTalk came just days after regulators threatened to block Virgin Media O2’s (VMO2) £2bn takeover of rival Netomnia. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) warned the deal risked pushing up prices in the broadband market.

InfraVia, which manages €20bn (£17bn) on behalf of investors, is involved in the Netomnia transaction. The deal is being carried out through Nexfibre, a joint venture between InfraVia and VMO2’s parent companies, Liberty Global and Telefónica. They have said the transaction would unlock £3.5bn of investment in the UK.

Mr Candès said the contrasting responses to the Netomnia deal and BT’s swoop for TalkTalk highlighted uncertainty in the UK market, adding that “neither inspires confidence”.

He took aim at the competition watchdog, which concluded in provisional findings that CityFibre, another broadband provider, would probably have bought Netomnia had VMO2’s deal not been in place.

The InfraVia boss argued that his company’s takeover was therefore being “weighed against an alternative that may never happen”.

He said that while so-called “counterfactual” assessments had a place in merger control, these needed to be “rooted in commercial and economic reality”. He added: “At some point this counterfactual has become a counter-fantasy.”

Mr Candès warned this uncertainty was undermining confidence in Britain, raising the risk that investors could pull funding. He also questioned whether the CMA was adhering to a government directive to prioritise economic growth.

He said: “To make long-term plans, investors need to know where they stand. Rules need to be clear, consistent and grounded in economic reality.

“If real, committed capital is held back in favour of speculative possibilities, investors will notice. They will invest elsewhere.”

VMO2 has called BT’s TalkTalk deal a “stitch-up” while Lutz Schüler, the chief executive, has written to Lisa Nandy, the Culture Secretary, demanding clarity on why she chose to intervene.

The company, which is BT’s largest rival, is calling for the watchdog to conduct an in-depth investigation into the impact of the deal on competition.

The CMA last week delivered a fast-tracked report to Ms Nandy, who will make a final decision. The regulator has separately accepted feedback on the Netomnia merger and will issue its final decision before Dec 15.

Mr Candès’s criticism comes just days before John Healey, the Chancellor, presents his first Budget.

The Department for Culture, Media and Sport and the CMA declined to comment.

Is the UK becoming uninvestable?

By Bruno Candès, partner at InfraVia

Investors can handle commercial risk. That is our business. Regulatory uncertainty is different.

The UK has spent years telling international investors it wants our capital. Good. We want to invest here.

But words are not enough. Decisions matter.

Two recent moves bring that into sharp focus.

First, the Government’s orchestration of BT’s acquisition of TalkTalk. I understand the desire to fix an immediate problem but the result strengthens the long-term position of the incumbent.

Second, the CMA’s interim position on consolidation in fibre. A real transaction, backed by £3.5bn of international investment, is being tested against a speculative future in which another buyer might emerge from a heavily indebted market.

One deals with today’s problem. The other bets on tomorrow’s hypothetical. Neither inspires confidence.

The Government’s strategic steer could hardly be clearer. It says the CMA’s approach should “clearly and unambiguously reflect the need to enhance the attractiveness of the UK as a destination for international investment”.

And the investment challenge is already significant. The Government itself acknowledges that infrastructure investment in the UK has been “too erratic and too low”. Its 10-year infrastructure strategy sets out at least £725bn of public funding in the coming decade, while making clear that private investment is critical to achieving the UK’s infrastructure ambitions.

That underlines the importance of investor confidence. We compete for assets. We win deals. And we accept that not every decision goes our way. That is investing.

To make long-term plans, investors need to know where they stand. Rules need to be clear, consistent and grounded in economic reality.

The UK has set the direction. Now it needs to follow it.

Our proposed transaction unlocks £3.5bn of international investment in UK digital infrastructure.

Real capital. Ready to put fibre in the ground. Yet it is being weighed against an alternative that may never happen.

Counterfactuals have a place in merger control. Of course they do. They are the CMA’s assessment of what the market would most likely look like if a deal did not happen. But that assessment needs to be rooted in commercial and economic reality.

At some point this counterfactual has become a counter-fantasy.

In rugby, you do not award a try because another team might one day find the money, assemble the players and cross the line. You judge what is happening on the field.

And what is on the field today? Committed capital. A credible transaction. A stronger competitor.

The right answer is already in front of us.

Competition does not live on a spreadsheet.

Fibre networks need capital, customers and scale. Without them, the economics do not work. And the investment stops.

That is why consolidation is not automatically the enemy of competition. Done properly, it can create a stronger alternative to a single dominant incumbent.

Competition is not a headcount exercise. What matters is whether the challengers are strong enough to compete.

Keeping more players on paper while leaving them weaker in the real world would be a hollow victory.

The goal should be competition that lasts. Not competition that exists only in theory.

International capital has choices. And investors judge countries by what governments and regulators do, not simply what they say. Confidence takes years to build, can be lost quickly and, once lost, is difficult to win back.

If real, committed capital is held back in favour of speculative possibilities, investors will notice. They will invest elsewhere.

An unpredictable market becomes an uninvestable market. The UK is in danger of becoming one. It does not have to be.

The investment is ready. The case for sustainable competition is clear. The decision is still there to be made.

Back real investment. Build real competition. Create real choice for consumers.

Let’s get on with it.

data.title: Coutts u-turns in debanking row with shipping tycoon
data.description:
Coutts has been forced to backtrack on key claims made in a debanking row with a shipping tycoon after admitting its information was inaccurate.

The lender, known as the “King’s bank” for its relationship with the British monarchy, is embroiled in a row with Philip Adkins, an international shipping executive.

He has alleged that Coutts, which is owned by NatWest, froze his accounts in 2024 and held erroneous information on him about his personal wealth.

Coutts had originally claimed that Mr Adkins divulged the details himself over the phone in 2021, but the bank has now admitted that this is inaccurate.

Lawyers for the bank have also accepted that Mr Adkins would be entitled to pursue damages against the bank under data protection rules, and that it would have to erase and remove the false information.

Mr Adkins, the former boss of Red Box Energy Services, claims that Coutts’s inaccurate information triggered an investigation into his finances by the US Department of Justice.

Coutts is alleged to have incorrectly put his wealth at £62m, said he owned an apartment in Hong Kong and said he had lost half his wealth in a credit line to Goldman Sachs.

Instead, he had never owned an apartment nor had a relationship with Goldman Sachs, his lawyers said, adding that he had been a Coutts customer for four decades. His lawyers also claimed his net worth figure was incorrect.

In response, Coutts has denied sharing any data with third parties, and maintains that Mr Adkins himself requested to close his accounts with the bank.

It also said it must comply with sanctions obligations and that the UK and US authorities sanctioned entities connected to Red Box Energy Services in 2024.

Although sources dispute that the case is about debanking, it has echoes of a similar episode the bank faced with Nigel Farage, whose account was closed by Coutts in 2023.

In that incident, it was revealed that Coutts spent months compiling evidence on the “significant reputational risks of being associated with him”.

Ultimately, the dispute led to the exit of Dame Alison Rose, the NatWest chief executive, who admitted discussing Mr Farage’s case with a BBC journalist.

Coutts is one of Britain’s most esteemed banks having been founded in 1692 during the reign of William III and Mary II.

In the Farage case, NatWest initially claimed the Reform UK leader had failed to meet eligibility requirements for access to the bank, but it was subsequently revealed that the closure was because of his political views.

A report by the law firm Travers Smith found that although NatWest had acted within the law, it had made “serious failings” in the incident.

Dame Alison later admitted a “serious error of judgment” after briefing a BBC journalist about Mr Farage’s case, which forced her resignation from the bank.

The bank paid Mr Farage an undisclosed sum to settle the dispute last year.

A Coutts spokesman said: “We cannot comment on ongoing legal proceedings.”

Mr Adkins said: “I would really like to know how Coutts can properly manage its financial data system and maintain an inaccurate financial profile of me for over five years which included an apartment in Hong Kong that I never owned.”

data.title: Lime riders joust as knights in London
data.description:
Lime bike riders have been filmed dressed as knights and duelling in London.

The company has said its bikes are “not for jousting” after videos circulated on social media showed hundreds of people gathered in London Fields, east London, to watch Saturday’s event.

Artist Jack Carden and actor Cameron Carnegie-Brown, known as Camtholomew, were filmed jousting whilst riding the green rentable e-bikes.

Dressed in chainmail, red and black cloaks and armour, including helmets, the pair ride towards one another, brandishing striped poles.

The assembled crowd can be heard chanting “joust, joust, joust” before one of the men strikes the other with a “lance”, causing them to fall from the bike.

A spokesman for Lime said on Monday: “We always love seeing Londoners come together and build a sense of community in unexpected ways.

“While we appreciate the medieval spirit, safety must always come first.

“Lime bikes are designed for getting around the city, not for jousting.

“We discourage anyone from attempting similar events, to help keep riders and those around them safe.”

Posting on social media before the event, Mr Carden said the “free public joust” was “performance art”.

In a video from the event posted to both competitors’ social media accounts, a voiceover says: “I want to remind you all why we are here. 

“Not only does this mean some artistic violence but to come together and celebrate art, to remind ourselves that we’re all the same and that what we need right now in this world is a little bit more love.”

A video on Mr Carden’s Instagram account of the joust has been watched more than four million times.

data.title: Toblerone owner accuses British rival of copying shape
data.description:
The owner of Toblerone is suing a tiny British chocolate maker amid claims its vegan bars copy the brand’s distinctive shape.

Mondelēz, the American food giant, which also owns Cadbury and Oreo, has launched legal proceedings against Catherine’s Originals, a small business based in West Sussex employing just 10 people.

The company has accused Catherine’s, which largely takes orders through Instagram, of trademark infringement, alleging that its O’bar chocolate is too similar to Toblerone.

The dispute centres on the appearance of the chocolate, which is divided into rounded segments rather than Toblerone’s signature triangular peaks.

Catherine’s Originals was founded in 2021 by Catherine Dodd, who was still a teenager at the time.

The scale of the David and Goliath legal battle is underlined by the vast difference in size between the two businesses.

Accounts filed at Companies House show Catherine’s Originals employed an average of just 10 people, including its directors, last year.

The business had around £105,000 in the bank at the end of December.

By contrast, Mondelēz employs around 91,000 people worldwide and made profit of $2.45bn (£1.8bn) on sales of $38.5bn last year.

Ms Dodd has denied copying Toblerone, insisting that the rounded segments of her chocolate bars were designed to resemble the letter O in her company’s name.

She told The Guardian: “We strongly disagree with the claim concerning O’bar and are working with our legal team to defend our position.

“Honestly, it’s fairly frightening for a small business we’ve put so much care and hard work into building. But being a smaller business does not mean being afraid to stand up for what we’ve created.”

A spokesman for Mondelēz said: “The iconic Toblerone shape is one of the most recognised and distinctive product designs in the UK and across the world, and has been a hallmark of the brand since 1929.

data.title: Lloyds: Bank tax will drive up mortgage costs
data.description:
John Healey’s bank tax will push up mortgage and loan costs for households, Lloyds has warned.

William Chalmers, the chief financial officer at the bank, said the tax rise was unhelpful and would impact the cost of borrowing.

He said: “It is ultimately important that we do what we can to reduce the cost of lending in order for the UK to grow, and that travels through into the cost of borrowing.

“It’s also important that we do everything we can to ensure international competitiveness. To be clear, additional taxes are unhelpful to achieving both of those two objectives – UK growth or international competitiveness.”

John Healey used his Budget on Wednesday to announce a doubling of the banking surcharge from 3pc to 6pc for 15 months from January to provide “immediate support on energy bills”.

The surcharge is levied in addition to corporation tax, which now stands at 25pc, bringing the total rate faced by the sector to 31pc – the highest level since at least 2015.

Mr Chalmers also questioned whether raising bank taxes would help households deal with the energy crisis.

“I didn’t see an obvious linkage between energy prices and bank taxes,” he said. “If anything, it makes it even more important that we’re able to lend into the real economy and secure growth, which is the best defence against energy price impacts that might otherwise prevail on the UK economy.”

The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) estimates that the higher bank tax will bring in an extra £1.5bn, though it believes that roughly £190m of bank profits would move out of the UK following the rise in tax.

Other banks have also criticised the tax increase, with JP Morgan saying it “lacks principle”. The Wall Street giant said it was unfair for the Chancellor to “single out” banks.

David Postings, chief executive of industry trade association UK Finance, said: “Increasing bank taxes is not, in our view, the best way to deliver growth.

“The Chancellor’s promise that this increase will be time-limited is therefore important, given we already have a tax regime that needs to be made more internationally competitive.”

Mr Chalmers’ comments came as Lloyds Bank almost doubled its pre-tax profit in the third quarter of the year to £2.3bn, boosted by income from higher interest rates.

Strong performance in Lloyds’ private bank, as well as its corporate and institutional division, also helped boost its profits.

Charlie Nunn, the bank’s chief executive, has been moving Lloyds Bank away from its dependence on interest rates by building out its wealth management and insurance operations.

Lloyds shares were down more than 3pc in early trading.

data.title: One million risk losing landline as digital switchover looms
data.description:
Have you been overcharged, struggled to get a refund, dealt with poor customer service or spotted something consumers should know about? Get in touch with us in the comments or email consumeraffairs@telegraph.co.uk*.

One million customers have just three months to upgrade their analogue phone lines as part of a UK-wide digital switchover.

Landline operators are switching home phones across the country to internet-based connections instead of copper-wire cables.

BT-owned Openreach, which operates the UK’s largest landline network, is scheduled to shut down its old system on Jan 31.

It told The Telegraph that one million customers, comprising both residents and businesses, were still on the old public switched telephone network (PSTN) despite the looming cut-off date.

Some customers who miss the deadline may be moved on to a temporary emergency phone service which does not have features such as voicemail. Others risk losing their connection altogether.

James Lilley, Openreach director of customer migrations, said that tens of thousands of customers were switching each week, but a rise in scams had made it harder to get consumers to respond to letters about the change.

“It’s very hard to get [customers] to read and react and do something,” he said.

Recently published data from Openreach showed that London had the greatest proportion of legacy lines still left to switch among major UK cities.

Business owners would also be affected as the PSTN system supports some payment terminals, emergency phones in lifts and door entry systems.

Although the deadline is nearing, Openreach insisted there would not be a single day when customers suddenly lose access to services.

Mr Lilley said: “There is no big red button that will switch everyone off on Jan 31.”

But the back-up line, known as the emergency voice access (Evac) service, does not include certain other features, such as three-way calling or call diversion.

The industry had originally targeted a switch-off date of Dec 31, 2025. After concerns were raised about rural households and vulnerable, often elderly, customers who rely on telecare alarms, this was extended.

Under the PSTN Charter, providers agreed not to switch users of telecare devices unless their devices, such as fall alarms, were compatible with digital landlines.

Telecom companies, including BT, have also been giving free back-up battery packs to vulnerable customers who rely on their landlines, which can keep phones working for an hour or more.

Campaign group Silver Voices has, however, called for another extension, saying it was necessary to address the needs of older customers and businesses where there may be complex engineering problems.

Earlier this week, MPs also warned that the plans could leave people in remote areas unable to contact help in an emergency such as a severe storm or a cyber attack.

Unlike digital services, the traditional landline network does not rely on mains electricity and so continues to work in a power cut.

The Government has said the migration to digital, which was first announced in 2017, was necessary because the ageing copper-based network had become less reliable.

But during a debate in the Commons on Tuesday, Torcuil Crichton, a Labour MP, who represents the Western Isles constituency of Na h-Eileanan an Iar, said: “Resilience is inbuilt in the islands but we have major problems with connectivity because of this move from analogue to digital phone lines.

“When the power goes out, people don’t have the phone, they don’t have the internet and often they don’t have a mobile signal either,” he added.

Julian Lewis, a Conservative MP, also raised concerns about the lack of a “back-up system” if digital phone services were not available.

He told Dan Jarvis, the security minister, that the copper-wire network “could have given us useful levels of resilience in an emergency”.

Mr Jarvis said he would “look very closely” at this point.

Ofcom said it expected minimal disruption for most customers.

A spokesman for the regulator said that it has clear rules that phone companies must follow when switching customers to digital landlines.

It said it was monitoring the process closely and had already fined one firm for “putting vulnerable customers at unacceptable risk of harm” during the changeover.

A BT Group spokesman said: “As we focus on the small minority of our customers yet to make the switch, protecting those who need extra support remains our top priority.”

data.title: ‘I can’t pay for anything’: 10-hour blackout exposes risk-taking Revolut
data.description:
Revolut has spent a decade telling customers it does things better than the high street.

The fintech, whose $115bn (£87bn) valuation makes it larger than Barclays, Lloyds and NatWest, pioneered the online-only approach to banking, leaving the established lenders struggling to keep up.

Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, the world’s biggest bank, went so far as to say he was “jealous” of the company because of its breakneck innovation and growth.

But a 10-hour outage last week, which left hundreds of thousands of customers unable to withdraw money, has raised concerns that Revolut’s rapid development has come at the expense of more basic functions.

The disruption, caused by a power issue at a Google Cloud data centre in London, affected 30 of Revolut’s core services, including signing in to accounts, transferring money, paying by card and withdrawing money from cash machines.

Revolut customers flooded social media to complain, with nearly 5,000 replies to the bank’s post on X about the disruption.

“I can’t even pay for anything. I just ate at a restaurant and can’t pay the bill. This is crazy,” said one customer on the social media platform.

It was a familiar kind of headache for Revolut, which has spent years trying to square breakneck growth with ever-closer scrutiny from regulators – a balancing act that will only get harder as talk of a stock market listing in New York and London grows.

However you splice it, Revolut’s outage was a very bad look for customers, regulators, potential investors in its mooted stock-market float and has raised fears that similar outages could happen again.

Alan Woodward, a specialist in computer science at Surrey University, said Revolut suffered more savagely in the Google Cloud meltdown than the traditional high street lenders.

This is because the old guard rely on older systems for their core banking services which sit outside the cloud, while Revolut relies more heavily on cloud services.

“If you look at people like Lloyd’s and HSBC, their core banking systems are actually quite old. A lot of them are still mainframe systems,” he said.

“What you see on the glossy web front end (for the high street banks) is actually what will run in the data centres. What’s running as your core banking is probably in their own data centre.”

It’s an issue that Revolut was aware of before the Google Cloud outage and had previously signalled plans to incorporate Amazon Web Services as a backup cloud provider next year.

High street banks are far from perfect on the IT front and their legacy systems often fail. There were at least 803 hours of unplanned tech outages between January 2023 and February 2025 from nine major UK banks and building societies, the Treasury select committee said last year.

Nik Storonsky, Revolut’s billionaire founder, has often been first in line to pour scorn on the old guard, criticising their fear of risk aversion and reluctance to transfer away from legacy core banking systems.

“They are stuck in limbo with a professional management who are extremely risk-averse. All their resources are spent on protecting what they have already,” he said recently.

But now the tables have turned on Revolut – and at an inopportune time for the company.

The fintech is in the process of trying to acquire a full US banking licence, while its application for a full banking licence from the Bank of England went through several tortuous years before it was approved.

It won’t be applying for any more in the EU, as it reckons licences in France and Lithuania will be enough to service the bloc.

Todd Baker, a former executive at global financial group MUFG and now lecturer at Columbia Business School, said US regulators would undoubtedly seek to discuss the nature of the outage.

“If the UK regulators initiate enforcement action against Revolut related to the outage, that will raise the salience of the problem for the US regulators and may well delay Revolut’s US launch until a satisfactory resolution of the UK situation is reached,” he said.

Revolut is wrestling with regulators on several fronts.

It emerged this week that the Bank of England had ordered a review of Revolut’s product approval processes. The order was made around the time that Revolut finally secured a full banking licence in March.

Its defenders, and Storonsky himself, argue that the firm takes risk seriously – but that regulators hold it back instinctively.

“We speak with regulators; they’re all kind of ‘growth is not a good mentality’. My answer is very simple. Every time when you think as a regulator that I am an excessive risk taker, it’s completely wrong,” Storonsky has said.

“I’m the one [most] motivated for this company to succeed and to survive, right? And that means I’m actually not going to take stupid excessive risks compared to professional CEOs or professional boards.”

In any case, analysts are closely watching the bank’s missteps, even as it continues to charge ahead at breakneck speeds.

S&P Global recently awarded the bank the best credit rating of any fintech, yet analysts said its rapid expansion left it with “significant exposure” to cyber risks.

“We pay a lot of attention to ... cyber security and regulatory compliance, which are critical for fintech companies,” Dmitry Nazarov, an analyst at S&P Global Ratings, said.

“Given Revolut’s growth and business model, we believe it has significant exposure to these risks.

“We are, of course, assessing very closely how well-prepared Revolut is to tackle these risks, and we think that, in general, they’ve made a lot of progress over the past three years.”

Revolut still has plenty else to focus on as it seeks to conquer the world, financial analysts say.

“They are kind of defying gravity at the moment; they are moving at a very rapid pace, opening in new countries every week, it seems. It is firing on all cylinders from a growth and customer numbers expansion standpoint,” said John Cronin, the founder of SeaPoint Insights, an independent research firm based in Dublin.

However, for a bank that boasts of its superiority to the high street, last week’s 10-hour blackout was an uncomfortable reminder to get the basics right.

Revolut declined to comment.

data.title: The West is hooked on Chinese drugs but they could save your life
data.description:
Sir Keir Starmer’s decision to invite Sir Pascal Soriot, AstraZeneca’s chief executive, to Beijing at the beginning of the year was a textbook piece of modern diplomacy.

The then-prime minister’s attempt to revive economic cooperation rested on a knockout deal that went beyond the usual warm words. Sir Pascal, a sworn Sinophile and one of the biggest cheerleaders of Chinese innovation, was only too happy to oblige.

Within hours of Sir Keir’s arrival, AstraZeneca had unveiled a plan to invest $15bn (£11bn) in China, building on its existing medical manufacturing and research capabilities in Beijing, Shanghai, Wuxi, Taizhou and Qingdao.

AstraZeneca’s pledge was the marquee announcement of Sir Keir’s trip. Sir Pascal said the “landmark investment” marked the next chapter for the company in China. For the politburo, it was further proof that their plan to turn China into a global pharmaceuticals leader has worked.

In the West, China has long been dismissed as little more than a dealer in cheap copycat medicines – both legal and illegal – and increasingly knockoffs too, such as unlicensed GLP-1 weight loss medication.

This portrayal no longer bears scrutiny, however. In recent years, the Chinese pharmaceutical industry has undergone a remarkable reinvention. Western industry leaders view it as a bona fide drug superpower at the forefront of discovery.

China controls an exciting pipeline of groundbreaking medicines and occupies a growing role as a globally important venue for clinical trials.

But for now, cooperation between East and West suits both sides. European and American drugmakers have rushed to embrace Chinese research, forging multi-billion licensing deals. Those with the appetite have opened their own labs and even set up manufacturing outposts.

Chinese science is now “the best in the world” and ignoring it is not an option, says one European pharmaceuticals chairman.

Few have led the charge as enthusiastically as Sir Pascal, AstraZeneca’s swashbuckling French boss. China is now its second-biggest market. Meanwhile GSK, the UK’s other national drug champion, has struck a series of partnerships with Chinese labs to licence promising drugs outside the country.

These relationships are critical for China’s pharmaceuticals industry, providing access to the lucrative markets that fund innovation. At home, their only customer is Xi Jinping, and he sets the price.

Yet this partnership is fragile. Amid growing concern in the US about the threat China’s new scientific prowess poses to drug supplies, innovation and even national security, industry executives fear an iron curtain will be drawn.

Drugs may be the next front in the superpower trade war that has already drawn in telecoms equipment, semiconductors, electric vehicles, rare earth minerals and solar panels.

For Europe, including Britain’s pharmaceutical giants AstraZeneca and GSK, the looming nightmare is that an American administration will sooner or later use its economic muscle to effectively outlaw their cooperation with China.

One senior figure says the possibility of a sweeping American crackdown is “probably the one question that keeps me awake at night”.

China’s rapid scientific progress

Dr Zhao Hong, a renowned Chinese cancer specialist, shocked thousands of Communist Party delegates in March last year: a Guangzhou-based biotech firm had developed a cancer drug that had outperformed the world’s bestselling equivalent in clinical trials.

The work of China’s Akeso Biopharma, lung cancer drug ivonescimab had shown that it could delay non-small-cell lung cancer progression for five months longer than US giant Merck’s Keytruda treatment – the world’s bestselling prescription drug in 2025.

The success of ivonescimab was hailed as a breakthrough moment for China’s pharmaceutical industry.

“China is at the best time of its biopharmaceutical sector’s development,” Hong told state media at the annual Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference.

The speed with which China is catching up in pharmaceuticals and biotech is astonishing.

By 2024, China had 1,255 drugs at the research stage, a nearly eight-fold jump in less than a decade. America had 1,441 – a 15pc rise – while the total in Europe had shrunk slightly to 400.

Experts attribute the leap to a fundamental shift in how the industry was perceived by the Chinese regime.

One veteran UK executive recalls how when he first used to visit China in the late 1990s, it was to complain about “counterfeits and pharmaceuticals that were really dangerous”. Today, China is seen as “a golden opportunity”, he says.

“They have moved deliberately to be at the leading edge of science,” he adds.

Beijing has provided vast support in the form of scores of state-financed biotechnology parks equipped with advanced laboratories and heavily subsidised hardware, together with a sweeping overhaul of the regulatory system beginning in 2015.

A study by Prof Yimin Cui, of Peking University, and colleagues found that the time taken to approve a drug for human trials fell to 87 days after the reforms, from 501 days previously.

Chinese researchers are helped by the sheer size of the country’s population – last counted at more than 1.4 billion – says Freddy Yip, a corporate lawyer at Cooley.

“In the US, it may take a long time to recruit sufficient patients, but in China, you have access to lots of different patients with different kinds of diseases, including many rare diseases,” Yip says.

Sir Pascal has said this combination of scientific capability and rapid execution – “China speed”, as he has called it – can help to dramatically accelerate drug development.

One of China’s leading biotech venture capitalists estimates clinical trials are “two thirds cheaper and half as quick in China”.

Progress has been spurred by a massive increase in spending on research and development – leaping from $35m in 2015 to $15bn in 2023 – and a “reverse brain drain” in which thousands of foreign-educated Chinese scientists and entrepreneurs have returned home, according to Porsche Consulting.

Chinese scientists are now at the vanguard of treatment for cardiovascular diseases and cancer, as well as spearheading drug development for metabolic conditions and neurological disorders, such as Parkinson’s, among many others.

Alarm bells in Washington

Mere months before Sir Pascal was lending heft to Sir Keir’s Beijing bridge-building mission, the Frenchman was being warmly welcomed at the Oval Office by Donald Trump.

Thanking the US president for welcoming him “in this beautiful office”, Sir Pascal was armed with another crowd-pleasing announcement: a pledge to cut drug prescription prices in the US, after Trump had accused other countries of “freeloading” at the expense of Americans.

Sir Pascal went further as well, unveiling a $50bn plan to expand the company’s existing operations in the US. In return, AstraZeneca received a three-year exemption from tariffs.

Privately, AstraZeneca executives acknowledge it was also an attempt to ward off growing concern in the White House about the deepening of ties with China.

“We are cognisant of some of the more hawkish commentary [from US politicians]. It is a delicate balancing act, and we are treading a fine line by recognising what the US is trying to achieve,” an insider says.

Yet, for all Washington’s alarm, dependency has become more pronounced, not less. Western companies have piled into the country, hoovering up clinical trial data and striking licensing deals to develop Chinese medicines outside the mainland, which they hope can then be used to treat patients across the developed world.

“This is the golden age of science and China is white-hot right now,” an industry source says.

Deal activity is being driven by anxiety among European and US companies as their pipeline of drugs peters out.

America’s biotech industry faces the alarming prospect of an estimated $350bn worth of medicines – equivalent to roughly one fifth of projected global prescription-drug revenue – losing patent protection by the end of the decade.

When patents run out, generic rivals are allowed to gatecrash the market, jeopardising sales.

Few have led the way with the verve that AstraZeneca has demonstrated.

Sir Pascal’s Beijing announcement was accompanied by a boast that it had signed 16 global licensing agreements with 15 Chinese partners since 2023 alone – thought to be the most of any overseas pharmaceuticals multi-national.

GSK hasn’t been far behind. Last year, the company struck an alliance with local giant Hengrui Pharma to develop a dozen new medicines outside the mainland. The value of the deal could eventually total $12bn.

The agreements are part of an industry-wide surge in deals totalling $138bn last year – a nearly tenfold jump since 2021 – according to data provider PharmCube. 2026 is expected to be another record.

Deal flow shows little sign of slowing.

A fortnight ago, GSK unveiled a $1.3bn pact with Hutchmed, a Hong Kong-based biopharmaceuticals company with research facilities in Shanghai, for the bulk of the licensing rights to what it called “first in-class” cancer treatments.

Brewing geopolitical storm

Amid the feeding frenzy, concern in Washington has turned to outright hostility in some quarters.

In December last year, Trump signed into law the Biosecure Act, a move widely seen as a sharp escalation in tensions and the moment the longstanding strategic rivalry between the US and China spilt into the biotechnology arena.

The act prevents US companies reliant on federal contracts and funding from working with Chinese biotech firms with ties to the Chinese military and any deemed to pose a national security risk. It also bars Chinese companies from accessing US government funding themselves.

US biotechnology companies with federal contracts are now engaged in a mad dash to purge their supply chains of equipment obtained from any Chinese biotechnology firms on the banned list.

Next up is the Biotech Investment National Security Act. Though not yet signed into law, it will subject licensing deals involving Chinese companies to national security reviews.

Though technically a screening mechanism rather than a ban on licensing Chinese drugs, it will effectively function as one, says Craig Garthwaite, a professor at Northwestern University’s Kellogg School of Management.

There is also pressure to bar the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) from accepting Chinese trial data, amid concerns about their reliability. The FDA has repeatedly rejected one of Hengrui’s cancer drugs, citing questions about quality control at its manufacturing sites.

As one senior City figure puts it: the White House has conjured up other reasons to “erect a wall around China”.

AstraZeneca’s attempt to navigate this geopolitical storm by investing in both China and the US divides opinion. Some see it as an inspired way to keep both Washington and Beijing happy at the same time.

“I think Pascal has been very smart in not allowing anybody to question his US credentials. He’s playing his cards very wisely,” the boss of a rival company says.

Others see it as a high-stakes gamble from a company that is more exposed than most of its competitors and has learnt the hard way the risks that come from operating in China.

Leon Wang, the former head of its Chinese operations, is awaiting trial on charges of illegal trading, unlawful collection of personal information and medical insurance fraud, alongside another former employee, having been arrested in 2024.

If the saga made Sir Pascal reconsider his appetite for doing business in China, there is little sign of it.

Alongside licensing deals potentially worth tens of billions of dollars, it has around 17,000 employees in China, two “global strategic” research and development centres in Beijing and Shanghai, and four advanced manufacturing sites in Wuxi, Taizhou, Qingdao and Beijing.

China is now AstraZeneca’s second-largest market after the US, accounting for roughly 12pc of the company’s global turnover, and its Chinese facilities supply more than 70 markets worldwide.

In a written submission to the Commons business and trade select committee in July, AstraZeneca described co-operation with China as a “win-win”.

But as one investor with extensive interests in China points out: “If you’re a big pharma company with a significant proportion of your licensing spend coming from China and the tap suddenly gets turned off, that’s obviously a problem.”

Europe’s wary response

Despite sharply rising tensions, there are concerns that European policymakers are still a long way off from having a coherent industrial strategy that addresses the China question.

Having been slow to react to the threat that cheap Chinese manufacturing poses to the continent’s steelmakers, solar panel producers and its car industry, the risk is that the pendulum swings too far the other way and Brussels takes a similarly antagonistic approach in trying to shut China out of other sectors, such as pharmaceuticals.

Calls by Oliver Blume, the chief executive of Volkswagen, for tougher trade measures against Beijing have been interpreted in some circles as a signal that EU-China relations are close to a tipping point after years of resistance to anti-Chinese duties from the continent’s car giants.

Yet, a senior industrialist says Europe lacks the “economic counterweight to be able to exclude China”.

“I don’t necessarily think it’s good in the long term for the US to do so, but I think it’s very dangerous for Europe,” he adds.

“We need a more nuanced industrial strategy that seeks Chinese expertise and cost effectiveness, and to somehow bring some of the economic benefit of that into Europe,” he says.

Such sentiment echoes a growing willingness among car manufacturers to partner with Chinese counterparts amid an onslaught of imports. Nissan’s decision to share its Sunderland plant with Chery, one of China’s largest car exporters, is expected to be among the first of many similar tie-ups.

Some believe the growing divide between Washington and Beijing because of pharmaceuticals may even present an opportunity for Europe.

“I’m sure Europe would be more than happy to take Chinese-developed products that are sold to them at a lower price than what they might otherwise get from the United States,” Garthwaite says.

As Brussels bureaucrats try to agree on a co-ordinated approach, the rhetoric, particularly among some influential Republicans, continues to harden.

Chris Klomp, a top lieutenant of Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, has likened the situation to “a war”.

Anxiety has been heightened by a so-called “hot mic” incident at a Beijing military parade late last year, in which Vladimir Putin and Xi were overheard discussing the possibility that humans could live to 150 years old, thanks to advances in biotechnology.

Some China hawks saw it as further evidence that the US risked falling behind in the global race for domination in advanced science.

The Council on Foreign Relations, an influential American think tank, has called for reliance on China’s biotech know-how to be treated as a strategic vulnerability akin to critical minerals.

“The US (and just about every other nation) faces a growing risk that China will deliberately withhold essential pharmaceutical inputs as a tool of economic or political coercion … as China has done with rare-earth critical minerals,” it warned in June.

The Atlantic Council, another US think tank with a history of shaping American foreign policy, points out that the US is reliant on China for three quarters of some imported drugs and as much as 99pc of some raw materials that are critical to the production of certain key medicines.

What’s more, China’s 2020 export control law and 2021 biosecurity law “grant broad authority to weaponise pharmaceutical exports”, it said recently.

‘All in or all out’

AstraZeneca declined to comment on its position, but there are signs it is more nervous than it is willing to acknowledge.

It emerged in August that the company had held detailed discussions with American rival Bristol Myers Squibb about a potential £300bn mega-merger.

In seeking to substantially deepen its US footprint, AstraZeneca may have concluded that the best chance it has of escaping any crackdown is if the company can demonstrate it is willing to take action to address Trump’s demands for the “reshoring” of pharmaceutical manufacturing.

Radical corporate restructuring plans have also been explored in China. AstraZeneca previously looked at the possibility of carving out its Chinese business into a separate legal entity and listing it on the Shanghai stock exchange. Though nothing came of those plans, they were seen as an attempt to insulate it from mounting geopolitical tensions.

GSK, meanwhile, sees no reason for such drastic action. Publicly, all a spokesman is willing to say is that it has “a longstanding presence in China, to make sure patients can access our medicines and vaccines”.

“China is also increasingly a source of cutting-edge biopharma innovation, and we have established several important collaborations for potential new treatments in oncology, respiratory, immunology and inflammation,” the spokesman adds.

However, like AstraZeneca, it too has fallen foul of Beijing after the company was engulfed in a bribery scandal in 2014.

GSK was found guilty of bribing Chinese doctors and hospitals to prescribe its medical products and was forced to pay a record $490m fine.

That ordeal prompted GSK bosses to take a much more cautious approach in which its activities were limited to strict licensing deals rather than the asset-heavy approach of others, such as AstraZeneca.

“It [GSK] went through a very difficult time in China. The experience damaged the company immeasurably in terms of its willingness to take risks,” a City source says.

By focusing on developing local collaborations, GSK believes it can still capitalise on the opportunities in China while being “less vulnerable” than rivals who are more “asset-exposed”, an insider explains.

Yet, the same person admits it ultimately boils down to one question: “Are they [China] helping us long-term or are they harming us? And I can’t answer that, which is why we can’t afford to be all in or all out.”

Industry figures hope common sense prevails between the two superpowers.

Garthwaite acknowledges deals that come with potential national security risk should be scrutinised, while attempts to reduce American over-dependence on Chinese antibiotics are also to be applauded.

However, he says the White House needs to distinguish between drug production and drug development, which “shouldn’t be too hard”.

Another investor says patients don’t really care where the drugs come from, “as long as they’re subjected to the same trials”.

In response to a recent US ban on imports of humanoid robots, China’s foreign ministry said: “Protectionism does not make the US more competitive … it will only hurt the interests of US companies and consumers.”﻿

Yet, nor is it in China’s interests to actively undermine American science. Chinese drugmakers simply cannot afford to be shut out of Western markets, particularly the US, experts say.

“China is really vulnerable too. It has to rely on its export machine because it doesn’t have sufficient levels of internal consumption,” one analyst says.

Ultimately, industry sources admit they are at the mercy of an unpredictable Trump administration whose appetite for trade wars shows little sign of waning.

As one boardroom veteran puts it: “It’s akin to walking a tightrope – we’ll continue trying to walk it and hope we stay on.”

data.title: BBC Today programme audience falls to post-pandemic low
data.description:
The audience for the BBC Radio 4 Today programme has fallen to a post-pandemic low, figures show.

The number of listeners fell from 5.61 million in April-June to 5.29 million in July-September, according to data from Rajar.

This amounts to the lowest quarterly figure since the research organisation resumed reporting data in 2021 after the Covid pandemic.

Elsewhere, audiences for the Radio 2 Breakfast Show held steady during Sara Cox’s first months as host.

The programme attracted an average of 6.44 million weekly listeners across July-September, up slightly from 6.37 million in April-June.

Cox took over as permanent presenter of the show on July 6, replacing Scott Mills.

He was sacked at the end of March, shortly before details emerged about a police investigation into the DJ that had been launched in 2016 amid allegations of serious sexual offences involving a teenage boy under 16.

The show continues to be the most popular radio programme broadcast in the UK at that time of the day, according to Rajar.

The slump in Today’s popularity follows the departure of several high-profile presenters this year.

The Telegraph revealed in September that Emma Barnett was leaving the Radio 4 programme in a fresh blow to the show after Amol Rajan left in January to set up his own YouTube channel.

Barnett joined the line-up in 2024. Before her imminent departure was revealed, she had been off work following a hysterectomy for endometriosis.

‘Clashing egos’

Her expected departure followed a rumoured rift with Nick Robinson, one of her co-hosts.

In March last year, it was reported that the pair had gone for 90 days without appearing on air together amid rumours of “clashing egos” and allegations that Robinson was “overbearing” towards her.

The matter was said to have been resolved with no action taken, and there was no suggestion that Robinson had done anything wrong.

Radio 2 also remains the most listened-to station in Britain, with a total average weekly audience of 12.67 million between July and September, up slightly from 12.37 million in the previous three months.

By contrast, 5 Live Breakfast enjoyed a jump in listeners from 1.33 million to 1.43 million, in a period coinciding with the closing weeks of the 2026 World Cup.

Spin-off station success

Two of the BBC’s three new digital spin-off stations also recorded an uptick in their weekly audience figures.

Radio 1 Anthems rose from 584,000 to 630,000 listeners, Radio 1 Dance climbed from 615,000 to 645,000, while Radio 3 Unwind slipped from 408,000 to 382,000.

All three have been available on digital radio since September 2025.

Kate Philips, the BBC’s chief content officer, said she was “delighted” for Cox and the Radio 2 breakfast team.

“These results underline the strength of BBC radio, which continues to bring audiences together through outstanding live events, trusted journalism and world-class music,” she said.

“Audiences spent 423 million hours with radio, podcasts and music on BBC Sounds, demonstrating the continued value of our content across live and on-demand listening.”

Radio 3’s audience rose slightly from 1.88 million in April-June to 1.96 million in July-September, according to the latest Rajar figures.

There were 1.41 million weekly listeners to Radio 4 Extra, down slightly from 1.43 million.

The BBC recently announced that Radio 4 Extra will close next year as part of plans save £500m by 2028.

A BBC spokesman said: “We’re pleased Today remains the most listened to breakfast radio news programme in the UK as millions of people continue to tune into the programme every week for trusted, impartial reporting and agenda-setting interviews.”

data.title: BBC licence fee on track to top £200 as millions switch off
data.description:
The BBC licence fee is on track to top £200 within five years as the public service broadcaster continues to lose viewers.

The annual charge is expected to rise from its current level of £180 to £202.60 by 2031, according to official forecasts from the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).

Meanwhile, the number of people paying the licence fee is slated to drop by 2.7 million over the next five years to just 19 million.

That marks a significant downgrade from the OBR’s previous assumptions in March, when it predicted that 21 million people would still be paying the licence fee by 2031.

The BBC is losing around half a million licence-fee payers every year, with bosses warning of a “steeper than projected decline” in recent months.

The corporation is grappling with an exodus of viewers to streaming rivals such as Netflix and Disney, while young audiences are increasingly turning to platforms such as YouTube and TikTok.

This has been compounded by a string of controversies at the broadcaster, including the doctoring of a Donald Trump speech that led to the resignation of Tim Davie, the director general, this year.

The latest forecasts underscore the scale of the challenge facing Matt Brittin, the new boss. The BBC is locked in negotiations with the Government over the future of the licence fee.

Mr Brittin has branded the compulsory fee a “busted flush” as fewer and fewer Britons are willing to cough up. The BBC has said that while 94pc of households use its services every month, only 80pc are paying the licence fee.

Ministers are considering reforms to the corporation’s funding model ahead of the end of its current charter period next year.

One proposal being looked at is extending the fee to cover streaming services such as Netflix, while some have called for the BBC’s funding to be linked to household bills such as broadband and council tax.

Proponents of this approach argue that the licence fee could be reduced if more households contribute.

Lisa Nandy, the Culture Secretary, has also considered alternative funding models such as advertising or subscriptions. The Government is expected to outline its proposals in a white paper expected to be published before Christmas.

The decline in the number of households paying has been compounded by recent freezes in the annual charge, leading to the BBC’s licence fee income dropping by around 30pc in real terms.

Mr Brittin is overseeing a major cost-cutting drive to save £500m over the next two years.

The cuts are expected to lead to up to 2,000 job losses, while the broadcaster has also begun cutting programmes and has announced the closure of the BBC Three channel.

However, the cutbacks risk triggering a revolt among beleaguered BBC staff. The National Union of Journalists (NUJ) is balloting staff on potential strike action after bosses announced plans to cut 100 roles from the broadcaster’s news division.

A BBC spokesman said: “We have consistently argued that the current funding model is outdated and needs reform.

“We will continue to engage with government to secure a new charter that provides sustainable, sufficient and universal funding so the BBC can deliver for audiences for generations to come.”

A Government spokesman said: “The BBC must be funded by a model that is sustainable and fair to all those that are paying it.

“Through Charter Review, we are looking at a range of options, including how the BBC can operate more efficiently, generate more commercial revenue, and how the licence fee could be reformed.”
