data.title: Ministers accused of concealing true scale of England’s green belt loss
data.description:
Ministers have been accused of covering up the true scale of England’s green belt loss as Labour pushes for more building.

Figures issued by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government this week showed that England’s green belt shrank by just 0.03pc in the year ending March 2026.

However, the Campaign to Protect Rural England (CPRE) said a grey-belt loophole meant swathes of lost land were not being counted in the figures.

Richard Hebditch, the CPRE’s planning representative, said the figures were “misleading” because they ignored the fact that green-belt land could now be built on if it was reclassified as grey belt. This land is not counted as lost in official statistics.

Mr Hebditch said: “Either the Government is happy for [the data] to be largely meaningless or they are deliberately deceitful stats, hiding what is actually happening.

“It doesn’t capture the significant amounts of land that we are losing from the grey-belt policy.”

The grey belt refers to sites in the green belt such as scrub land, disused car parks or petrol stations that are deemed to be of little natural value and instead are ideal for property development.

Under planning reforms made by Angela Rayner, the Housing Secretary, introduced in December 2024, land judged to be grey belt can be built on while remaining officially designated as green belt.

New planning rules introduced in August made it even easier to undertake construction projects near “well-connected” railway stations, including in the green belt.

None of this was included in the Government’s headline numbers.

Its researchers admitted in the report that they could not estimate how much of the green belt had been identified as grey belt and said that statisticians were exploring whether to collect these data.

The Government’s figures only looked at formal changes to green-belt boundaries, which happen when councils draw up new local plans for their areas.

Seven councils did this during the 2025‐26 period, with Tunbridge Wells, Kent, losing the most protected land at 220 hectares.

A grey-belt designation does not necessarily mean all of that land will be developed. Nonetheless, Mr Hebditch argued that the figures should be included as the designation opens the door to possible building work on the area.

Figures from Channel 4 News showed that 96pc of protected land in Guildford, Surrey, was potentially grey belt, alongside 92pc in Stoke-on-Trent and nearly 80pc in Solihull, West Midlands.

“There is a real lack of transparency to communities about what will be happening to land around their towns and villages,” Mr Hebditch said.

“It’s important for them to know what effect the policy changes are having ... and what’s actually being decided about the use of that land.”

The Government’s 0.03pc estimate compares with a 0.04pc loss of green belt land in the previous year.

A Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government spokesman said: “The Government remains committed to protecting the green belt, with brownfield land the first choice for development.”

data.title: Property giant halts £3.6bn development project
data.description:
One of Britain’s largest property firms has paused construction at a £3.6bn development in London as it struggles to find buyers for its apartments.

British Land, listed on the FTSE 100, will not go ahead with the second phase of construction in Canada Water, south-east London, as the company grapples with rising costs and sluggish sales.

The property group is understood to be waiting for a clear improvement in market conditions before resuming work on the project’s mix of homes, offices and retail spaces.

The decision is another blow to the capital’s housebuilding industry, amid a steep decline in construction and claims that the market is “fundamentally broken”.

The first phase of British Land’s 53-acre development at Canada Water includes 245,000 sq ft of offices, along with 186 new homes at a project called The Founding. Nearly 80 affordable homes are also included in the development.

Approval has been granted for up to 4,184 new homes on the site, but in its annual report released in May this year, British Land said it had sold just 57 apartments.

It also admitted that challenging market conditions, difficulties with leases and sales, as well as changes to the development had caused the project’s valuation to fall by 6.9pc in the last financial year.

British Land jointly funds the development alongside pension fund AustralianSuper. Both companies have been contacted for comment.

The decision brings one of London’s largest regeneration projects to a halt, at a time when London is on course to build just 20pc of the Government’s annual homes target of 88,000, according to figures from Molior.

In recent months, a succession of property developers has warned that London is becoming increasingly unviable for new house-building projects.

Landsec shelved a £1.5bn plan this week to rebuild a shopping centre and create 1,700 new homes in Lewisham, south-east London, after the borough’s Green-led council demanded more affordable housing.

Jennie Daly, the boss of housebuilder Taylor Wimpey, also said this month that building in the capital was “fundamentally broken”, and that the incentive to take on risky projects had “evaporated”.

Berkeley, another major housebuilder, recently said it was grappling with “extreme uncertainty” after authorities delayed or blocked plans for thousands of new London homes across different projects.

Buyers are struggling with mortgage costs which have increased rapidly since the start of the Iran war, while construction companies are feeling the pinch from rising material costs.

It comes after home completions across England dropped to their lowest level since 2016.

Figures from the Office for National Statistics show that 142,050 new homes were completed in England in 2025, a nine-year low.

The slowdown in housebuilding casts further doubt on Labour’s 2024 manifesto pledge to build 1.5 million new homes by the end of the decade.

data.title: BBC journalists to vote on strike action in revolt over job cuts
data.description:
Journalists at the BBC are to vote on strike action in protest against sweeping job cuts at the embattled broadcaster.

The National Union of Journalists (NUJ) is to ballot its members on a potential walkout amid concerns about compulsory redundancies.

The BBC has outlined plans to cut 100 jobs from its news division in the coming months as part of a wider effort to find £500m in savings.

“We’ve backed that up with action too – a large majority of the redundancies agreed to date have been achieved on a voluntary basis.

“But faced with a £500m financial savings challenge and significant operational pressures, we cannot offer a guarantee that there will be no compulsory redundancies.”

The dispute marks the latest clash between the BBC and its union, which is already balloting members in a row about the broadcaster’s 1pc pay offer.

The BBC is preparing to cut up to 2,000 jobs in a cost-cutting programme overseen by Matt Brittin, its director general.

As well as removing roles, it has begun cutting programming and last week confirmed plans to shut down the BBC Three channel for the second time in the last decade.

The public service broadcaster is seeking to shore up its balance sheet as it grapples with a sharp decline in income from the licence fee, which now stands at £180 a year.

Licence fee income has declined by 30pc in real terms since 2010, while bosses have pointed to a gap between the number of UK households using the BBC’s services and those who pay the fee.

The corporation is in discussions with the Government about the renewal of its charter, with ministers considering reforms including extending the licence fee to cover viewing on streaming services such as Netflix.

data.title: ‘Ozempic face’ powers revival of a fading British giant
data.description:
A surprise discovery may have saved one of Britain’s oldest chemical companies from sliding into irrelevance.

Croda, founded more than 100 years ago, was once known as the “mini ICI”, a powerhouse industrial giant with 70 factories in Lancashire and Yorkshire.

But like so much of Britain’s chemical industry, its star has been fading in recent years.

A share price rally during Covid – after it teamed up with Pfizer to produce one of the first vaccines – has been fizzling out, with its stock declining for four consecutive years.

Now, however, a surprise discovery is reversing Croda’s fortunes, giving the biotech-to-chemicals group a new lease of life as a beauty giant.

Croda recently discovered that one of its old chemicals can be used to treat “Ozempic face”, the often alarming facial transformation associated with the fat-jab craze.

For about a decade, Croda had been producing a skin-plumping chemical derived from the root of the plant anemarrhena to limited sale success.

Known as Volufiline, the agent swells the skin by chemically expanding fat cells and is used mostly in body creams.

But after users of GLP-1 drugs complained of hollow cheeks and sunken eyes, doctors discovered that Volufiline can combat the gaunt features associated with rapid weight loss.

The discovery has led to an explosion of sales for Croda, turning Volufiline into a TikTok sensation, in demand from the French and South Korean cosmetics industry.

Steve Foots, Croda’s chief executive, said the success of Volufiline had taken everybody by surprise.

“It had been in our portfolio for a decade,” he admits. “Ozempic coming on the market has created a big opportunity, which we’re capitalising on. It can lead to facial hollowing, but we can innovate around that by plumping your skin.”

Revenue from Volufiline sales jumped 270pc in the first half as more than 150 companies signed up to use it in their products.

Videos tagged #Volufiline have also generated 200 million views on the US TikTok Shop app in 12 months.

It has prompted Croda to lean into its new profile as a key force in the burgeoning TikTok influencer economy, helping send shares up 25pc from their August 2025 nadir.

Unlike Botox, Volufiline is applied as a face cream or in a lipstick-style tube.

Estée Lauder, the cosmetics giant, is hooked and has started selling a 92pc concentrate version of Croda’s agent under the Volufiline name.

Croda has even managed to sell it to the Korean “K-beauty” industry, which pioneered the skin-transforming agents and exports $11bn (£8.3bn) every year.

Foots said that while the fat-jabs windfall was unexpected, it had resulted from a decades-long repositioning of Croda from traditional chemicals into a supplier to customers, including L’Oréal, Procter & Gamble and Unilever, as well as Estée Lauder.

Next up is hair care. Alongside Volufiline, Croda is pushing KeraBio, a synthetic form of biotech-derived keratin, as its next miracle product.

While Volufiline was an existing ingredient that found a new use, Foots said KeraBio – developed at Croda’s research facility in Daresbury, Cheshire – will be its “first big product launch in the beauty industry”.

A similar serum from an American rival sells for £80 a shot.

“It’s solving the problem of repairing hair that’s been damaged through combing and heating and colouring, which breaks the keratin bonds,” Foots said.

“It strengthens your hair in a chemical way by creating new bonds, and stops it from ageing, which is a bit of a holy grail in the industry.”

For Croda’s proud British roots, its re-emergence as a cosmetics force is a major boost for the nation’s chemicals sector.

Foots said that while Croda’s business was driven by breakthroughs made at a plant in Daresbury and a second research lab at its headquarters near Goole, East Yorkshire, still not enough was being done to make the UK a chemical powerhouse.

Only 950 of Croda’s 5,500 employees are UK based, and while it has three British plants, most production takes place at factories scattered around Europe, the United States and Asia.

While the beauty industry may be Croda’s new frontier, the firm is also expanding the plant in Leek, Staffordshire, that was so critical in producing lipids used to deliver the Pfizer jab.

A recent breakthrough by Moderna and Merck in developing a melanoma vaccine that uses the same mRNA gene therapy principles shows the potential of the sector, Foots said.

He said: “We were prominent in solving the biggest medical crisis of a generation with the biggest innovation of its time, which was gene therapy drugs. And it’s still advancing.

“Flu vaccines, cancer treatments. The science is there. It will take time to get to market, but we’re excited because Croda is provital in many of these programmes.”

Croda may be one of the few independent British chemicals groups still standing, but its Ozempic discovery proves there’s life in the old dog yet.

data.title: Ex-Adidas boss sues builder after being told to partly demolish £1.3m home
data.description:
A former Adidas boss who was ordered to demolish part of his £1.3m home because it is two metres too long is suing the developer who sold it to him.

Edward Nixon, a former managing director of Adidas in Korea, and his wife, Sally, bought West Barn in East Haddon, Northamptonshire, and commissioned Barry Howard to convert it into a home.

Mr Howard, the head of Barry Howard Homes, a Northampton-based development company, sold the couple the £600,000 parcel of land on which West Barn stands and had already built a “shell of a house” on the site.

He struck a £700,000 deal with the couple to “finalise the construction of the house in accordance with drawings provided to the Nixons”.

The couple say they were told by Mr Howard during a video call in July 2020 that “the house is built and the planners are happy with it”.

But in June the following year, West Northamptonshire council imposed an enforcement notice, demanding that the Nixons either demolish their new home or carry out comprehensive alterations, telling them that the 36-metre barn conversion was two metres bigger than the approved plans.

The Nixons are now suing Mr Howard for £900,000 for “fraudulent misrepresentation” on the basis that he must have known the house was bigger than it should have been.

However, the developer is disputing the couple’s claim, insisting he had no idea the barn’s dimensions had gone over the limit when he sold it.

Daria Gleyze, the couple’s barrister, claimed at Central London county court that Mr Howard made a series of misleading statements which induced her clients to go ahead with buying into the conversion project, including the video call in July 2020.

And in September that year when filling out the standard inquiries form questionnaire accompanying the sale contract, Mr Howard answered “no” to the question, “are you aware of any breach of planning law in relation to the construction, use or occupation of the property”, the barrister said.

Ms Gleyze told Judge Nigel Gerald that the council demanded drastic alterations because of “its sheer bulk and mass deviating from the character and form of the original approved building”.

The court heard that the house also exceeded its permitted ridge height, where two opposing sloping roof planes meet, by just under one metre.

The local authority decided that the changes had “detracted from the character and appearance” of the original barn, and in December 2020, three months after completing the barn’s purchase, the Nixons discovered that the planning rules had been broken.

In June 2021, the council imposed an enforcement notice and the following year approved “remedial works” that would result in a “significant decrease in size and a different layout of the house”, Ms Gleyze explained.

“Their new house will have to be much smaller,” she told Judge Gerald.

Representing himself in court, Mr Howard insisted that he “had no knowledge that this building was being built in breach”, and claimed that Mr Nixon was “involved in every detail of the building’s design”.

Ms Gleyze called his defence “demonstrably untrue”, arguing: “It is inconceivable, and wholly fanciful to assert, that Mr Howard, who prides himself on being a professional builder with ample experience of building houses, would not have realised that he had deviated from the plans approved when he constructed the house, especially given the very significant discrepancies between the house as built and as approved.

“It is clear that the claimants suffered loss as a result of these misrepresentations. They were forced to incur significant costs in attempting to remedy the breach of planning and they will end up with a property significantly smaller and less valuable than what they had purchased.

“A valuation dated Oct 13, 2025, estimated a difference of £350,000 between the value of the house as built and as it would be after remedial planning measures are implemented.”

During a court hearing last week, Judge Gerald was asked to order “summary judgment” against Mr Howard on the grounds that he had “no realistic prospect” of defeating the claim against him.

But after a brief hearing, the judge agreed to Mr Howard’s request to have the case adjourned in order for him to gather more evidence and instruct solicitors.

“It seems fair to give Mr Howard a relatively brief opportunity to find new solicitors and put in a witness statement,” he said.

“The essence of his witness statement would be to explain why he didn’t know at the time that the representation which was made was wrong.”

The judge also noted evidence produced by the Nixons from the project’s architect “on one reading to the effect that prior to Sept 22 Mr Howard had been told that the planning regulations had been breached”.

The judge adjourned the case until late November.

data.title: Burnham demands answers as Poundland faces collapse
data.description:
The Prime Minister is demanding answers about Poundland’s insolvency after its directors filed a notice to appoint administrators, putting thousands of jobs at risk.

Andy Burnham has asked Gordon Brothers, the discount chain’s owner, to explain why bids for the company that would have kept it afloat were rejected.

He has raised concerns along with Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary.

Both are demanding answers as to why Gordon Brothers rejected a solvent bid from Ireland’s Martin Property Group for the entire Poundland business earlier this week.

Speaking after the retailer filed a notice to appoint administrators on Thursday, Mr Burnham told The Telegraph: “This is a deeply worrying time for Poundland staff and their families.

“We want to see jobs protected. If there was a potential owner to avoid this that hasn’t been accepted, then the Business Secretary and I want to know why that is the case.

“We stand ready to support the workforce however we can.”

His concerns were echoed by Mr Reynolds, who said: “If it is true that it was not necessary to put the business into administration then the present owners will have to account for that.”

Mr Reynolds said he was “keeping a close eye” on the situation, which threatens to become the biggest retail collapse since BHS went bust in 2016.

Poundland has 600 stores and employs 12,000 people.

The company’s collapse could directly affect workers in Mr Burnham’s Makerfield constituency, which is home to Poundland’s biggest distribution centre.

The Telegraph revealed on Thursday that Poundland’s directors had filed a notice to appoint administrators, 24 hours after John Healey, the Chancellor, delivered his first Budget.

This legal process will now trigger a 10-day moratorium that automatically prevents creditors from calling in their debts.

However, it will also allow bosses to consider bids to break up the business, casting doubt over its 600 stores and raising concerns for its 12,000 employees in the run-up to Christmas.

The consulting firm AlixPartners will handle any insolvency if the last-gasp survival attempt fails.

Employees and union officials launched a protest outside Poundland’s headquarters in Walsall, West Midlands, on Thursday afternoon.

They are particularly concerned by the fact that Poundland is heading for administration despite a run of strong trading.

One source said they were fearful that a “solvent business was being turned insolvent”.

In a private update aimed at reassuring suppliers on Thursday, bosses revealed that Poundland achieved sales growth of 6.7pc in September.

This was then followed by 8.4pc growth in the first three weeks of October.

Barry Williams, the chief executive of Poundland, has been spearheading turnaround efforts at the business since it was put up for sale by Gordon Brothers two months ago.

However, in a statement on Thursday, he and chief financial officer Shaun Wills confirmed the prospect of the Poundland brand vanishing from the high street.

They said: “Over the past two months, initially prompted by interest from several parties, we have been working on a formal sale process for Poundland.

“Despite enormous efforts it has not been possible to identify an acceptable offer for the business as a whole.

“The process has however attracted several established retail operators who have made formal offers, collectively these cover a significant part of the business, and we believe offer the best available prospects for shareholders, creditors and to preserve jobs.

“We recognise any sale process creates uncertainty and particularly when set against a challenging UK economic environment. We thank all stakeholders, and in particular our people for their support during this period.”

It comes after a period of growing tension between Poundland’s management and its owner.

It emerged earlier this week that Gordon Brothers had sought to starve the business of critical day-to-day funding, in a move Mr Williams branded “unexpected, unwanted and wholly avoidable”.

In a letter to staff, he said he was disappointed by Gordon Brothers decision to reject a “fully funded, ready-to-go bid that would have kept the business intact and able to continue the remarkable progress we have made”.

The solvent bid in question was from Martin Property Group, which previously owned a shopping centre in Mr Reynolds’ Stalybridge and Hyde constituency.

However, this was ultimately rejected after Martin Property Group refused to meet Gordon Brothers’ demands for immediate full repayment of a £30m shareholder loan, which it acquired for just £1 as part of its original buyout.

The next 10 days will now see a number of bidders return to the sale process in search of stores.

This is likely to include Poundstretcher owner Fortress, TG Jones’s Modella Capital and The Range’s CDS Superstores.

data.title: The clean power push to supply Britain with the cheapest gas on Earth
data.description:
On the wall at Rivan Industries is a list of promising start-ups that failed despite raising huge sums of cash.

The “hardware graveyard”, as the British manufacturing company calls it, is sobering: “Northvolt, batteries $15bn [£12.5bn], dead; Theranos, medical diagnosis, $700m, dead; Nikola, automotive, $2bn, dead ...”

“That’s to remind us that capital isn’t enough,” says Harvey Hodd, Rivan’s 30-year-old founder.

“It’s extremely difficult to build hardware in the real world. You can raise capital for it, as all these companies have done, but the litmus test is whether you can properly deploy it.”

Like many of the start-ups on the list, Rivan certainly has a lot of promise.

Founded in London just two years ago, the energy-tech firm raised $47.5m from investors including $34m in a single funding round last April.

The company’s backers include John and Patrick Collison, the co-founders of digital-payments giant Stripe, European venture fund IQ Capital and Bolt founder Markus Villig.

But to avoid the fate of the doomed start-ups on Hodd’s list, Rivan is going to have to prove his central thesis: that climate-friendly, synthetic gas can be produced cheaply, and at scale, from air and water.

It wants to provide these synthetic fuels for sectors of the economy that are the hardest to decarbonise, from heavy industry to aviation, using shipping container-sized plants.

As well as the obvious environmental benefits, Hodd argues that his company can produce synthetic gas for less than it currently costs Britain to import the real thing.

That is a big claim, and would differentiate Rivan from other businesses currently proposing to produce alternative fuels such as hydrogen and ammonia for eye-watering prices.

“We will be cheaper than anywhere on Earth, way beyond that, and way faster than that,” Hodd says.

“It can be cheaper than importing today. Then, in a year or two, we’ll be cheaper than gas has basically ever been in the UK. But we still need a bit of time for that.”

With the Iran crisis and low European storage levels driving the price to four-year highs, natural gas is changing hands for €95 (£80) per megawatt hour on the Continent.

It has been at elevated levels since 2022, however, when the invasion of Ukraine scrambled supplies and forced Britain and its allies to rely more heavily on liquefied natural gas from America, Qatar and other far-flung places.

This is one reason Hodd’s promise to make gas cheaper than it has ever been in the UK is striking.

He is effectively claiming Rivan will be able to produce its synthetic replacement for pre-crisis levels of anything between €10 and €20 per megawatt hour, or less.

So how will they do it?

“This place will get us there,” says the entrepreneur, sitting in a meeting room at the company’s brand new factory in Bermondsey, south-east London.

At a separate site in Swindon, Rivan has also been proving the viability of its synthetic gas plant and will soon begin feeding what it produces into the national gas grid. It says it is now ready to scale the business up.

It moved into the Bermondsey factory over the summer and is preparing to serve various customers across Britain and Europe, although Hodd says he can’t currently name any of them.

Each plant, effectively a mini-factory, is situated alongside a solar farm and combines renewable electricity, rainwater, and carbon dioxide captured from the atmosphere to produce the synthetic gas.

Clean power is used to power an electrolyser that breaks down rainwater to make hydrogen, which is then combined with carbon dioxide in a reactor to produce the gas.

Because the CO2 that makes the gas is drawn from the atmosphere, it is technically carbon-neutral.

“As soon as you burn it, the exact same amount of carbon that you pulled to make it is released, and it keeps going round and round and round,” Hodd says.

The machines have been completely developed in house by Rivan, which also owns the solar plants that supply them.

Experts have generally been sceptical that making fuels using energy-intensive processes like this can ever be more economical than simply drilling in the North Sea.

But Hodd says the company has kept its costs ultra-low by doing everything itself: owning the power supply and building every part of the tech.

“Fundamentally, you can’t argue with the laws of physics,” he agrees.

“But if you think about how people have looked at this before, they’ve said, ‘OK, we’ll focus on say a singular part of that, which is a reactor.

“We’ll do the design in-house because we have brilliant engineers. We’ll go and send it to a manufacturer, and they’ll fabricate it for us.’

“We can’t afford any of that, because we’re cost sensitive. We have to make everything: All the calculations, all the design, all the manufacturing, all the hardware, all the electronics, all the software.

“And number two, we said, ‘We need access to an unprecedented amount of renewable, cheap electricity.’ So that’s why we focused on permitting all of our own solar.

“It means we can get very, very cheap decentralised electricity, and they’re the two core components to making any chemical process.”

Perhaps the biggest advantage of the company’s idea is that it works exactly like the natural gas we use today.

Factories and power plants can pump it through their existing pipes and burn it in their current machines without having to buy expensive, new net-zero equipment.

Meanwhile, Rivan’s gas plants can also feed what they make directly into the pressurised national gas transmission network – meaning no expensive equipment for storage or transport is required.

For now the company is focused on gas alone. But there is no technical reason why it cannot also produce other products such as diesel or jet fuel, says Hodd.

“You can make any synthetic fuels as long as you’ve got carbon and hydrogen. They’re the only two constituent parts you need,” he says.

“Right now, we’re focused on natural gas for obvious reasons. But we will expand into loads of other things.”

Rivan expects to become profitable off the back of producing its first 50 plants, having struck 10-year contracts to supply various customers including steel makers, cement companies and chemical manufacturers with its synthetic gas.

Some of its other clients include airlines and data centre operators. The plan is to produce one fuel plant a week – with plans already under way for a second factory that will be “40 times bigger”.

Hodd claims that eventually, Rivan’s technology could help to wean Britain off its dependence on gas imports for the industries it supplies – serving as a forward-looking alternative to the North Sea.

“Everything is downstream of energy access and cost,” adds Hodd. “So we need to solve the problem of energy security in the UK.

“There is available funding, and there is huge demand. Stage one of the business was to deploy our hardware, show that we can validate the costs.

“Now we need to take that and scale it, and really show the world what we can do.”

data.title: Thousands of jobs at risk as Poundland heads for administration
data.description:
Poundland directors have filed a notice to appoint administrators, The Telegraph can reveal, threatening thousands of jobs.

Barry Williams, the chief executive, and Shaun Wills, the finance director, made the submission to the High Court on Thursday afternoon.

The court filing will now trigger a 10-day moratorium that automatically prevents creditors from calling in their debts.

This will give directors breathing space to mount a last-ditch effort to save as many stores and jobs as possible.

However, sources close to the negotiations cast doubt on Poundland, one of Britain’s biggest biggest retailers, surviving in its current form.

The prospect of Poundland’s collapse will dent John Healey’s hopes of supporting the high street. The Chancellor vowed to support “hollowed out” town centres in his Budget on Wednesday.

The consulting firm AlixPartners will handle any insolvency if the last-gasp survival attempt fails.

Mr Williams confirmed on Thursday that a break-up is likely as “it has not been possible to identify an acceptable offer for the business as a whole”.

He said: “The process has attracted several established retail operators who have made formal offers, collectively these cover a significant part of the business, and we believe offer the best available prospects for shareholders, creditors and to preserve jobs.”

‘Wholly avoidable’

The move was prompted by Gordon Brothers’ decision to starve the business of critical day-to-day funding after Poundland’s independent directors initially thwarted its attempts to push it into administration.

The funding squeeze marked a further escalation in an increasingly bitter dispute over Poundland’s future.

After foiling the plot to appoint administrators, the independent directors Andrew Kirkpatrick, Stephen Welch and Dominic Young all resigned on Tuesday in protest.

Hours later, Mr Williams revealed in a letter to its 12,000 employees that Gordon Brothers had begun restricting access to a key lending facility used to meet the company’s everyday bills.

He described the move as “unexpected, unwanted and wholly avoidable”.

At the time, Mr Williams said: “I’m disappointed to have to tell you that Gordon Brothers have restricted access to funds that we would in normal circumstances expect to access fully under our existing loan agreement.”

He said management was now “seeking legal advice on what the correct course of action is”.

The breakdown in relations is the result of a fierce battle to determine whether Poundland is sold to new owners or broken up.

The former would ensure it survives, while the latter is expected to lead to the loss of thousands of jobs and the disappearance of one of the high street’s most prominent retailers.

Rival retailers have expressed interest in snapping up some of the estate, but it is unclear how many of its 600 stores would be sold.

Management has thrown its backing behind an offer from Ireland’s Martin Property Group that would have secured its future and allowed it to continue trading.

Mr Williams told staff it was a “fully funded, ready-to-go bid that would have kept the business intact and able to continue the remarkable progress we have made”.

However, Gordon Brothers has rejected the offer, fuelling expectations that Poundland will be pushed into insolvency and broken up.

It is understood the firm believes it can recoup more under a break-up.

“To say I am disappointed is an understatement,” Mr Williams said. “This business simply does not deserve to go into any kind of administration.

“Despite the actions of others, it is my intention to work to create the best outcome I can for you all.”

Gordon Brothers’ refusal to accept Martin Property Group’s offer relates to a disagreement over how much it would pay upfront.

The firm is seeking full repayment of a £30m loan facility that it acquired for £1 from Poundland’s previous owners, Pepco, the Polish retail giant.

However, Martin Property Group has said it is only willing to pay half in advance, with the other half deferred for two years when the loan matures.

Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, is understood to have sought answers from Gordon Brothers about its intentions.

data.title: BBC accused of hoarding radio airwaves
data.description:
The BBC has been accused of “hoarding” radio airwaves even as the struggling broadcaster grapples for extra income to offset its declining licence fee.

The corporation, which is in the throes of a £500m cost-cutting programme, is under growing pressure to rent out some of its spectrum to other radio operators.

Rivals argue that the BBC’s current stranglehold on radio infrastructure is “wasteful”, adding that the public service broadcaster is overlooking a chance to generate much-needed additional revenue.

Phil Riley, co-founder of Boom Radio, has written to Matt Brittin, the BBC director general, urging him to open up capacity in exchange for fees.

He said any move to open up spectrum for commercial rivals could be “financially very advantageous” for the BBC and generate as much as £15m in revenues each year.

The windfall would come at a critical time for the BBC, which is racing to strip out £500m in costs in the next two years.

‘Hoarding capacity’

The broadcaster last week announced the closure of channels including BBC Three, while a further 100 jobs will be cut from its news operation. However, it remains less than halfway to its cost-cutting target.

Jason Bryant, founder of Nation Broadcasting, which operates more than two dozen local radio stations across the UK, also said the BBC’s refusal to rent out the spectrum was “absolutely an issue”.

“They are effectively hoarding a whole load of capacity,” he said. “Clearly, if there was willing, there is the opportunity to squeeze a greater number of services on the BBC.”

Mr Bryant said he had suggested such a move to Tim Davie, the former BBC director general, in 2023.

Britain’s radio stations are bundled into transmission groups known as a “multiplex”.

The BBC’s national multiplex runs primarily on the traditional digital radio spectrum, known as digital audio broadcasting (DAB).

However, the commercial version runs on the more efficient DAB+, which allows around twice as many commercial stations to fit onto their multiplex as on the BBC equivalent.

Commercial rivals say the BBC could free up more capacity by upgrading to DAB+.

Additional slots have opened up as the BBC starts to close stations such as Radio 4 Extra as part of its cost-cutting drive.

It is understood that there are no regulations preventing the BBC from renting out space on its multiplex.

However, the corporation has so far resisted any such move, with industry sources suggesting it was afraid to leave behind the small number of listeners who do not have DAB+-enabled radios.

Mr Riley said: “There is a reality here, which is that the BBC multiplex is very wasteful in its use of the capacity that they have.

“If the BBC were to embrace DAB+ for their services rather than DAB, they would free up a significant amount of capacity, and there are definitely commercial services which would want to rent that capacity off them.”

He added that the refusal stood in stark contrast to the corporation’s push to switch off terrestrial TV signals and move to streaming in 2034.

Mr Riley said: “That sits ill with the other side of the BBC where, along with ITV and Channel Four, they’re talking about the wholesale destruction of the digital television infrastructure in the space of the next eight years.”

The BBC declined to comment.

data.title: Shell posts second-highest profit ever after oil price surge
data.description:
Shell recorded its second-highest profit ever after the Iran war pushed up oil and gas prices.

The British energy giant reported profits of $10.8bn (£8.1bn) between July and September, the company’s best quarterly performance since the 2022 energy crisis.

That was up from $5.4bn in the same quarter last year and above analysts’ expectations of $10.3bn.

The rise follows the Middle East conflict, which has pushed oil prices to $114 a barrel, while European gas prices have also jumped above €100 for the first time since 2022.

Shell told investors on Thursday that its refining margins, the profit from converting crude oil into useful products, hit a record $42 a barrel last quarter, up from $24 earlier this year.

Its chemicals and products division, which includes oil trading, also saw profits jump to $3.86bn, its highest on record.

The results led Wael Sawan, Shell’s chief executive, to announce a $5bn buyback for investors, up from $3bn last quarter. This pushed the company’s share price up by 2.8pc in early trading.

Mr Sawan said: “Shell’s relentless focus on operational performance enabled very strong results in a quarter with continued severe disruption to the global energy system.”

Like other oil majors, Shell has increased fossil fuel production in recent months to benefit from rising global prices.

Sinead Gorman, Shell’s chief financial officer, said Gulf of Mexico production platforms had “delivered the highest monthly production in over two decades”.

Shell’s new LNG Canada site also ramped up output to meet surging demand from Europe and Asia, which are seeking alternative energy sources after being cut off from Middle Eastern supplies.

The latest profit surge has come despite significant hits to the company’s balance sheet.

Shell reported a $2.5bn pre-tax impairment charge in its latest results. The charge is believed to relate to its decision not to restart construction of a planned biofuels facility in Rotterdam.

This is part of a broader retreat from net zero, which has led the company to offload its entire European onshore renewables portfolio, spanning the UK, Italy, Spain and the Netherlands.

BP is expected to report a similar earnings jump when it releases its third-quarter results on Friday.

The results have triggered widespread criticism from environmental and consumer groups, which accuse the energy industry of profiting from war and disaster.

Simon Francis of the End Fuel Poverty Coalition said: “The sixth winter of the energy bills crisis benefits the influential shareholders of fossil fuel giants but leaves ordinary households struggling yet again.

“Getting Britain off gas is the only way to end this.”

data.title: Labour gives railway trade union activists a ‘blank cheque’
data.description:
Labour has been accused of giving rail union activists a “blank cheque” to campaign during work hours.

Groups including the RMT, the Transport Salaried Staffs’ Association and the Aslef train drivers’ association will be allowed to carry out trade union work while being paid as if they were in their day jobs.

Keir Mather, a junior minister, said that the Department for Transport (DfT)’s passenger train agency, DfT Operator, had signed a “voluntary recognition agreement” with the three main rail unions.

That agreement, the minister said, had no limits on taxpayer funding of trade union activism during normal working hours. The funding will be supplied via Great British Railways, the planned state body unifying the rail network.

Richard Holden MP, the shadow transport secretary, said: “It’s crystal clear that Andy Burnham’s Labour Government is repeating Keir Starmer’s mistakes and giving a blank cheque to their trades union paymasters on the trains – this time with so called ‘facility time’ which, in reality, means political campaigning at the expense of passengers and taxpayers.

“Rather than raising taxes and fares to pay for union activity, the Government should be concentrating on making railways cheaper, safer and more reliable for passengers and taxpayers,” the Conservative MP added.

“Sadly under Labour, serving the unions rather than the public will always be their top priority.”

Union sources say that facility time consists of up to 50 per cent of a worker’s normal contracted hours which can be spent performing activities such as identifying health and safety problems or dealing with workplace disciplinary problems.

This is claimed to save employers money by avoiding the need to hire more HR staff.

Previously, under the Civil Service’s wider Facility Time Framework document, government departments were not allowed to spend more than 0.1 per cent of their annual salary bill on trade union activists’ facility time.

This would have limited DfT and its agencies, such as DfT Operator or the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency, to a maximum of about £58,000 per year being spent on facility time.

But Mr Mather confirmed that all limits have been lifted. In a parliamentary response to a question posed by Mr Holden, he said: “The [trade union] agreement does not prescribe a fixed facility time entitlement, budget or payroll percentage.

“Instead, reasonable paid time off for accredited representatives will be managed in line with legislation, Acas guidance and operational requirements.

“As facility time will vary according to operational need and levels of trade union activity, it is not currently possible to provide a reliable estimate of its annual cost or proportion of payroll,” he added, saying that such paid time off “will be managed proportionately, balancing statutory obligations, operational delivery and value for money considerations”.

Facility time includes activities such as attending union conferences during working hours, as well as “union facing” projects such as branch meetings.

Critics have said Labour’s watering down of rules ensuring that public sector union members are not paid for non-work activities during work time effectively channels cash into the unions’ pockets.

Trade unions fund the Labour Party and individual Labour MPs to the tune of millions of pounds per year.

Key taxpayer protections against union misuse of facility time were torn up by Sir Keir Starmer’s government, including laws ensuring departments revealed how much facility time was granted to union activists.

Labour also weakened transparency laws around trade union financing, making it harder for the public to understand and scrutinise how much money unions are pouring into political donations, as well as identifying the sources and targets of that funding.

A Department for Transport spokesperson said: “Any suggestion that these arrangements provide a blank cheque for facility time is wrong.

“The voluntary recognition agreement that DfT Operator has reached applies only to union representation for a small number of predominantly former DfT employees who transferred into DfT Operator and does not extend to the whole industry.

“We are taking a pragmatic approach that reflects established industrial relations practice and means workplace issues can be dealt with constructively.”

The spokesman also denied that the agreement applied to DFT Operator staff who were members of the RMT, TSSA or Aslef unions, without giving further detail.

data.title: Meta’s AI raid triggers monopoly abuse investigation
data.description:
Meta’s AI assault on news publishers has triggered an investigation into potential competition abuses by the tech giant.

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) will examine whether Meta is abusing its dominant position by imposing “exploitative” terms on publishers and advertisers.

Billionaire Mark Zuckerberg’s company has said it will introduce new terms allowing it to deploy bots to scrape any website associated with a business account on Facebook, Instagram, Messenger or WhatsApp.

Any business that does not accept the terms would be forced to stop using Meta’s sites for commercial purposes.

Meta originally planned to introduce the new rules on Friday before delaying them until Nov 20. It has now paused the rollout pending consultation with industry groups.

The CMA said it was concerned that forcing news publishers and other websites to accept the terms could be an “unlawful imposition of unfair trading conditions” for thousands of UK businesses that rely on Meta’s apps to reach customers and audiences.

It will consider whether Meta holds a dominant position in the market and, if so, whether its actions amount to an abuse of that position.

The watchdog has the power to block Meta’s new terms and impose fines if the company is found to have broken competition law.

The intervention follows a fierce backlash from the news industry, which accused Meta of mounting an “outrageous assault on journalism”.

Publishers warned that the terms would allow Meta to access vast troves of their journalism to train AI models without paying.

Some have considered closing their accounts, but this would have significant financial consequences given many outlets rely on Facebook for traffic referrals.

Publishers face ‘invidious choice’

Local publishers would be hit hardest as up to a third of their audience comes from the social media platform.

The News Media Association (NMA), which represents titles including The Telegraph, The Times and The Guardian, wrote to ministers this week, urging them to back the CMA in tackling Meta’s behaviour.

Theo Bamber, NMA chief executive, said: “Meta has given publishers an invidious choice of giving away their content for free to power its AI products or leaving a platform which millions of Britons use to get their news.

“We applaud the Competition and Markets Authority for taking action to protect British businesses and UK citizens’ access to high-quality news, and ministers must back them all the way. There is still a lot more work to do, but now is the time to start bringing the dominance of big tech to an end.”

Dame Caroline Dinenage, chairman of the culture select committee, said: “News publishers are absolutely right to be up in arms about the prospect of AI models being able to exploit their intellectual property without permission or fair payment.

“This risks not only undermining the commercial value of journalism, but could also allow disinformation to flourish if publishers decide to pull their accounts from Meta platforms.”

Sarah Cardell, chief executive of the CMA, said: “We’ve heard concerns from news publishers and other businesses and are acting swiftly to investigate whether Meta’s proposed changes may breach competition law, using the most appropriate powers available to us to examine these issues in detail. We will be working to reach a swift and satisfactory resolution to this case.”

The CMA separately said it was seeking information about Meta’s new business subscription service after small businesses raised concerns about a restriction on how many external links can be shared on Facebook and Instagram.

A Meta spokesman said: “There are no grounds for a competition investigation. We’ve already committed not to change our terms without consulting publishers and other stakeholders. We welcome the opportunity to explain our approach to the CMA.”

data.title: Nvidia to prop up British AI giant as data centre boom unwinds
data.description:
Nvidia is poised to prop up the British AI giant Nscale amid signs that the data centre boom is beginning to unwind.

The world’s biggest chip company is reportedly in discussions to provide financial backing for Nscale’s new flagship US data centre that Anthropic plans to use.

Nvidia would provide credit support to backstop the construction and electricity costs of the new complex in West Virginia, which will be equipped with its chips.

The support, first reported by The Information, would hand a much-needed boost to Nscale after Microsoft pulled the plug on a separate agreement for a major data centre in Essex.

The US tech giant, which is one of Nscale’s two largest customers, was to become the anchor tenant at the company’s first data centre in its home country as part of a broader pledge to invest £22bn in the UK.

But The Telegraph revealed this month that Microsoft had pulled out of the project, which has faced delays and is now in limbo.

The decision has cast a shadow over Nscale’s plans to debut on the New York stock exchange in a flotation worth up to $35bn (£26bn).

It comes amid wider concerns about whether AI infrastructure businesses will deliver sufficient returns.

Australian rival Firmus cancelled plans for its $30bn initial public offering earlier this month, citing market conditions. Other “neocloud” companies, which build data centres for AI, such as CoreWeave and Nebius, have seen their shares and bonds slump.

Soaring interest rates have driven up the cost of debt-funded AI infrastructure projects, fuelling concerns about the sustainability of the neocloud business model.

The rapidly-growing AI sector has also faced scrutiny for “circular financing”, where tech giants make significant investments in companies that are also major customers. Nvidia is already an investor in Nscale.

This has triggered warnings from investors such as Michael Burry, who was depicted in the Oscar-winning film The Big Short, about an AI bubble and the looming threat of a market crash.

Nscale was founded by Australian entrepreneur Josh Payne, a former coal miner, and has appointed Sheryl Sandberg and Sir Nick Clegg, both former Facebook executives, to its board.

The company has been privately valued at $15bn and a stock-market float could make it one of Britain’s most valuable AI firms.

However, the success of its listing will be viewed as a critical test of investors’ continued appetite for debt-fuelled AI businesses.

Nscale and Nvidia were contacted for comment.

data.title: China blamed for loss of half a million German factory jobs
data.description:
China has been blamed for the loss of half a million German factory jobs since 2019, as experts have warned that Europe’s manufacturing engine is losing momentum.

German industry shed 496,000 jobs between 2019 and 2025, according to the Ifo Institute in Dresden, representing a drop of 7.1pc.

Joachim Ragnitz, the managing director at Ifo Dresden, said: “Employment is shrinking in almost all industrial sectors, which is likely a result of declining competitiveness, particularly vis-à-vis China.

“Traditional German core sectors, such as the automotive industry and mechanical engineering, are particularly hard hit.”

The figures follow warnings of a “China shock 2.0” as the world’s second-largest economy pumps out cheap advanced-manufacturing exports that threaten to crush Western industry. China’s trade surplus with Germany has doubled in the last year.

It brings back painful memories of the first shock in the early 2000s, when China unleashed a wave of cheap toys, clothes and manufactured goods into Western economies.

In addition to growing competition from China, the Ifo Institute also blamed vanishing factory jobs on a fresh wave of de-industrialisation triggered by high energy prices and changing demographics.

Europe’s biggest economy has suffered several shocks in recent years, reeling in particular from losing access to cheap Russian gas after the Ukraine war.

As factory jobs have disappeared, hiring in less productive sectors has risen significantly.

The services sector employs 2.2 million more people than in 2019, mainly in health and social care and public administration.

Mr Ragnitz warned that this would spell trouble for the future, as these jobs were unlikely to provide a significant boost to growth.

He said: “The new jobs are for the most part not being created where Germany is especially productive and innovative. That may slow down our growth potential in the future.”

Car manufacturers and their suppliers have cut 123,500 jobs since 2019, a plunge of 13pc. Meanwhile, metal products manufacturers cut 115,600 jobs, and mechanical engineering another 64,500.

These three sectors account for 60pc of the job losses.

By contrast, service providers saw strong growth with 391,000 new jobs in healthcare and 357,000 in social services, including nursing homes.

Mr Ragnitz said the country’s ageing population was the key driver of this trend.

Germany has for years had a relatively low fertility rate. It improved briefly for a few years before and during Covid, before plunging again to its current level of 1.3 children per woman.

A fierce backlash against immigration means politicians may struggle to offset such demographic pressures.

Industrial decline has caused job losses in every part of Germany apart from Hamburg. Jobs are also falling faster in the east than in the west, at 8.4pc vs 6.8pc. In Thuringia and Saxony-Anhalt, overall employment has even declined.

These are both states where the Alternative for Germany (AfD) is popular, with the hard-Right party winning the largest vote share in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt last month. It also won the state election in Thuringia in 2024.

data.title: Volvo loses £1bn in value as it slashes 2,500 jobs
data.description:
Volvo has announced plans to slash 2,500 jobs after a sharp fall in sales triggered a share price slump that has wiped £1bn from its value.

Shares in the company, which is owned by Chinese group Geely, plunged as much as 31pc after it revealed revenues fell by 23pc in the third quarter.

Volvo announced a 5bn Swedish kronor (£376.4m) cost-cutting plan that will result in around 2,000 job cuts in Sweden and another 500 globally “through natural attrition and by targeted exit packages to employees”.

The car manufacturer warned it may have to take “additional actions” after revenues in China fell by almost 50pc and it was hit by the loss of electric car subsidies in the US.

Volvo issued a profit warning and pulled its annual guidance earlier this month as sales declined.

Hakan Samuelsson, Volvo’s chief executive, said on Friday: “We continue to operate in a very tough environment with strong external challenges: de-globalisation, hypercompetition and climate change.

“The third quarter of 2026 was very disappointing and reflects a year that has become far more challenging than originally anticipated. Our ongoing turnaround plan therefore needs ​a decisive reinforcement.”

Volvo is the latest European car manufacturer to announce sweeping job losses. In July, BMW revealed it would cut 8,000 jobs in an attempt to reduce costs. Earlier this year, Volkswagen said it would cut as many as 100,000 roles out of a total workforce of 650,000. The move is expected to result in the closure of four factories.

Jaguar Land Rover, Britain’s largest car manufacturer, said in September that it would cut 4,000 jobs over the next two years.

Volvo’s revenues in the three months to the end of September slumped to 66.9bn Swedish kronor (£5bn), a 23pc decline from the same period a year earlier.

The car manufacturer also fell to a net loss of 5.7bn kronor (£429.2m) in the third quarter, down from a net profit of 4.5bn kronor (£338.8m) a year earlier.

Volvo, which had bet heavily on electric vehicle sales, said the axing of customer incentives in the US under Donald Trump had dented its revenue.

In 2024, the carmaker scrapped a target of transitioning to selling only electric cars by the end of the decade.

Last month, Volvo said that Mr Samuelsson would leave as chief executive next year, with Klaus Zellmer, the boss of Skoda Auto, due to take up the Volvo chief executive of the Swedish car manufacturer “no later” than October next year.

data.title: The 33-year-old at the forefront of Britain’s defence revolution
data.description:
To see the future of Britain’s defence industry, you have to visit a four-storey building found on what used to be a car park off Old Kent Road. This clean and functional edifice is the biggest new factory in London since the Second World War.

A Union Flag overlooks the factory floor, where 12 machines are silently engaged in turning steel, aluminium and titanium into precision components for jet engines, drones, robots and much more.

Presiding over them is Alexander Fitzgerald, the 33-year-old founder and chief executive of the company, Isembard, which he established in late 2024.

Like everyone who creates a successful business, the T-shirt-wearing entrepreneur spotted a problem and proposed a solution. “What’s happening across every single sector right now – from aerospace to defence to robotics to energy to semiconductors – is that demand is massively increasing, but the supply of manufacturing capacity to make those components is reducing,” he says.

Isembard’s driving purpose is to provide some of that desperately needed extra capacity. The opportunity is all the greater because of a revolution sweeping Britain’s defence industry.

For generations, the sector has been dominated by a handful of large “prime contractors”, such as BAE Systems, which specialise in the slow and hugely expensive production of a relative handful of advanced jet fighters, tanks and warships, designed to stay in service for decades.

But the lesson from Ukraine is that there are increasing – and critical – advantages for countries that can speedily produce an abundance of smaller and cheaper systems, such as drones, then constantly improve and redesign them, and turn out new and better models every few months. This requires a multitude of small and medium-sized enterprises that can compete to be the most innovative and efficient by deploying AI to make an ever-changing array of components as quickly and cheaply as possible.

Isembard is already doing exactly that. Companies send 3D designs for the parts they need, and Isembard manufactures them according to those designs. “We build our own software and AI to make setting up our factories and running our factories really efficient,” says Fitzgerald.

At present, about 95 per cent of components for manufacturing are produced by small and medium-scale businesses. It is an extraordinary fact that the average age of the owners of these companies in the UK is 65 – and that no less than 40 per cent of them plan to retire within five years.

At the exact moment when Europe is rearming – with all Nato countries, including Britain, pledging to spend at least 3.5 per cent of GDP on defence by 2035 – the supply chain for new components is contracting.

Hence, Isembard is expanding rapidly to meet pent-up demand. Fitzgerald opened his first factory last year, and today his company has 18 worldwide – eight in Britain, eight in America and one each in France and Germany.

This growth has been accelerated by Isembard’s unique business model, which allows for franchised factories. All but five of the existing plants are not owned by the company, but franchised to individual operators. The newest, in Swindon, took a mere 90 days to set up, and Fitzgerald aims to get this down to one or two weeks.

Speed and agility are everything. Fitzgerald notes that what has allowed Ukraine to resist the Russian invaders is not one kind of exquisitely engineered drone, but rather a vast and constantly changing array of different models. “In Ukraine, it’s not one type of drone – and 10 billion of them,” he says. “It’s a zoo of different types of drones, at all classes and all stages. Then you need to be able to scale up.”

Fitzgerald adds: “You need a manufacturing base, which is fundamentally a question of, ‘Have you got enough stuff that can make stuff? Have you networked them enough to be more efficient?’ That’s really the core of our business.”

Reindustrialising Britain by reshoring production is, he believes, the key to the country’s future prosperity. “The grand theory of everything is manufacturing because it’s the root of our prosperity, security and purpose,” he says. “I subscribe to the manufacturing dream – that means security and prosperity [depend on] your ability to make stuff.”

Nearby, the computer numerical control (CNC) machines – which have affectionate nicknames such as Cathy and Big Bertha – on the factory floor are playing their part in reindustrialising Britain by turning out the precisely shaped objects that will soon be flying at high speed as the components of jet engines or drones.

The factory, which covers three floors and 160,000 square feet, aims to triple its workforce to 200 by the end of next year. Taking delivery of the hulking CNCs required Fitzgerald to install a bigger loading door in the building, which was previously used as a grocery depot. The machines had to arrive in the early hours of the morning, since there are timing restrictions within three miles of Charing Cross for loads of that weight and size.

Fitzgerald emphasises that Isembard is not a “defence tech company”, but rather a “manufacturing company”. About 60 per cent of its customers are in aerospace and defence, while most of the rest are in robotics.

But Russia is unlikely to be interested in that distinction as its intelligence services carry out their escalating campaign of sabotage and subversion across Europe, including in Britain.

Is Fitzgerald concerned about that threat? “Yes, and I think the Government should be concerned,” he replies. “We have good security protections in both the cyber and the physical side. We’ve had a lot of support from the Government, and from the police and other agencies, as well.”

Fitzgerald has personal experience of Whitehall, since he spent three years as a Treasury civil servant after graduating from Nottingham University with a degree in biochemistry. Earlier, he had also tried his hand at journalism as an intern at City AM.

He enjoyed his time working in the Government, but cannot help remembering: “When I thought I had the right answer for something, it still had to go through six pairs of hands to get to someone to make a decision. That frustrated me.”

He left the Treasury to start a broadband company that amassed almost 100,000 customers before he sold it to Octopus Group in 2022. Fitzgerald founded Isembard soon afterwards, and the company now makes components for customers like Anduril, which manufactures drones and autonomous weaponry, and Oxford Space Systems, which produces the antennae for satellites.

In the past, certain British investors and banks had a fastidious disdain for any businesses linked to defence, some of which were denied financial services. Fitzgerald, who is also an Army reservist, has encountered no such difficulties, and he believes that attitudes have changed. “I think Ukraine has changed that,” he says. “Geopolitics has changed that.”

Something else that has changed is the attitude towards manufacturing in general. One of Andy Burnham’s central priorities is “reindustrialisation” and recapturing the dynamism of former years.

In that spirit, Fitzgerald named his company after the great Victorian engineer, Isambard Kingdom Brunel, though he adapted the spelling of his hero’s Christian name because the original domain had already been taken.

Today, he keeps a black top hat on his desk in tribute to the man whose individual drive and genius powered Britain’s first industrial revolution.

His other inspiration is Lord Beaverbrook, the minister for aircraft production in 1940, who galvanised British industry into delivering 100 Spitfires and Hurricanes every week, making him an architect of victory in the Battle of Britain and changing the course of the Second World War.

“The Air Ministry didn’t like him. He was threatening to resign the whole time, but he got the job done,” says Fitzgerald, who notes that Beaverbrook tripled production in a matter of months by distributing the manufacture of Spitfire and Hurricane components between hundreds of superbly innovative and cost-efficient small and medium enterprises across the country.

That formula saved Britain in 1940. It might yet do the same again.

data.title: British baked beans ‘under threat from Burnham tariffs’
data.description:
British baked beans are under threat from Andy Burnham’s decision to cut tariffs on imported food, manufacturers have warned.

On Tuesday, the Government announced the suspension of tariffs on more than 100 food products, including cutting the 16 per cent levy on tinned beans.

The move was part of a package of measures the Chancellor announced in his Budget to give families “breathing space” amid the cost of living crisis.

However, British food bosses have warned that cheap exports from the US and China could undermine the country’s major bean processing industry.

The Heinz baked bean plant in Wigan, Greater Manchester, employs up to 850 people and produces 1.5 million tins a day. The Princes Group, which makes Branston baked beans, is owned by Italian food conglomerate Newlat and is one of Britain’s biggest food manufacturers with around 2,000 UK staff.

Karen Betts, chief executive of the Food and Drink Federation (FDF), said Mr Healey’s Budget had done “nothing to ease the pressures food and drink manufacturers are under”.

“One of the Chancellor’s flagship announcements, removing tariffs from some food and drink products, will have no meaningful impact on consumer prices,” she said.

“But it will undermine British factories and their workers, grappling with much higher costs, producing the same products.”

A spokesman for the Princes Group said: “Based on our understanding of the proposals so far, removing tariffs on imported finished baked beans is unlikely to have a meaningful impact on prices, particularly as there are currently no tariffs on the imported haricot beans used by UK manufacturers and no tariffs on EU imports.

“We believe measures that help address the higher costs of manufacturing food in the UK, particularly energy costs, would have a greater impact for both consumers and British businesses.”

The tariff announcement was made days after the Prime Minister said he would put the British family favourite in his emergency box in case of a national disaster. Asked what items he would stockpile, he picked baked beans, soup and Twiglets.

The FDF said it was also concerned about the lifting of tariffs on boiled sweets, toffees and caramels and pressed sweets like Love Hearts and Parma Violets, as well as chocolate.

Last year, the UK and US both applied a tariff of up to a 10 per cent on chocolate imports from the other country. Since then, the US has increased its tariff to 20 per cent and the UK has just removed it for most products.

In addition, the FDF said there were concerns around jams, marmalades and purees, tomato ketchup, tomato sauces, soups and broths.

“Food and drink manufacturing should be central to the Government’s growth and reindustrialisation agenda,” said Ms Betts. “But time and again, we are treated as an afterthought.

“The Treasury, in particular, has persistently failed to recognise the importance of food and drink manufacturing to jobs and prosperity across the length and breadth of the UK.”

The FDF said that particular companies that could be affected, including confectioners Nestle in York and Halifax, Haribo in Bradford, and Cadbury in Bourneville and Tiptree jam in Colchester.

The Government says the tariff suspensions, taken together with others announced earlier this year, will reduce consumer costs by up to £595m a year, saving households up to £21 on their annual food shop.

In its response to a consultation on the changes, the Government said it recognised there “may be some limited impacts on domestic producers of goods”, but said it “considers the benefits of this to consumers, through reduced costs, outweigh those risks”.

data.title: JP Morgan lashes out at ‘unprincipled’ bank tax
data.description:
JP Morgan has criticised John Healey’s tax raid on banks, saying it “lacks principle”.

The Wall Street bank said it was unfair for the Chancellor to “single out” banks after Mr Healey announced an increase in the surcharge on bank profits in the Budget.

JP Morgan reportedly faces paying an additional £100m to £150m because of the higher surcharge. It has paid £5.5bn in bank-specific taxes since 2011.

Mr Healey will temporarily double the surcharge from 3pc to 6pc for 15 months from January to provide “immediate support on energy bills”, he said.

The surcharge is levied in addition to the top rate of corporation tax, which now stands at 25pc, bringing the total rate faced by the sector to 31pc – the highest level since at least 2015.

Singling out banking

The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) estimates that the higher tax rate will bring in an extra £1.5bn, though it believes that roughly £190m of UK profits would move out of the UK following the rise in tax.

Responding to the Budget announcement, a JP Morgan spokesman said the bank was “committed” to the UK and recognised the cost of living challenges facing the country.

But they added: “To single out this industry for additional taxes again, one of the UK’s biggest generators of growth and jobs, lacks principle.

“It also overlooks that the banking industry operates in a highly competitive global marketplace.”

International banks, including JP Morgan and Citi, have been among the most high-profile critics of increasing bank taxes, warning that it could drive investment and jobs abroad.

Jamie Dimon, JP Morgan’s chief executive, has been amongst the staunchest critics of the policy.

In July, he said there would be “adverse consequences” if Andy Burnham targeted lenders with fresh windfall taxes to help fund his spending plans.

“I always thought it was wrong. We’re a great citizen [in the UK]. We hire people there. We want to be bigger there. We train people there. We hire veterans there,” he said.

“So if a government decides to do it, there’s nothing I can do, but it will over time cause decisions made that they may not like.”

Much of the City had feared that the Chancellor would raise the bank surcharge to 8pc, where it had sat until Jeremy Hunt, the then Conservative chancellor, lowered it to 3pc in 2023.

News of Mr Healey’s plans leaked to Bloomberg hours before he announced them in Parliament, which led bank shares to rally. 

Dame Meg Hillier, the chairman of the Treasury committee, wrote to the Treasury and Financial Conduct Authority demanding answers over the leak, which she said was “deeply concerning”.

Bank shares rallied further on confirmation that the increase would be smaller than expected and time-limited. Barclays rose by 3.2pc, while Lloyds Bank and NatWest were both up closer to 4pc.

Lloyds Bank and NatWest are the most exposed to any rise in the bank tax, according to Gary Greenwood, an analyst at Shorecap, with Barclays slightly less affected. HSBC and Standard Chartered, which make much of their money overseas, are even less exposed to the tax increase.

The reprieve on bank taxes was one of the few good pieces of news in the Budget for the City, which was explicitly aimed at giving families and businesses “breathing space”.

The Budget had a number of other measures focused on “bloody minded entrepreneurs”, as Mr Healey termed them, but not all of them were positive.

Founders’ relief for capital gains tax will offer them a reduced 10pc rate when selling their businesses. However, tax analysts said the criteria for achieving the relief were so narrow that very few founders would qualify.

Nimesh Shah, the chief executive of Blick Rothenberg, the tax consultancy, said it was “very narrow in scope and many successful owner-managed businesses are unlikely to qualify”.

At the same time, the more widely used business asset disposal relief has been made less generous. The threshold for tax relief was cut from £1m to £500,000.

The Chancellor said that he would increase the generosity of tax-advantaged employee share option schemes.

The Government has also overhauled the way businesses can write off the costs of equipment against their tax bills, slowing the rate at which businesses can offset the cost of equipment against their tax bills while offering a bigger upfront write-off on some new investment. Ultimately, the policy will raise £1bn for the Treasury.

data.title: Airbnb owners hit by £800m tax raid
data.description:
Hundreds of thousands of Airbnb owners will be hit by John Healey’s Budget tax raid on landlords, piling yet more pressure on Britain’s tourism industry.

Treasury sources confirmed that short-term holiday lets will be hit by the 4pc additional tax on property income, as well as landlords renting out houses and flats for tenants to live in.

The surprise raid on the rental sector was one of a series of Budget tax grabs announced by the Chancellor on Wednesday, which will be used to fund headline giveaways such as the £100 energy bills handout to households.

Basic-rate income taxpayers will see the tax rate on property income rise from 20pc to 24pc from next April. Those in higher tax bands will see the rates on rental income rise to 44pc and 49pc.

Rachel Reeves had already signalled a 2p increase in her Budget last November, but Mr Healey went further in his Commons statement on Wednesday.

Industry leaders said the extra tax would be another significant blow for a sector still reeling from the prospect of a “holiday tax” on overnight stays from 2028.

Alistair Handyside, of the Professional Association of Self-Caterers, said: “It is incredibly unhelpful at a time when tourism is under so much pressure; it’s yet another payment to find.

“A lot of people are going to say, ‘I’ve done the maths, it’s just not worth it any more.’ It’s not any individual straw that breaks people; it’s the cumulative impact.

“All the costs are going up and now the Government is taking more, and of course we’re not able to put up prices, so everyone’s margin decreases again. They can’t keep doing that; it just doesn’t work.”

OBR estimates suggest the new higher rates of property income tax will raise around £1bn in the 2028‐29 tax year before settling at around £800m in later years.

Pavan Mandir, at advisers UK Landlord Tax, said an Airbnb owner in the higher-rate tax band making a typical £24,000 profit will see their tax bill rise by £960 from £9,600 to £10,560.

An estimated 450,000 Airbnb properties in Britain are available for short-term lets.

Alongside rival online platforms such as Airbnb, Booking.com and Expedia-owned Vrbo hosted more than 100 million stays last year.

Many are owned by businesses or do not yet earn enough to pay income tax, leaving around 130,000 individuals declaring a total of £2.5bn in profits from holiday lets last year, according to HMRC.

Short-term holiday lets had not been classified as property businesses until April last year when a more generous tax treatment under the furnished holiday lettings regime was abolished.

Mr Mandir said: “Since the furnished holiday lettings regime was abolished from April 6 2025, holiday lets and Airbnb-style lets have formed part of your ordinary property business.

“That means there is no separate treatment for short-term lets.”

Airbnb declined to comment.
