data.title: ‘Pay me or I’ll kick your face in’: The growing menace of cowboy builders
data.description:
Have you lost money to a rogue builder? Tell us your story at money@telegraph.co.uk*.

When he hired a builder to redo the façade of his new home in Kent, Greg Coates* thought he had done his homework.

He obtained seven quotes, then checked his chosen trader out on Companies House and read online reviews of his work. “He seemed really, really friendly and knew his stuff,” Coates recalls of their first meeting.

But then things quickly soured. The work – which was expected to take a fortnight – began a week late because of the builder being on holiday in Mexico, and the delays kept mounting.

More than a month in, Coates, a 33-year-old engineer who had been researching each step of the process, pointed out that some of the work did not adhere to building regulations. He was fobbed off.

So when the contractor texted to ask for the final chunk of the fees, Coates said that he would pay, minus £1,500 until the parts that weren’t up to code were certified.

“Within about two minutes, he called me up, screaming down the phone,” Coates says. If he didn’t pay within the hour, he said, “I’m going to send the boys round, we’re going to rip everything off the walls. We’re going to tear your house to pieces; I’m going to kick your f------- face in. You’re going to wish you never messed with me.”

At the time, Coates was out and his partner was at home on her own, so “blind panic” was running through his mind. “I was really, really concerned for my partner’s safety.”

The couple had only moved a few months earlier. “The last thing I wanted was for the next 20 years to be tainted by this idea of somebody coming round or this looming threat,” he says. So he transferred the £1,500 and called the police. They gave him a crime reference number and told him to call back if further threats were made.

The £10.3bn cost

Coates is among the half of all British homeowners to have been burnt by cowboy contractors, who set clients back to the tune of £10.3bn in 2024 alone, according to figures from the Federation of Master Builders and the National Centre for Social Research.

In August, the Government launched a voluntary scheme that builders can join to “help people identify and hire trusted traders with confidence”. But critics have noted that similar schemes already exist and that, because it is optional, nothing stops those outside it from continuing to threaten customers without recourse.

In July, James Fuller, a builder, pleaded guilty to harassment without violence and two counts of criminal damage after being accused of causing £164,000 worth of damage to former clients’ home after a dispute over the cost of the renovation.

He was filmed on their roof hurling tiles to the ground, allegedly stole the couple’s dog, and made death threats. After a hearing last month, he is awaiting sentencing.

For most who fall foul of builders’ threats, like Coates, it is easier to give in to financial demands than to face further fallout with people who have access to your home.

Some cowboy builders take on more projects than they can manage at once, using the incomplete status of each job for leverage so that homeowners are backed into a corner. They are forced to either pay up so they’re not trapped in a building site, or hire someone new who can plainly see that a first attempt has gone awry, and will charge extra to step in.

Homeowners also report being asked to front cash outside agreed payment plans to cover builders’ personal costs.

Coates’s builder called back an hour after his tirade to apologise, then suggested that he return to do other jobs in the house – at additional cost.

“I said: ‘You’re not welcome at the property any more; [If you come back] you’ll be trespassing and I’ll call the police.’” The builder never returned.

“In all, I paid about £22,000 for a job that I’ve got no paperwork for,” says Coates.

‘He skipped off with our life savings’

For many, fighting back simply isn’t possible. Cal Dunmore*, 44, was going through cancer treatment and caring for his three-month-old baby when he received a call saying that his builder’s staff wanted to go and watch the heavyweight boxing, and “he needed money to pay them so that they could go out and enjoy themselves”.

Dunmore pointed out that they had agreed a payment plan for taking down a dry-stone wall at his 18th-century property in North Wales, building a retaining wall and backfilling it.

The builder then became extremely aggressive over the phone, Dunmore says. “He was swearing at me and all sorts, and threatening to send people around the house and dismantle the bits of the wall that he had built. He was very threatening.”

He then came to the house demanding money before sending his son to do the same, despite the fact that the work was not yet complete.

Given what he and his wife were navigating in their personal lives, they felt that they were stuck with the builder, despite the damage he had already done to their property.

When the last wheelbarrow was being pushed off the property, he transferred the final part of the £24,000 sum – double what he had been quoted. By the time he’d gone back outside, the wall had fallen.

With what was left of it posing a serious risk, Dunmore contacted his council, which he says wouldn’t get involved. He also went to the platform he had hired the builder through, which he says wanted to work as mediators and have a discussion, but the builder just ignored them.

Dunmore readied himself to go to court before being told that costs were likely to be around £20,000. “How are you supposed to take someone to court when they’ve stolen all your money?”

He feels that laws around limited companies enable bad actors, too. “I could set up a company now and rob a whole bunch of people and then just close the company and set up a new one. And there doesn’t seem to be any laws around it. It seems very cowboy-like,” he says.

Dunmore was forced to hire a secondary contractor, ultimately paying £55,000 in total for a job that was expected to take three months, but lasted five years.

His wife also suffered two miscarriages during that time, which Dunmore believes were the result of the stress they endured. “That guy has literally skipped off with our life savings, and set us back as a family,” he says.

Both Dunmore and Coates are frustrated they can’t speak openly about what has happened for fear of further intimidation. “What stings the most is that I want to warn other people; I want to make his life difficult,” Coates says. “But I have to put mine and my partner’s safety first.”

His situation is far from a one-off, he knows. Yet given the lengths he went to in order to avoid falling into this trap, he admits: “I’m surprised it happened to me.”

*Names have been changed.

data.title: ‘Millionaire row’ neighbours in court battle over basement cinema
data.description:
Neighbours on a “millionaire’s row” are locked in a High Court battle over plans to build a basement cinema and gym under their garden.

Acting on behalf of the house’s freehold and residents’ group, directors Piers Calvert and Lisa Erickson are fighting against the owner of the ground-floor flat who unveiled plans for the basement beneath the garden of their shared building in west London.

They live in a five-storey Grade II-listed Victorian house in Holland Park, where flats recently sold for more than £3m, which sits in the vicinity of homes belonging to celebrities such as the Beckhams, Sir Elton John and Robbie Williams.

Mr Calvert, a photographer, and Mrs Erickson, a choral singer and former banker, are carrying out the dispute through 51 Holland Park Residents Ltd against Montana International Properties Ltd, an offshore entity of which few details are public.

Sitting at London’s High Court, Master Francesca Kaye must rule whether the company owns only the surface of the garden, or the soil beneath it “to the centre of the earth”.

The freehold company argues that, despite having planning permission for the basement, Montana International has no right to dig deep enough to build the room as the soil beneath the surface of the garden goes beyond the limits of the property.

David Nicholls, the barrister for 51 Holland Park, said: “The demise of the garden [the specific area the company owns] does not carry with it the subsoil to the centre of the earth or to any level beyond that reasonably required for use as a garden.

“The subsoil at 20ft or 100ft or 1,000ft below the surface cannot properly be said to be ‘garden’.”

Mr Calvert owns the lease on the attic flat, while Mrs Erickson, 69, owns the lease on the maisonette below.

Since 2014, the lease on the final flat, which covers the ground and lower ground floors as well as the garden, has been owned by Jersey-listed Montana International Properties Ltd, the owners of which lawyers have refused to reveal.

Planning permission for the 2.5m-deep basement beneath the garden, which also includes a shower room and storage space, was granted to the company in 2018.

Mr Nicholls told Master Kaye: “In short, 51 Holland Park contends that the demise includes the subsoil beneath the garden to no greater depth than is reasonably required for the use of the garden as a garden.”

He added: “There is a presumption that applies particularly to freehold conveyances, namely that the owner of land is presumed to own everything up to the sky and down to the centre of the earth.

“But that presumption does not automatically apply in the leasehold context. The correct starting point is the lease, the actual words used, and the overall context.”

Mr Nicholls said the word “garden” had featured in Montana International’s lease for the property, rather than something that might be thought to include what is under the surface such as “land”.

Lease ‘naturally includes’ subsoil

Daniel Dovar, the barrister for Montana International, argued that in a “plain and natural” reading of the company’s lease, the company’s ownership of the garden extended below the ground “without limitation”.

“The demise is of the whole garden, which naturally includes all the subsoil. There is no lease which provides any alternative construction,” he told the judge.

He continued: “If that were not sufficient, then there is the legal presumption that a conveyance of property includes the airspace above and the subsoil below.”

After three days in court, Master Kaye reserved her decision on the dispute until a later date.

data.title: Exposed: Britain’s shoddy new-build epidemic
data.description:
Have you bought a new-build home with defects? Do you regret your purchase? Get in touch at money@telegraph.co.uk*.

“I can already point out five issues with this house,” Tom Britton says within a few seconds of stepping out of the car. “And that’s without going into the state of the pavement, the road... and look at this grass.”

Britton and his specialist surveying team are here to root out snags in a brand new home in Corby, Northamptonshire. But from the outset, they are less than impressed.

He squats and pulls up some of the front garden, rubbing a crumbling mixture of tarmac and soil between his fingers. The grass is dead, leaving behind an ugly brown strip.

“That’s not because we’ve had a drought. That will never grow because they’ve laid tarmac underneath,” Britton says wearily. Every house along the new street has the same issue.

Charlie Jones, a first-time buyer, has lived in the property barely a week. Yet despite the property having been built by a “five-star” developer, Britton’s team at new-build inspection company HomeSnag expects to encounter a litany of issues.

“We’ve been to new homes worth as much as £4m that have had problems,” says Britton, who estimates that just 5-10pc of the properties he inspects meet the housebuilding industry’s standard for genuine five-star build quality.

The data his team has collected across 2,000 inspections make for disturbing reading: 70pc of new homes have uneven ceilings, 60pc have ventilation issues and half lack sufficient loft insulation.

Incredibly, nearly a third have mould, including the one we visit. Marius Neculaes, one of 14 surveyors at HomeSnag, discovers it after pulling down panelling under the kitchen units. “That would start to really smell in a few months,” he says.

Some homes have even posed serious safety risks to Britton’s surveyors, including gas and carbon monoxide leaks, live exposed cables and loose brickwork.

Labour has promised to drive a housebuilding revolution, with 1.5 million new homes by 2029. But many of the homes being churned out are blighted by defects.

For those who have paid a premium to avoid the draughty rooms and faulty boilers that often plague older properties, it can prove deeply disheartening.

Jones, who is 28, says a large part of the reason he and his partner forked out £310,000 for a home on a new-build estate was for the “peace of mind” that came with buying box-fresh.

“You’re in your house all the time, so there’s going to be a timescale of when you’re going to start to find faults,” he says. “But you expect a brand new property to not have those for at least 10, 15 years-plus.”

Yet when the report from Britton’s survey comes back, it raises dozens of issues with the house, several of which are flagged as “significant”, including uneven ceilings and a missing extractor fan in the utility room. There are eight defects identified on the roof alone.

HomeSnag’s Britton, who says the average new home has around 130 defects, is indignant.

“This is supposed to be a five-star builder. They know they’re cutting corners, but they rely on the fact most homeowners won’t know what they’re looking for. They’re only looking for cosmetic issues, like marks on the wall.”

Owners typically have two years from the date of completion to flag issues of any size to their developer. After that, there is a further eight-year window in which the builder is no longer responsible but homeowners can appeal to warranty providers who serve as a form of insurance.

Steve Turner, at industry body the Home Builders Federation (HBF), says that this gives new-build homeowners a distinct advantage over those moving into existing housing stock where “if the roof’s leaking, you’ve got to pay for it”.

Yet in the past, warranty providers and housebuilders have been accused of being inextricably linked, raising questions about the independence of decisions over compensation and remediation.

‘Not much quality control’

Housebuilders have faced an onslaught of rising costs in recent years. The average cost of constructing a low-rise house has jumped by £76,000 since 2020, with the soaring price of materials and labour responsible for around half of that increase, according to the HBF.

To keep a lid on bills, volume developers have historically relied heavily on subcontracting. The Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (Rics) estimates that around 85-90pc of all construction work is subcontracted, rather than relying on in-house staff.

While site managers are expected to ensure a minimum standard of quality, Jeremy Gray, at the Federation of Master Builders, a trade body for SME builders, says ad-hoc training on sites raises the potential for problems.

“[The volume builders] have got quite a few apprentices coming in, they train them on the edge of the site in these sheds, and then there’s not much quality control. It’s all speed, because the money’s in the land, it’s not really in the houses.”

This, he says, differs from smaller housebuilders where reputation is everything and in-house staff are more common.

Rics identifies subcontracting as a risk when building new homes, warning that “main contractors lose a degree of management and control over specialist work”.

However, Turner, at the HBF, which represents housebuilders, dismisses the idea that subcontracting is to blame for defects.

“New-builds aren’t like cars – they’re not made in factories,” he says. “They’re built in fields, in all weathers, by numerous trades over a period of time. Everything in each different new-build is in some respect different. So you do sometimes get relatively minor snags.”

Britton is more sceptical, believing that builders intentionally cut corners where they believe they can get away with it. “They’re dealing with plots, rather than people,” he says. “It’s a faceless process.”

Help to Buy 2.0

More than half of the British public believe older homes are better quality than new-builds, according to a survey by the Chartered Institute of Builders (CIOB), while almost a third describe new housing as “poor quality”.

There are fears in the sector that Labour’s dogged pursuit of headline delivery figures will only exacerbate this issue at a time when sales of new-builds are already at rock bottom.

“It’s imperative that we stop thinking of housing just in terms of raw delivery, because when you get the product right, you stimulate the market demand,” says David Parry, at the CIOB.

Andy Burnham’s recent announcement about a revived Help to Buy-style scheme – called Your First Home – answered long-held calls from developers for state-led buyer support.

While naturally this has been welcomed by the housebuilding industry, there are concerns about a repeat of the fallout from the previous scheme, in which a rush to build resulted in severe structural and cosmetic defects in new homes.

This led to the creation of industry bodies the New Homes Quality Board (NHQB) and New Homes Ombudsman, which set a more exacting code for housebuilders and allowed homeowners to more easily challenge problems, with the threat of fines if developers failed to respond in good time.

The Ombudsman received 1,800 complaints last year, up from 593 the year before.

However, Turner warns that despite continual promises from the Government, signing up to these regulators is still voluntary.

Earlier this week, the NHQB wrote an open letter to the Government, signed by a number of housebuilders including Vistry, urging the code to be made statutory, with the NHQB chief saying “quality must keep pace with quantity”.

Meanwhile, back in Corby, first-time buyer Jones is just relieved to have called in the professional help of Britton and his team when he did. Once he sends HomeSnag’s report to the developer, as paid-up members of the NHQB, it will have an obligation to remediate the snags within a few weeks.

Only then will Jones and his partner be able to enjoy the home they have worked so hard to pay for.

data.title: Great British Railways chairman to earn £250k – without any rail experience
data.description:
A banking executive will become the chairman of Labour’s Great British Railways (GBR) quango on a £250,000 salary – despite never having worked in the rail industry.

Sir John Kingman, the chairman of Barclays Bank UK, took up the post on Friday with a brief to shape the new organisation.

GBR is being set up by Labour’s Railways Bill to oversee Britain’s entire rail network, integrating track management with passenger train operations. It will be the UK’s third-largest public sector organisation, behind the NHS and the military.

Heidi Alexander, the Transport Secretary, said Sir John had an “exceptional record” and added that the appointment was a “defining moment in our mission to put passengers first and rebuild Britain’s railways”.

However, the decision to appoint someone with no transport background to such a sensitive post will fuel the growing controversy over the new quango.

Richard Tice, the deputy leader of Reform UK, said the appointment was a “civil service stitch-up”.

Richard Holden, the shadow transport secretary, previously warned that GBR would be a costly monopoly undermining competition and passenger choice, whose sheer size would make it unaccountable.

Sir John’s appointment was the latest step in setting up the quango, after the site of its headquarters in Becketwell, Derby, was revealed last week.

However, the organisation will only be formally established once the Railways Bill is approved, which is expected to take another year.

It means the existing state-owned organisations that it will replace – track managers Network Rail and DfT Operator Ltd (Dfto), which oversees 10 train operating companies – will remain in situ.

Their chairmen – both also appointed earlier this year – will also stay on so taxpayers will be funding the salaries of all three overlapping roles for at least a year.

Richard George, Network Rail’s chairman, is paid £315,000 a year, while Sir Andrew Haines, Dfto’s chairman and the former boss of Network Rail, gets £160,000 a year.

Sir John, a former Treasury mandarin, will also retain his existing job as non-executive chairman of Barclays Bank UK, for which he was paid £600,000 last year. Barclays recently extended his term by another three years.

Sir John’s early career includes a spell as a columnist for the Financial Times. He also worked in the chief executive’s office at BP from 1997 to 1998, later rising to become a permanent secretary at the Treasury. There, he played a central role in the UK government’s response to the 2008 financial crisis, including the nationalisation of Northern Rock.

Sir John said: “The opportunity to lead Great British Railways is one I could not let pass. It is a privilege to be involved in rail’s next chapter making sure that public ownership of the railways delivers change that people can see.

“I want to help to build a simpler, more unified railway that puts the interests of the passengers and customers first, supports growth and creates opportunity across the country.”

However, opponents of the GBR plan were critical. Mr Tice said: “A fat cat with zero rail industry experience is made chair of the new railways quango on a massive salary. It’s another fine stitch-up from the civil service.”

data.title: Why 200 passengers were ejected from the world’s first ‘endless’ cruise
data.description:
An “endless” world cruise that left Belfast two years ago has ground to a halt, with around 200 passengers ordered to leave with all their belongings.

Villa Vie Odyssey, which was due to circle the globe continuously, has entered “temporary lay-up” in Cambodia, the chief executive of Villa Vie Residences, Kathy Villalba, announced. Residents, who had paid up to £700,000 each to live permanently on the ship, were given seven hours to disembark because the company was “unable to secure the fuel necessary to continue operations”.

Holly Hennessy, a founding member of the project, posted a tearful video from her cabin balcony in which she hugged her cat, Captain, and said: “Our dream may be dying.”

She wrote on Facebook: “The truth is that we don’t know what’s going to happen with the ship. We love Odyssey and hope it can overcome all the issues. It’s been very tough going of late, particularly given the fuel crisis.

“We’ve had a few months to anticipate this happening; most shipmates have got to a place of acceptance. It’s still utterly heartbreaking though.”

Another passenger, Randy Cassingham, wrote on his blog, ResidentialCruising.com: “It didn’t come out of the blue – it was a cascade of problems piling up on one another, from the business model to mistakes by management to the crisis in fuel cost and availability and more.”

He told The Telegraph that residents were so concerned about the crew’s salaries being paid that some sat outside the restaurant at mealtimes collecting cash for them.

Mr Cassingham added: “We’ve run the full spectrum of the darker moods, from anger to resentment to bewilderment to ‘What am I going to do?’ Many feel betrayed – how could they leave such a safe and easy-to-deal-with place like Thailand to drop us in Cambodia?

“A few residents are shell-shocked, because they spent the majority of their nest eggs to be here and don’t know how they’ll live. But I really think the overwhelming mood is that it was a fantastic adventure and great while it lasted. We made some wonderful friends and have amazing memories, and saw things we never would have seen otherwise.”

A rocky start

Odyssey’s voyage was troubled from the beginning, with a four-month delay in sailing because of problems discovered when the former Fred Olsen ship, Braemar, entered dry dock in Belfast. One woman was banned from embarking because of complaints she made in a private WhatsApp group.

When Odyssey eventually set off in October 2024, initial issues included having no hot water and not being able to flush the toilets, leading one passenger to dub it “SS Clusterf---”.

Later in the trip, the ship had to skip bucket-list destinations of the Galapagos Islands and Antarctica, as well as an 800-mile journey along the Amazon.

But, as the voyage progressed, residents began excitedly posting on social media about visiting new destinations. In its first three and a half years, Odyssey was due to visit 425 ports in 147 countries, before circumnavigating the Earth again and again for up to 15 years.

Buoyed up by the reaction, Villa Vie Residences announced plans for a second ship, as well as the launch of an ultra-luxury vessel, Lumina, under a separate brand.

Escalating costs

However, escalating costs on Odyssey meant repeated calls for residents to contribute more money. Then, in an email to them dated October 26, Villalba said the company was £50,000 short of the amount it needed to keep the ship running.

She wrote: “As a result, the Odyssey will enter a temporary lay-up this afternoon, with crew remaining on board to maintain the vessel and its essential systems.

“All residents must disembark by 2pm today. For those who are unable to collect all their belongings before disembarking, please co-ordinate with guest services to arrange an orderly return using the shuttle buses, which will remain available until 6pm tomorrow.”

Statistics from the site MarineTraffic show that, in the past year, Odyssey has travelled 35,885 nautical miles. However, its time at sea compared with being in port fell to 34 per cent over the past 30 days, compared with 51 per cent in the past 12 months, while its average speed dropped from 8.2 knots to 6.9.

In a press release, Villa Vie Residences said it was working “to address extraordinary increases in fuel costs and evaluate restructuring and recapitalisation alternatives”.

It noted that the price of marine oil in parts of Asia had soared from the equivalent of around $1,800 a cabin to $8,000. “The company cannot simply pass increases of that scale on to residents, and the resulting shortfall has placed its current operating model under unsustainable financial pressure,” the statement said.

It added: “The company is working with residents to co-ordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew and employees while we work toward restructuring and recapitalisation over the next 60 days. That work is ongoing and no outcome is assured.”

Villa Vie Residences did not respond to a request for comment.

data.title: NatWest slashes 1,000 jobs as it rolls out AI
data.description:
NatWest has cut 1,000 jobs in the last three months as it pushes forward with AI advances.

The bank said on Friday that it had cut a total of 1,400 jobs so far this year, with the majority coming in the last quarter. The figures did not include the impact of the acquisition of wealth manager Evelyn Partners.

A quarter of the role reductions were down to a recent sale of Mentor, the bank’s business consultancy service.

Paul Thwaite, the chief executive of NatWest, said: “We’ve acquired some businesses and we’ve also sold some businesses. But there’s no single change that’s influencing the numbers.”

The job cuts come as NatWest rolls out AI across the bank, including for customers.

Its fraud triage agent, called Cora, has dealt with 52,000 credit card customer issues since it was launched at the end of August, the bank said.

“Roles are changing. We’ve got new roles that are very much dedicated to AI,” Mr Thwaite added.

“We’ve got other roles that are being changed because of AI. My job is to make sure we get the right people with the right skills doing the roles.”

NatWest is the latest bank to announce significant job cuts. Earlier this week, Barclays said it was planning to cut 5,000 jobs this year in an AI-related cull.

HSBC is planning to use AI to reduce the ranks of its UK financial advisers by almost 70pc, it emerged last month.

Bill Winters, the boss of Standard Chartered, was criticised earlier this year for referring to AI replacing “lower-value human capital” as he announced 8,000 redundancies.

Mr Thwaite said: “The way that we’re using AI is for the benefit of our customers and for the benefit of our colleagues. It’s helping manage our risk better and protect our customers better.”

Job cuts across banking also come ahead of new laws that will make it harder for companies to let staff go from next year.

Rules on unfair dismissal have been strengthened under the Employment Rights Act 2025. Several surveys show that companies are expected to be more cautious about hiring as a result.

Some evidence also suggests companies are considering workforce reductions before the new rules take effect. A study commissioned by Acas, the public body that advises on workplace relations and dispute resolution, has found that almost half of large businesses are likely to make staff redundancies by January 2027.

NatWest’s job numbers came as the bank reported pre-tax profits of £2.2bn in the third quarter, flat year-on-year. The results were slightly above City estimates.

‘We need strong banks’

From next year, banks will face higher taxes as John Healey plans to double the bank surcharge from 3pc to 6pc for 15 months from January.

While Mr Thwaite refrained from criticising the increase directly, he said it was important that it remained time-limited.

“If we genuinely want a strong economy, we need strong banks, and that means banks using the capital they’ve got to support customers whether they’re households or whether they’re businesses because ultimately, that’s what drives the underlying growth picture,” Mr Thwaite said.

“The Chancellor laid out, obviously, an increase in the surcharge but also that it was a temporary increase. I think that’s very important because the time limit provides welcome clarity both to banks and businesses so we can plan.”

Other banks have criticised the tax increase, with JP Morgan saying it “lacks principle”. The Wall Street giant said it was unfair for the Chancellor to “single out” banks.

Shares in NatWest dropped by as much as 9.4pc, with trading briefly halted, after the bank said that it expected a slowdown in interest income next year.

Katie Murray, the chief financial officer, said on a call with analysts that the bank expected its net interest margin, the difference between what it earns from lending and what it pays on deposits, to be “flatter” in 2027.

Since Mr Thwaite took over as chief executive in 2023, he has made developing the bank’s wealth management capabilities a major part of its plans to diversify away from income tied to interest-rate changes.

This year, the bank completed the £2.7bn acquisition of Evelyn Partners, Britain’s third-largest wealth manager, its largest acquisition since the disastrous takeover of ABN Amro just before the financial crisis.

data.title: North Korea blamed for largest heist in history as hackers steal $6bn
data.description:
North Korea has been blamed for the largest heist in history after hackers stole $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from the cryptocurrency giant Binance.

The world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange is racing to recover funds and has blocked customer withdrawals in the wake of the theft, which analysts said had been planned by elite North Korean hackers.

The company said hackers had compromised an engineer’s laptop, using it as a route into the company’s systems and making billions in unauthorised withdrawals.

The hack is more than four times the $1.5bn Bybit hack of February 2025, which was previously the largest on record.

It also eclipses the largest physical heist in history, when Saddam Hussein’s family stole $1bn from the Bank of Iraq in 2003 before the US invaded.

Analysis group TRM Labs said most of the heist had taken place within 20 minutes, beginning at around 8pm on Thursday. It blamed a “premier hacking unit” from North Korea called TraderTraitor.

North Korea has been blamed for a series of cyber attacks on cryptocurrency exchanges, with state-backed hackers stealing billions of dollars each year to fund the country’s illicit weapons programmes.

Analysis firm Elliptic said the stolen funds had moved through digital wallets tied to the hacking of Bitget, another cyber attack linked to Pyongyang’s hacking groups.

The FBI said it was investigating the incident.

Binance insisted customer funds were safe, adding it would cover any losses from company reserves.

The UK’s Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) said it was in contact with Binance over the incident. It is understood the Bank of England is monitoring the fallout.

Richard Teng, the co-chief executive of Binance, said on Friday that the cyber attackers may have broken into an engineer’s laptop and used it as a means to gain wider access to the company’s systems.

However, he insisted it was not just a “one-click” attack on a single employee but involved a “more complex attack process”.

He wrote on X: “We’re working closely with law enforcement to ensure the matter is handled appropriately.”

Binance said on Friday morning that withdrawals would be frozen for a further 45 hours – meaning customers will not be able to access their money until Sunday.

Founder says Binance will cover losses

After the hack, coin providers Tether, Circle, Ripple and World Liberty Financial froze about $2.8bn in so-called stablecoins.

World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to Donald Trump and his family, also said it had worked to freeze funds stolen in the Binance hack.

However, TRM said hackers had stolen 18,270 bitcoins and more than 420,000 ether, putting it “beyond any issuer’s reach”. Elliptic estimated that around $3.3bn in assets appeared to have evaded attempts to freeze the funds.

The price of Bitcoin fell more than 4.3pc after the hack emerged while the price of ether dropped by more than 5.7pc.

Yi He, the co-founder of Binance, said the exchange would “cover all hacking losses”.

A company spokesman said: “Rest assured that user funds are completely safe.

“Binance’s initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised dev-ops engineer’s laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorised withdrawal transactions.

“We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak.”

Binance is one of the world’s most popular cryptocurrency exchanges, offering customers a platform to buy, sell, trade, and stake a range of crypto assets.

It was founded by Changpeng Zhao, a Chinese-born Canadian businessman, in 2017 and has grown quickly into a global hub for crypto trading.

Mr Zhao said it appeared that Binance had been hacked but reassured its users that it “will cover” losses. He no longer runs the company but remains its largest shareholder.

Investors ranging from beginners to professionals are able to access an extensive list of digital currencies on Binance, trading tens of billions of dollars of assets on its platform every day.

Analysts said the hackers had tried to cover their tracks by shifting the coins between different cryptocurrencies.

They also sent the money to cryptocurrency lending services, effectively borrowing against their stolen gains to evade attempts to freeze the assets.

Mr Teng said Binance was working with law enforcement on tracking and recovering the funds.

Binance is based off-shore and is not allowed to operate in the UK.

An FCA spokesman said: “While Binance wasn’t registered with the FCA to provide crypto services in the UK, we’re aware of the reported incident and engaging with them to understand the impact.”

The National Crime Agency declined to comment.

data.title: The signs that Britain has hit peak Padel
data.description:
Padel, the racquet sport taking over Britain, is growing so fast that a new court opens somewhere in the country every nine hours.

From abandoned warehouses to rugby-club car parks, entrepreneurs have been turning almost any available patch of land into somewhere to play the voguish game, which combines elements of squash and tennis.

But what began as a gold rush is now claiming its first victims, with fears that Britain has hit “peak padel”.

Operators are collapsing, rents are rising, and competition threatens to drive prices down. Industry figures warn that Britain’s padel bubble is about to burst.

“We’ve all benefited from the hype. We’ve all enjoyed the hype,” says Andy Knee, the chief executive of padel operator PadelStars. “But it will be healthy that it starts to grow a little bit more slowly.”

Originally a game played in Latin America, padel and its sister sport pickleball have come out of nowhere to become the trendy game played after work or on weekends by thousands of Britons.

It’s relatively easy to pick up – rackets are larger than both tennis and badminton – and the large number of available courts has helped it boom in popularity since Covid-19.

Since 2020, the number of courts has exploded from 69 to 1,825 in May this year, according to the Lawn Tennis Association, an increase of 2,500pc.

Separate figures from booking-data specialist Playskan show that a further 674 courts opened between January and August this year alone, about one every nine hours.

At least £225m has been invested in UK padel in recent years, according to Bloomberg, with celebrities including rapper Stormzy and Sir Andy Murray, the former tennis champion, backing operators.

Financial challenges

Yet the first cracks are already appearing.

Social Sports Society, which operated five venues across Britain, entered administration following a dispute with its financing partner. Its flagship club near Wembley Stadium closed following reports of unpaid rent.

Padel XO, a business founded by Max Evans, a former Scotland rugby player, has also gone into liquidation.

Speaking from a fashionable co-working space in Clapham, south London, one of several neighbourhoods where padel has become a fixture of the social scene, PadelStar founder Knee warns that investors are already building too many courts in certain areas.

“There’s a street in Watford which has got 19 courts on it now,” he says. “Is that the most judicious use of capital? I would question it.”

The danger is not necessarily that Britons will stop playing padel. It is that too many businesses are competing for the same customers after spending millions of pounds opening clubs.

Much of the initial expansion has involved operators snapping up disused warehouses, which can be converted into indoor padel clubs relatively quickly.

But while these buildings offer the space and high ceilings needed for courts, they come with expensive rents, business rates and maintenance bills.

Knee says warehouse operators can pay five or six times as much rent as PadelStars, which generally builds courts on cheaper land alongside existing sports facilities.

He estimates that some warehouse clubs need to book their courts for 50pc to 60pc of available hours simply to stay afloat.

That leaves expensive indoor clubs particularly vulnerable when rivals open nearby and begin cutting prices.

Jessica Hill, a leisure property expert at Savills, warns the problems could worsen when operators face their first rent reviews.

She says landlords who bought warehouses for industrial use may demand rent increases based on what industrial tenants would pay, rather than what padel clubs can afford.

“There is definitely a risk for people that have gone into industrial units [who have] potentially not understood the risk they’re taking,” she says.

Smaller businesses are also facing competition from established leisure giants with much deeper pockets.

David Lloyd, Britain’s largest padel operator, had 169 UK courts at the end of last year and planned to add another 87 across its wider estate during 2026.

Meanwhile, Mike Ashley’s Frasers Group is pursuing an ambitious expansion of its Slazenger Padel Clubs business.

In August, it opened a nine-court club inside a former 3,252 sq m retail unit in Exeter, following earlier openings in Leeds, Swindon and Blackburn. The company has outlined plans to build a network of around 150 courts.

Hill warns that Frasers could prove particularly dangerous for smaller competitors.

“They have the force behind them in terms of their ability to expand, fund operations, fund cheaper court hires as well, to cut prices, to cut competition,” she says.

‘Don’t tend to be loyal’

Operators also can’t necessarily rely on customer loyalty.

Unlike the generations of football, cricket and rugby players who return to the same clubs year after year, Britain’s padel enthusiasts can be a fickle bunch.

Hill says operators have found that players happily abandon their regular indoor courts when the sun comes out, seeking games outdoors.

“People don’t tend to be loyal to a court,” she says. “If they want to play outdoors, they will go out and find an outdoor court to play in.”

Some clubs are responding by installing saunas, plunge pools and co-working facilities, hoping to persuade customers to spend more time and money on-site.

The sums involved can be substantial. Savills research found peak court-hire prices reaching £72.50 an hour, while some premium London venues charged considerably more.

Yet the problem is not necessarily that Britain has too many padel courts overall. It is that they are being built in the wrong places.

Savills found in an earlier study that 72pc of courts were concentrated in southern England, leaving large parts of the country underserved. But the North West has also become a padel hotspot, with courts springing up in Manchester, Liverpool, Blackburn and Preston. The region now has more courts per head than London, according to figures from Padel Britain.

Hill believes Britain’s notoriously slow planning system may also have prevented an even more reckless, rapid expansion of court building.

While operators complain about the delays, she says the system “could be considered a good regulator of speed of growth”.

In Sweden, where padel boomed during the pandemic, almost 90 businesses connected to the sport went bankrupt in 2023 after operators built more courts than local demand could support.

Diminishing novelty

Questions also remain about how long Britain’s enthusiasm will last once the novelty wears off.

Tom Farquharson, co-founder of The Padel School, believes this reflects how much of Britain’s growth has been driven by casual players rather than the sort of established club culture found in Spain and Argentina.

While padel is easy to pick up, he warns that people who never progress beyond playing occasional social games may eventually drift away.

“Players who don’t improve and plateau can potentially stop playing the game,” he says.

For now, Knee remains confident that padel has years of growth ahead.

But he says the industry’s most exuberant investors could be in for an unpleasant surprise.

“I think inevitably, when the sport is growing quickly, people sort of get giddy about it and think the good times are just going to keep rolling.”

data.title: Norway is all the proof we need that Rosebank must be approved
data.description:
It was great to read this week about how well one of the major players in the North Sea is doing, and how much the whole country is benefiting from its success. Output is booming, it has reported its strongest profits in four years, plenty of skilled jobs are being created, and the government is raking in hundreds of millions in extra revenue both as a shareholder, and, of course, from all the taxes it pays.

There is just one catch. The company is Norway’s Equinor, and it is our Scandinavian neighbours who are benefitting from its success.

The Norwegian giant is a template for how we could be managing our own energy resources – if only our political leaders stopped dithering and had the sense to follow its lead.

Equinor reported another strong set of results this week. Its earnings before tax for the third quarter doubled to $12.4​bn (£9.3bn) from $6.2bn, the highest level since 2022. Production is up, and its pipeline is strong.

“The basis for this result is, of course, that we have increased production and, ​just as importantly, that prices have risen significantly,” according to Anders Opedal, its chief executive. Indeed, there is plenty more where that came from. On Thursday the company announced that estimates of the amount of recoverable gas in its Afrodite field were more than double the earlier estimates. It will be keeping the pipelines full for many years to come.

Given all that, it is no great surprise that its shares are up by 86pc so far this year, and keep hitting all time highs. The Norwegian government owns 67pc of the company, so at a rough estimate it has made more than £20bn this year alone from its shareholding. 

On top of that it has collected corporation tax, as well as the petroleum taxes which, when taken together, means the government takes in more than 70pc of any profits made by its energy giants. In short, it is not just that the company is doing well. So is the whole country. Indeed, all the money Equinor is generating helps explain why Norway has a huge budget surplus and has been cutting taxes.

The contrast with Britain could hardly be more painful. While a company such as Equinor is booming on the back of strong oil and gas prices and rising production, we have been running down our own resources.

Equinor itself has always been a major player in the fields off the Aberdeen coast, but only last month it repeated that a combination of punishing taxes and activist-led lawfare meant the industry was “uninvestable”.

Overall North Sea production has been in steady decline for years, and all the so-called renewable experts keep telling us that it is pointless to think about preserving it because there is hardly any oil and gas left in its exhausted fields, and even if there were it wouldn’t make any difference to the global price. Even leaving aside our “global leadership” on combatting climate change there isn’t any money to be made.

The Norwegian example tells that is not, to be put it politely, quite the whole story. We have, in fairness, taken one tiny baby step towards boosting production again in the British section of the North Sea.

After years of tortured delays the Jackdaw gas field has finally been approved. But we are still waiting on a final decision on the Rosebank field, even though, bizarrely, both the Chancellor and the Office for Budget Responsibility have already pencilled in the tax revenues that will start flowing once it starts production. Apparently it is still being held up while Labour’s boneheaded backbenches fight a rearguard action to try to delay it all over again.

That is simply not good enough. There is no reason not to approve the field immediately. Dithering and delaying doesn’t help the workers in Aberdeen who need jobs, it doesn’t help a Treasury that needs the money, and it doesn’t even help the climate, given that we just import fossil fuels instead. All it does is reinforce the impression across the energy industry that Britain is no longer a serious country, and not one worth wasting time and money on. and money on.

Our approvals should not stop with just those two fields, there is so much more that we could be doing. Offshore Energies UK has identified more than 100 projects in the North Sea that we could be exploiting, while the Norwegian experience tells us that once you start drilling, and using the latest techniques, there is always more energy locked up in the ground than initially expected.

In reality, Equinor is a role model for how to manage the North Sea while gradually transitioning to wind, solar and nuclear power. Extend the life of existing fields for as long as you can and develop new ones where possible.

Tax the industry so the Government makes plenty of money, but not at such a high rate that it is impossible for the companies investing their capital to make a decent return or to reward their shareholders for the risks they are taking. And, if possible, take a significant government stake in the main exploration and development company so that the state benefits as a shareholder and doesn’t have any incentive to punish the operators with sky high taxes. It is hardly complicated stuff.

All we need are the political leaders with the basic intellectual curiosity to take a look at something that is working really well for a close neighbour, and one with almost exactly the same geographic resources we have. Given the track record of this Government, we won’t hold our breath – but the template is right there in front of us.

data.title: How Labour’s nationalising of South Western Railway made things worse
data.description:
Davor Palic has become wearily used to leaving ridiculously early for work. The 38-year-old estate agent lives in Woking, regularly taking the recently nationalised South Western Railway (SWR) service to London Waterloo. But he’s developed a fairly simple rule of thumb over the years: if he needs to be somewhere on time, he probably shouldn’t trust the SWR timetable.

“Sometimes it’s delayed more than 30 minutes,” he says, shaking his head. “Usually it’s five or seven minutes, but even that’s enough to make me miss the bus at the other end. It’s annoying because I can be late for work a lot.”

And even when the train is on time, Palic says it can sometimes arrive at one of the busiest stations on the South Western Railway network with just five carriages rather than the full advertised length of up to 12.

“In the morning it’s so busy,” Palic explains. “It makes the overcrowding worse and it’s very hard to get a seat.”

It wasn’t meant to be this way. When Labour brought SWR into public ownership in May 2025 – the first operator to be taken in-house by the Labour Government – Heidi Alexander, the Secretary of State for Transport, promised a “cultural reset” for the railway, a “new dawn moving away from 30 years of inefficiency, delayed services and failing passengers, and moving confidently into a new era – the era of Great British Railways”.

A year down the line on June 11, 2026, Alexander was forced to accept in the House of Commons that performance at South Western Railway had “not been up to scratch”. She promised, as many have before her, to “leave no stone unturned” to improve the travel experience in future.

What’s happened since, though, is even more worrying for the likes of Eileen Taylor, 81. She travels on the line every week with her husband. “It has actually got worse with delays and timetabling,” she points out. “Someone told me they’d been standing for three hours on a service recently.”

All of which isn’t just anecdotal, it’s a failure of a nationalisation project borne out by facts published by SWR itself.

In the latest four-week performance period, only 65.34 per cent of its services arrived on time. In the quarter before nationalisation this figure was at 67.8 per cent. On the main line – the routes carrying passengers between places such as Woking, Guildford and Waterloo – the figure is just 50.98 per cent.

Even if you use the industry’s more forgiving measure of a train arriving within three minutes of schedule, SWR achieved 81.78 per cent across the network and just 68.86 per cent on the main line. Again, in the quarter before nationalisation it was empirically better, at 85.7 per cent.

It’s only when that measure is extended by up to a 15-minute delay that the figures rise above 90 per cent, tallying with Palic’s experience of regular small delays, and causing SWR to miss its punctuality targets.

So much for improving the experience of passengers. Jeremy Varns from campaign group South Western Railway Watch (SWR Watch) meets The Telegraph outside Guildford Station, and immediately points out a limp, ripped National Rail flag outside.

“Look at the state of that,” he says. “Replacing it won’t make trains run on time but it symbolises the indifference; they haven’t even bothered to replace it.”

Recently, Varns pulled together the many complaints he hears from passengers into a 12-point letter to SWR management, categorising everything from dirty trains and unusable toilets to delays, broken information screens and failures of communication. What happened when he met the directors to work through some of these issues was revealing.

“They were kind of grilling me and asking whether I thought they were incompetent,” he laughs. “And I said, ‘No, I’m not necessarily saying you’re incompetent, but you’re clearly not delivering for your passengers – what you’re telling us is happening is completely different to what’s happening on the ground.’

“My biggest concern is that there’s still no published contract for members of the public to go and read what South Western is required to deliver,” he says. “That smacks of an obvious lack of transparency.

“It means there’s no consequences for failure. Yes, they have these big initiatives like drones being sent to investigate track problems. But when passengers get onto a train and none of the toilets are working, and it’s a bit grubby, and the information screens are not being repaired when they go wrong for several weeks… it gives this whole impression of, well, a railway that is a bit rubbish. Neglected.”

Which is not what nationalisation was supposed to deliver. Last month SWR published an “Improving Your Railway” plan to “make the short, medium and long-term changes that will deliver a railway you can rely on to get you where you need to be every day”.

It talks about how South Western will become part of Great British Railways next year, and focus on “fixing the fundamentals”.

Which is in line with Andy Burnham’s current attitude towards railway performance. He acknowledged during an interview in September that the entire rail network had “a difficult summer” and the situation wasn’t “good enough”. According to figures released by the Office for Rail and Road in September, punctuality improved for just three out of 25 operators between April and June this year, in comparison with the same period in 2025.

“I’ve lost count of the number of times someone has stopped me to tell me about the train that never came,” Prime Minister Andy Burnham admitted. When he was later asked by BBC South specifically when SWR would improve, he said: “It will get better… the railways are in need of repair and that will take some time. I realise passengers can’t wait forever, which is why I’m calling a rail summit for later this year.”

The problem is, those passengers waiting forever have little confidence, based on long experience, that any of these improvements will happen.

“Rail nationalisation is an ideology without an actual delivery plan behind it,” says Varns. “It’s meaningless in that sense, all of this is just people saying they understand that things aren’t very good and they will get better, when in fact it’s poor management and poor oversight at the heart of these problems.

“Ministers come and go, they’re looking for short-term fixes, when really what the railway infrastructure needs is a long-term plan, solving long-term funding.”

These are exactly the kind of concern Will Forster, the Liberal Democrat MP for Woking, hears all the time from his constituents. The Woking MP established an All Party Parliamentary Group to scrutinise SWR before nationalisation, and, he says, since then: “Things have got slowly, steadily worse… in fact it’s quite noticeable how bad things have got since it was nationalised.”

Forster has since launched his own constituency survey, and it revealed a service that is struggling to meet demand – particularly during the working week – alongside widespread frustration about unreliability and a continual lack of communication during disruption.

“In June I said in the Commons that nationalisation has not gone to plan. I wanted to know why and was told by the Leader of the House that we didn’t need a debate because things were expected to improve. But improve by what? There’s no measurement there, no KPIs, which is absolutely shocking.

“Now I’m not even sure there is a plan. At the moment it feels like this is being done by Labour because instinctively it will make them feel better as a party – which doesn’t seem to be helping.”

“I don’t expect next month all trains on SWR will run on time,” he adds. “But I do expect them to maintain performance, then improve it. This is not about Labour feeling better about themselves, this is about people arriving on time for work.”

Rail industry expert and author, Christian Wolmar, agrees with the need for a long-term plan, but thinks it is too early to write off nationalisation.

“South Western was a malfunctioning railway beforehand so you can’t expect it to turn around overnight. Actually, you can point to other franchises such as Southeastern which are back in public ownership where things have improved. Greater Anglia is doing very well.

“Ultimately improving railways is about structural change... the key question really is whether government allow – and create – a structure that allows the railways to be run by railway people.”

Forster says he will continue to press Government for answers and transparency, but when we put the questions and concerns that passengers tell us to the Department for Transport (DfT), the response comes with exactly the kind of unfettered optimism that infuriates the likes of SWR Watch’s Jeremy Varns.

While admitting there was “more to do” in a statement to The Telegraph, a DfT spokesman added: “South Western Railway passengers are seeing the benefits of public ownership, with 60 new 10-car Arterio trains now in service, increasing capacity across the London commuter network by more than a third and replacing a 40-year-old fleet with modern, more comfortable trains.

“This summer, traincrew-related cancellations were reduced by almost 84 per cent compared with last year, while the number of trains running with fewer carriages than planned fell by around 40 per cent.”

And if it seems like there is “more to do” is doing a lot of heavy lifting in that statement, then it’s the response of Lucy, returning home from a busy day’s work in London that sums up just how low confidence has become in South Western Railway since privatisation.

“For me, I hate travelling by train because of the poor service,” she says. “I try to use South Western just once a week now. It could be a lot better.”

Additional reporting by Blaise Cloran

data.title: People who blare out music on public transport warned of £1,000 fines
data.description:
Passengers who play loud music on trains will be threatened with fines of up to £1,000 in a drive to stamp out anti-social behaviour.

Rail companies will target noisy commuters with announcements reminding them to put on headphones or face being thrown off at the next station.

Andy Burnham said that tackling inconsiderate travellers would help “make journeys that little bit better for all of us”.

The Prime Minister will front the launch of a government-backed campaign on Monday urging passengers to “share the carriage, not the noise”.

Train companies, including state-owned Great British Railways, will put notices across the network warning that playing music can be an offence.

Rail staff will be encouraged to first ask any traveller breaking the rules to put headphones in.

If they refuse to comply, they will be told they can be thrown off the train at the next station and face prosecution, with a maximum fine of £1,000.

Incidents where passengers refused to comply would initially be dealt with by train guards, with prosecutions brought by the British Transport Police.

Separate rules are also in place for buses, where loud passengers can be hit with on-the-spot fines of £100 by police for playing music aloud.

Drivers are not responsible for enforcing the rules, but are able to call in transport safety officers and the police to deal with incidents.

Mr Burnham said: “We’ve all been on the train when someone starts blasting music or videos from their phone. It gets on your nerves and can quickly spoil the journey.

“So, we’re launching a nationwide campaign reminding passengers to use headphones on trains. On top of that, we’re giving local leaders new powers to tackle loud music, vaping and littering on buses.

“It’s a simple thing, but one that will make journeys that little bit better for all of us.”

‘Share the carriage, not the noise’

Railway and bus companies are expected to promote the campaign on their services, as well as on their websites and across social media.

They will put up posters, and announcements have been recorded to play to passengers on trains.

One example provided by officials says: “This is a friendly reminder that you are in a shared space, so please consider those around you and wear headphones if you want to listen to music or take calls. Let’s share the carriage, not the noise.”

Heidi Alexander, the Transport Secretary, said: “It is so frustrating when the actions of an inconsiderate few spoil journeys for the rest of us, whether that is vaping, littering or blasting music out loud. 

“Even small changes in behaviour can make a massive difference to people’s experience on public transport.

Union concerns

But unions expressed concerns about the plans, warning they risked adding to the “avalanche of escalating abuse” that public transport workers faced.

Unite has demanded that bus drivers be given “the same protection from violence as emergency workers” when dealing with disruptive passengers.

Sharon Graham, the union’s general secretary, said: “The government’s proposals are well-meaning but wholly inadequate to tackle the challenges and violence bus workers are facing on a daily basis.

“The proposed penalties are not going to deal with the issues facing workers. Our members are demanding and deserve protections at work that these proposals do not address.”

data.title: Tesco sells central European arm for £1.5bn in global retreat
data.description:
Tesco has nearly completed the breakup of its once-sprawling global retail empire with the £1.5bn sale of its Czech and Slovak stores.

Britain’s biggest grocer ended 30 years of operations in the two Central European countries through a deal with Dutch supermarket giant Ahold Delhaize.

That leaves only Tesco’s Hungarian business in an international division that once had strongholds in 17 foreign countries.

However, the company has steadily withdrawn from overseas territories over the past 15 years to focus on its core business in the UK.

Only 190 Irish supermarkets are expected to remain part of its estate outside the UK.

Tesco built a substantial overseas network in the 1990s and 2000s.

Its foreign offshoots included stores in China, India, Malaysia, Thailand, Turkey and the United States, where an ill-fated attempt to establish its Fresh & Easy brand ended with its sale in 2013.

The businesses in South Korea, Thailand ‌and ⁠Malaysia were sold in 2015, while its remaining stake in its Chinese joint venture was offloaded in 2020.

Tesco operates more than 360 supermarkets, hypermarkets and convenience stores in the Czech Republic and Slovakia, and 114 franchise stores in the Czech Republic.

Tesco bought the business in 1996 when it purchased the regional operations of the American retailer Kmart for $117.5m (£88m).

Last year the two territories generated sales of around £2.9bn and accounted for the bulk of the £115m operating profits made by the Central European division. The Czech and Slovak businesses together employ around 14,000 people.

However, in its latest annual report, Tesco flagged “increased competition, particularly in Slovakia and ongoing regulatory pressure”.

The stores sold a range of locally sourced products, including, in Slovakia, live carp kept in tanks before Christmas, although the practice ended in 2023 after protests by animal rights groups.

Ken Murphy, the chief executive of Tesco, said: “The transaction will further simplify the group, increasing our focus on our core UK and Irish businesses and supporting our continued investment in our food-first retail ecosystem and the capabilities that will drive future growth, while enabling a further return of capital to shareholders.”

In addition to the stores, the sale includes offices and distribution centres in Kralupy, Czech Republic, and Prešov and Beckov, Slovakia. The sale is expected to be completed in the fourth quarter of next year.

Tesco will receive around £1bn in cash, with most of the proceeds returned to investors through a buyback.

Tesco said it would “continue to review all options for the future of our business in Hungary”.

Tesco shares rose around 1.5pc after the deal.

data.title: Water bosses lose bonuses after worst pollution on record
data.description:
Several water bosses will be blocked from receiving bonuses after their companies were awarded the worst possible environmental rating.

One-star ratings at Southern Water, Thames Water, South West Water and Yorkshire Water were all confirmed by the Environment Agency on Thursday.

This means they will now be blocked from paying executive bonuses as part of a government crackdown launched last year that seeks to prevent companies rewarding failure.

The latest ratings were confirmed as part of the agency’s annual performance review. The best possible rating is four stars, which was only achieved by Severn Trent.

The agency announced on Thursday that pollution incidents are still far too high across the UK, with six category 1 incidents reported in 2025.

These are incidents deemed to have had a major effect on the environment or on households, and also lead to a ban on bonuses.

Both Severn Trent and Anglian Water were found liable for category 1 incidents in 2025, meaning they will also be barred from handing payouts to their bosses.

Overall, the EA found that there were 74 serious sewage pollution incidents in 2025, only slightly fewer than the 75 in 2024.

Alan Lovell, the chairman of the Environment Agency, said that the companies awarded one-star ratings had fallen “well short of the standards rightly demanded by both us and the public”.

Ministers are now set to visit a number of sites to interrogate companies’ performance.

Dame Angela Eagle, the Environment Secretary, said she will also be looking at options to strengthen the ban on executives’ bonuses.

It follows the first ever joint report from the Environment Agency, Natural Resources Wales, the Drinking Water Inspectorate and Ofwat, which leaves nowhere for underperforming companies to hide.

In total, there were 2,666 sewage and water supply incidents that took place in 2025, with Thames Water responsible for more than any other supplier: 464.

That was down from 2,801 in 2024.

James Wallace, the chief executive of River Action, said: “Another year, another record low.

“In 2025 almost every water company in England has been ranked as performing poorly, and the sewage kept flowing into our rivers just as it has done for years.

“This year’s figures show that performance is getting worse, not better.”

PM vows to introduce more ‘public control’

Mr Wallace said the latest pollution figures are further evidence that Thames Water, which released 108,000 hours of raw sewage into Britain’s waterways last year, should be put into special administration.

The latest pollution failures have emerged despite £5bn of investment from water companies, which has pushed households’ bills.

The figures come at a critical moment for the water industry after Andy Burnham vowed to introduce more “public control” over the sector.

A spokesman for Water UK, which represents the sector, admitted that improvements were needed.

He said: “Today’s report shows the lowest level of leakage in history. However, the fact remains that the environmental performance of some water companies is not good enough.”

Dame Angela said: “Water companies have let the public down time and time again, and today’s report is further proof that root-and branch reform cannot wait.

“People are sick of excuses. I am demanding answer from the companies that are failing.”

data.title: GSK plots £400m Cambridge research hub in push for cancer breakthrough
data.description:
GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) will invest £400m in a major new science hub in Cambridge as part of plans to pour more money into developing new cancer drugs.

The pharmaceuticals giant said it planned to acquire a new 300,000 sq ft site on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus, which will house most of its research and development (R&D).

The new centre of excellence will employ more than 1,000 scientists, GSK said, with its researchers developing new vaccines, HIV treatments and cancer drugs.

However, the move will also end the FTSE 100 company’s 50-year relationship with Stevenage, Hertfordshire, which was previously its main UK research base. Some Stevenage staff will be asked to relocate to another lab in nearby Ware.

The investment in Cambridge comes as GSK seeks to ramp up its pipeline of medicines under Luke Miels, its new chief executive, who took on the role from Dame Emma Walmsley at the start of the year.

The company has been accelerating investment in cancer drugs after it acquired US-based Nuvalent in June for nearly £8bn.

GSK won approval from US medical regulators last week for Jideytro, a lung cancer treatment secured as part of the takeover of Nuvalent.

The decision to open a new Cambridge campus will bolster the Government’s efforts to turn the 100-mile corridor between Oxford and Cambridge into an economic powerhouse.

GSK said the investment would build its presence “in the heart of the UK’s life sciences ‘Golden Triangle’” – made up of Oxford, Cambridge and London.

Earlier this year, Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, set out Labour’s ambition to turn the area into a hub for science businesses, building new homes and transport links to create Europe’s “Silicon Valley”.

The Cambridge Biomedical Campus already employs more than 22,000 people and hosts treatments for one million patients each year. GSK hopes to build its links with research hospitals in Cambridge and benefit from proximity to the University of Cambridge.

Mr Miels said: “This investment will accelerate our R&D and help us deliver new, competitive products.”

On Tuesday, GSK also announced plans for a major cost-cutting drive aimed at saving £1.9bn by 2029 to fund the development of new drugs. The savings are expected to include job cuts around the world, including reducing some back-office roles.

Alongside the plans for a new Cambridge site, GSK said it had launched 20 phase three trials as part of its plans to expand its pipeline of treatments.

These trials are the final stage of clinical testing before a drug is submitted to the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency for approval.

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, said the £400m investment was “a vote of confidence in British business”.

Life science is one of eight sectors that form part of the Government’s modern industrial strategy.

The investment from GSK comes after its rival AstraZeneca announced that it would pour £200m into its Cambridge site, along with £100m for a project in Macclesfield, Cheshire.

GSK’s relocation to the Cambridge Biomedical Campus means Britain’s two largest pharmaceutical companies will neighbour each other in the city. GSK said it would keep its global headquarters in London.

data.title: Bake Off to air on Disney+ as Channel 4 strikes streaming deal
data.description:
The Great British Bake Off is to air on Disney+ under a new deal aimed at luring more young viewers to Channel 4.

The hit baking show, which now counts Nigella Lawson among its presenters, will be available to watch live on Disney’s streaming service in the UK and Ireland from early next year.

Under the terms of the partnership, Channel 4’s main TV channel will broadcast on Disney+, allowing viewers to tune in live to favourites such as Bake Off and Gogglebox, as well as the broadcaster’s news coverage.

The agreement also includes on-demand access to selected new shows, including upcoming comedy series Stepping Up, starring Denise Welch, and reality show Celebrity SAS: Who Dares Wins.

In addition, Disney+ subscribers will be able to access hundreds of hours of programmes from Channel 4’s back catalogue, such as Big Mood, Tip Toe and 24 Hours in A&E.

Channel 4 is hoping to tap into new audiences as it scrambles to reverse an exodus of young viewers to streaming rivals and social media apps such as YouTube and TikTok.

While the broadcaster has a remit to serve 16 to 24-year-olds, official viewing figures show that more than three quarters of its total viewing hours come from people aged 45 or older.

By contrast, young people aged 16 to 34 account for 39pc of viewing on Disney+, while a further 17pc is from children aged 15 or younger.

Priya Dogra, the chief executive of Channel 4, said the youth-focused broadcaster was “leaning into partnerships with like-minded organisations”.

She told The Telegraph: “Audience habits are evolving and Channel 4 needs to evolve to meet those habits. This is about how we are taking action to own our future.”

Ms Dogra has previously said Channel 4 was open to putting its shows on iPlayer, but has pushed back against suggestions that the broadcaster could be merged with the BBC.

Karl Holmes, Disney’s European streaming boss, said the deal would give Disney+ subscribers access to Channel 4’s “innovative, buzzy and talked-about shows”.

He said it underscored how the US media giant was “doubling down” on local programming to help bolster its catalogue of blockbusters and animated favourites.

Disney+ has already enjoyed major success in the UK with Rivals, which is scheduled to return for the remainder of its second series next month.

It follows a similar deal struck between ITV and Disney last year as Britain’s beleaguered public-service broadcasters seek partnerships with streaming giants in an increasingly competitive market.

Channel 4 and Disney did not disclose commercial terms of the licensing deal, though the broadcaster will retain advertising revenues from its live channel while Disney will keep ad sales from on-demand programmes.

Channel 4 programmes will be available from a dedicated section of the Disney+ app under the broadcaster’s branding.

It comes in the midst of heavy cost-cutting at Channel 4, which is cutting around a quarter of its workforce in the biggest redundancy round in its 40-year history.

Bosses are seeking to shore up the company’s balance sheet after it posted a £10m deficit last year.

The broadcaster, which is publicly owned but commercially funded, has also secured permission from the Government to access the remaining half of a £150m debt facility.

Ms Dogra, who took over as chief executive in March, is also seeking to breathe new life into Channel 4’s programming.

She has appointed David Brindley, the TV producer behind Educating Yorkshire and Race Across the World, as Channel 4’s new director of programmes, replacing Ian Katz, the long-serving content boss.

data.title: Energy Secretary’s former employer doubts North Sea wealth fund
data.description:
A think tank once led by Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, has criticised her plans for a North Sea wealth fund, saying it would be ineffective.

The New Economics Foundation (NEF), which Ms Fahnbulleh led between 2017 and 2023, said the proposed Energy Wealth Fund would fail in its aims because tax revenue from oil and gas drilling was too small to fund net zero plans.

The new fund was announced by the Energy Secretary this week alongside her decision to approve the Jackdaw gas field, with future North Sea tax receipts going into the vehicle.

But Blai Avià-Novoa, an economist at the New Economics Foundation, said: “Redirecting a small and declining revenue base to the national wealth fund will not be enough to deliver the green investment that the UK so desperately needs.

“It’s important to remember that North Sea oil and gas revenues are declining at an accelerated rate. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) says that revenues in 2028-29 will be just £0.2bn, less than a tenth of what they were in 2023-24.”

A think tank veteran, Ms Fahnbulleh left the NEF in 2023, shortly before she was elected to Parliament as MP for Peckham in the last general election.

The Treasury is launching the Energy Wealth Fund, which will sit within the existing National Wealth Fund, with a £2bn injection.

It is unclear whether only a share or all North Sea tax receipts will be redirected into the fund, or whether John Healey, the Chancellor, could unveil a new surcharge on the sector.

Mr Healey said on Wednesday that if Britain had invested revenues from the North Sea since the 1980s, “we’d have a British sovereign wealth fund now that would be worth probably a trillion pounds”.

The figure is based on internal Treasury modelling, assuming North Sea receipts of £200bn had been invested and left to grow at a similar rate to Norway’s $2.4tn (£1.8tn) sovereign wealth oil fund.

Britain’s decision to launch an Energy Wealth Fund long after North Sea revenues peaked is unlikely to yield any such results, sceptics have said.

Simon French, an economist at Panmure Liberum, said: “If the UK wants to start now then it shouldn’t be buying green energy assets but probably a global equity ETF, a global bond fund, and buy back some of that gold sold 25 years ago.”

Britain’s initiative will pour money into green energy projects, though the sums fall far short of what is needed.

The OBR has estimated that the Government needs to spend £257bn in 26 years up to 2050 to hit net zero.

Mr Avià-Novoa said: “To truly shift the dial, state investment vehicles like the National Wealth Fund will need to be able to borrow on the capital market, like they already can in other European countries.”
