data.title: Parking fines capped at £100 in purge on ‘cowboys’
data.description:
Parking penalties are to be capped at £100 as Andy Burnham cracks down on so-called “cowboy” companies.

Motorists will also be given 10 minutes to leave car parks without facing a penalty once their paid-for time is up, under new legally binding rules due to come into force by the end of the year.

The Private Parking Code of Practice will give drivers the right to have charges cancelled on appeal for honest mistakes.

These include a breakdown in a car park, a medical emergency or a broken ticket machine, as well as stopping briefly to check directions and issues outside the driver’s control.

Mr Burnham said: “Being a few minutes late back to your car or typing one digit of your numberplate wrong shouldn’t end with a hefty fine landing on your doormat.

“These charges leave people feeling ripped off and out of pocket, so I’m putting a stop to them.

“We are introducing clearer rules, longer grace periods and lower charges for genuine mistakes, while going after the deliberate scams that rip drivers off.”

Under the code, drivers who make mistakes such as forgetting parking permits, entering a vehicle registration wrong or forgetting to confirm it in a parking machine, will face a maximum charge of £20, the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said.

At present, Westminster council, for example, issues penalties of up to £130. These increase to £195 for a single contravention if not paid within 14 days.

Simon Williams, the RAC’s head of policy, said the code was a “step in the right direction” to protect drivers from the practices of some private parking companies, but “not the leap” the motoring services company had been campaigning for.

He said: “We’ve long called for the banning of debt recovery fees being added on top of parking charge notices and a single independent appeals body to replace the two industry-run ones, but neither have been included, which is disappointing.

“That said, the fact we finally have a code seven years on from the Private Parking Code of Practice Act becoming law is positive.”

A similar parking code of practice was issued in 2022 by the Conservative government. The parking industry robustly challenged it, prompting that set of rules to be withdrawn almost straight away.

Yet over-aggressive parking enforcement has been one of the nation’s biggest bugbears for many years.

In 2017, a Scottish woman was given a £24,500 penalty after ignoring more than 200 penalties, while in 2025 a nurse was taken to court by a private parking company after she “repeatedly” took more than five minutes after entering the car park to buy a ticket.

Will Hurley, the chief executive of the International Parking Community trade body, said: “I genuinely hope the new code is a good thing for the industry. We’ve put so much work into making sure that the Government understands the importance of it.

“For years I’ve been trying to change this mindset within the sector,” he added.

“Instead of looking for a reason to issue a charge, or instead of looking for a reason to reject an appeal [against a parking penalty], look for a reason not to issue a charge, or look for a reason to cancel a parking charge on appeal. And it’s just a slightly different mindset that I genuinely think makes a difference.”

A record 16.9 million parking tickets were handed out by private businesses in the 12 months to the end of March, according to analysis of government data by the Press Association and the RAC Foundation.

That is up from 14.4 million the year before, and 6.8 million in 2018-19. The parking industry attributed the rise to an increase in the number of car parks being managed.

Each ticket can be up to £100, meaning the total cost to drivers may be more than £4.6m per day at the current rate.

Alison Tooze, chief policy officer at the British Parking Association, said the new code was an “an important step forward for motorists, communities and responsible parking operators”.

“Overall, the code strikes the right balance between stronger protections for motorists and effective parking management, helping keep communities, businesses and local economies moving,” she said.

Jack Cousens, the head of roads policy at the AA, said: “After seven long years, drivers finally have something which could offer them better protections against the worst private parking operators. For too long, many private parking operators have aggressively attacked drivers to the point where many simply pay up if they receive a charge from one on the doorstep.

“While this is a good first step, there is still a huge amount of work to do, such as tackling the scourge of debt recovery fees. Ultimately, we need to stop charges being issued in the first place, especially where the driver has done nothing wrong.”

data.title: Burnham’s crackdown on headphone-dodgers ‘impossible to enforce’
data.description:
Labour’s plan to fine bus passengers £100 for playing music out loud will be impossible to implement without recruiting a costly army of enforcement officials, industry bosses warned.

Only a handful of local authorities have their own transport safety officers trained in tackling antisocial behaviour, while there are no plans to involve bus drivers in the campaign.

Alison Edwards, of the Confederation of Passenger Transport, said bus firms backed the crackdown but that the success of the scheme will “come down to budgets”.

She said: “We welcome the recognition that it’s an issue and the powers to tackle that, but what they need now is the ability to enforce that meaningfully.

“There’s a question mark because there’s a cost involved. Have they got the funding to have transport safety offices where they need them?”

She added: “Bus drivers are not security guards and it would be wrong to expect them to enforce the law.”

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, launched the campaign on headphone-dodgers last week, saying that “blasting music or videos” gets on people’s nerves “and can quickly spoil the journey”.

The campaign builds on legislation introduced last year giving local leaders new powers to tackle loud music, vaping and littering on buses, backed by the threat of a £100 penalty.

Antisocial behaviour on trains can attract £1,000 fines, enforceable by the British Transport Police, which works only on the railway, even though buses attract more passengers.

Phil Southall, a managing director at Go-Ahead, which runs buses throughout England, said he was “sceptical” about the scheme given the funding crisis at local authorities.

He said: “The Government says the responsibility for enforcing this falls to councils. But if the councils haven’t got the resources then nothing’s going to change.

“The bus drivers won’t do it because they’re not required to. If they don’t feel safe they’re not going to get out of the cab, and they’re certainly not going to be levying the fines.

“We will brief them on the change in legislation but the briefing will be ‘it’s not your responsibility’, basically.”

He added: “The whole definition probably needs a bit of clarity, too. A grandmother playing a TikTok video because she forgot her headphones, is that the same as a load of yobs?”

Metroline, which operates mostly in London, said that while eliminating antisocial behaviour was a long-term goal, the scarcity of funding meant the industry needed to pick its targets.

Using mobile phones on loudspeaker is a ‘low-level’ concern

Sean O’Shea, the chief commercial officer at parent group ComfortDelGro, said: “There aren’t those huge resources that would enable us to cover the whole spectrum. I don’t know if it’s going to end up being that big a priority.

“In terms of the hierarchy, violence against women and girls is far more important. If we can tackle the big issues and crack that, then let’s work our way down the list.”

He said habits such as people using mobile phones on loudspeaker might be seen as antisocial but were “low level and just something that people do because the technology enables it”.

Greater Manchester’s Bee Network, established when Mr Burnham was mayor, is one of the few bus services with a fully fledged enforcement operation, partly funded with government grants for which it became eligible after pioneering a London-style franchising model.

The city has 150 enforcement officers who respond to everything from drunks on buses and trams to violent disorder.

Even then, resources are spread thinly, with the force split into three divisions, each working four shifts to target the morning rush, end of the school day, evening drinkers and night buses.

Kate Green, the head of policing and community safety at Transport for Greater Manchester, said a live police chat room for concerned passengers currently redirects reports of vaping, smoking and noise away from a police response.

She said: “We patrol those routes and warn people they’ll have to leave if their behaviour continues. There’s no fine, but I do wonder how much that is going to change.”

The Department for Transport said those local authorities that elect to take up the new powers will also be responsible for their enforcement.

data.title: AstraZeneca dumped by investors over £300bn US merger talks
data.description:
AstraZeneca shares have taken an £18bn hit after investors baulked at reports it was plotting a mega-merger with a US rival.

Shares in Britain’s second-most valuable company slumped on Monday after it emerged that AstraZeneca had held talks about a potential $400bn (£300bn) tie-up with Bristol Myers Squibb.

If completed, the merger would create one of the world’s largest pharmaceutical businesses. The potential deal would also raise fears that AstraZeneca could shift its business to the US in a blow to Britain.

However, analysts said it was a high-risk deal that risked destroying more value than it created. It would be one of the biggest mergers of all time, meaning any missteps could prove hugely costly, and would be likely to draw the attention of competition regulators and politicians.

News of the talks, first reported by the Financial Times, sent AstraZeneca’s shares plunging 9pc on Monday to their lowest level since September 2025.

Markus Manns, a portfolio manager at Union Investment and an ‌AstraZeneca ⁠shareholder, told Reuters: “A combination with Bristol ​does not make strategic or financial sense.

“Many past mega-mergers have destroyed value and there is no apparent need for Astra to do it.”

Jefferies analysts said in a note: “If there is ​one company that doesn’t need financial engineering, it’s AstraZeneca.”

Michael Leuchten, an analyst at Jefferies, said he was “perplexed” by the potential takeover. He said investors backed the company because of its consistent sales growth, not because management “go out and do big deals”.

AstraZeneca is worth around £184bn on the London Stock Exchange, while New York-listed Bristol Myers Squibb has a market value of $133bn.

Bristol Myers Squibb shares surged as much as 3.8pc on Wall Street on Monday.

Analysts said competition concerns would be the biggest hurdle to a deal as both companies have large cancer treatment businesses.

The potential deal could also trigger a political backlash from Donald Trump’s administration, Jefferies warned.

Mr Leuchten added: “AstraZeneca would effectively be a UK-based acquirer of one of America’s large Pharmas, at a time when US policymakers are focused on domestic manufacturing and strategic industries.”

The deal would raise questions about AstraZeneca’s continued links to Britain as Sir Pascal Soriot, its chief executive, pushes ahead with a pivot towards the US.

AstraZeneca upgraded its listing on the New York Stock Exchange last September to let American investors buy its shares directly, while keeping its listing in London.

The move put AstraZeneca’s New York listing on a par with that of London, in what was seen as a blow to the UK’s struggling stock market.

AstraZeneca subsequently struck a $50bn deal with the Trump administration to invest in US manufacturing and transatlantic research facilities.

At the time, Sir Pascal described the drugmaker as a “very American company”.

The business subsequently agreed to sell some medicines at a discount to the US Medicaid programme to avoid being hit with tariffs.

Despite this, Britain’s biggest drugmaker has insisted that it intends to remain headquartered in Cambridge and retain its listing on the London Stock Exchange.

Mr Leuchten said buying Bristol Myers Squibb as a way to shift permanently to the US would be “a fairly drastic way to go about it”.

However, Neil Birrell, the chief investment officer at Premier Miton, an AstraZeneca shareholder, said the likelihood of the pharmaceutical business shifting its shares to the US would increase if the Bristol Myers Squibb deal went ahead.

Mr Birrell added: “There hasn’t been a huge amount that I’ve seen coming out from any of the authorities – whether it be the Government or the London Stock Exchange – of any great substance to try and keep these sort of companies here.”

The Prime Minister said the talks were “a private matter for the companies involved”.

A No 10 spokesman said: “More broadly, the UK life sciences sector is one of our greatest national assets, driving innovation, skilled employment and investment across the country while developing medicines that improve health outcomes and save lives.”

AstraZeneca has around 10,000 staff at five UK sites, including 4,000 at its main facilities in Cambridge and Macclesfield and another 2,000 in London and Luton.

Steve Boden, a regional organiser at GMB Union, said he was seeking urgent assurances from AstraZeneca that jobs would be protected.

“These reports of a merger are causing great concern amongst AstraZeneca’s loyal workers. While no deal has been formally announced, mergers can create pressure to cut costs, so staff are understandably worrying about what this could mean for them.”

The proposed mega-merger will evoke memories of Pfizer’s attempts to take over AstraZeneca a decade ago.

The US company’s acquisition ultimately collapsed after a wave of resistance from the board and politicians alike.

Ed Miliband, then Labour leader, said at the time that Pfizer’s assurances about protecting research and saving jobs were “worthless”.

Bristol Myers Squibb is headquartered in Princeton, New Jersey, and was started in 1858, making it one of the US’s oldest pharmaceutical companies.

data.title: Violent shoplifters avoiding prison because of Labour delays
data.description:
Violent shoplifters who attack retail workers are being spared prison sentences because of “inaction” by the Government in the face of jail overcrowding.

In April, Parliament passed new laws introducing a standalone offence of assaulting a retail worker with a maximum penalty of six months in jail.

It also gave courts powers to impose criminal behaviour orders for first-time offenders, which carry a maximum five-year jail term if breached.

However, the law change has yet to be implemented, and there is no fixed date when it will take effect.

It comes as the Government is seeking to reduce prison overcrowding with the early release of 4,500 criminals in the next 10 months.

Lucy Whing, the crime policy adviser at the British Retail Consortium, said: “Progress on tackling shop theft is still too slow. Theft is not a victimless crime – it fuels violence against shop workers, and adds costs that ultimately hit shoppers’ pockets.

“With 1,600 incidents of violence or abuse against retail workers every day, the human toll remains unacceptable.

“The Crime and Policing Act granted police new powers to intervene and prosecute offenders, including a long-overdue offence of assaulting a retail worker.

“Yet six months after the new law passed, these protections have still not come into force. Retail workers face abuse every day – their safety must not be the price of Government inaction.”

A nationwide week of action against retail crime begins on Nov 9.

Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, said: “The Government is leaving our streets unprotected. Police numbers are down 2,000 since the election and criminals are being let out of jail early. Now it turns out the Government can’t even commence their own laws because they have mismanaged the system so badly.”

The police reported more than half a million shoplifting offences between June 2025 and June this year, data show.

However, the British Retail Consortium says this underestimates the true level of crime because so many are not referred to police. Last year it estimated that there were 5.5 million detected incidents of shop theft.

One in seven thefts involve abuse

Data from Auror, a crime reporting platform that helps police and shops identify prolific thieves, showed that one in seven store thefts involved abuse.

One in 10 thefts involved violence, weapons, assault, arson, hate crimes, harassment or aggression in 2024, up from one in 12 the previous year.

Repeat offenders are up to four times more likely to be violent with knives or other sharp implements, the most common weapons used by thieves.

Earlier this year, The Telegraph revealed calls by Stuart Machin, the Marks and Spencer chief executive, for the Government and city mayors to crack down on shoplifting and violence towards staff.

Mr Machin called for police to be given more resources, saying criminals were getting “more brazen, more aggressive and more organised”.

A Home Office spokesman said: “For too long, retail crime has been dismissed as low-level offending. It harms shopworkers, damages businesses and hollows out communities.

“Shop theft is down 2 per cent on last year, and charges are up 25 per cent. We are making it a specific criminal offence to assault a retail worker because no one should go to work fearing for their safety. Further details on these new protections will follow in due course.”

data.title: ‘I took out a loan to save my start-up. Now I worry I may lose my home’
data.description:
When Callum Vincent, an entrepreneur, went looking for fresh funding to keep his sports science business Lumi Therapy afloat, he turned to a growing band of alternative lenders.

Lumi, which manufactured ice baths and infrared saunas, had enjoyed rapid success, winning investment from England footballer Harry Maguire and celebrity endorsements from the likes of Tommy Fury.

But when one of its main lenders pulled the plug, Vincent had no choice but to seek funding from outside the mainstream banking sector.

“It was literally the last resort. We were really squeezed by the middle of 2024. I had to take out a loan with them, which had crazy high interest rates, Vincent says.

“The idea was that we were going to pay it off in the next two to three months [with] the sales we were going to do over Christmas.”

After speaking with financial advisers, the entrepreneur took out loans from a number of lenders, including Iwoca and Funding Circle, two fintechs serving the small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) sector.

But the emergency lifeline wasn’t enough and Lumi collapsed into administration in 2025.

Now Vincent’s attempts to salvage his business have come back to haunt him.

Like many business owners, he agreed to personally guarantee the loans offered by Iwoca and Funding Circle, meaning his assets could be used to repay the loan if his business was unable to do so.

Vincent faces the risk that his house may have to be sold to repay Iwoca.

Although Iwoca is simply trying to protect its financial interests – Vincent agreed to the terms of the loan – the case highlights the dangers of entrepreneurs agreeing to personal guarantees.

His story is by no means unique.

Non-bank lenders such as Iwoca and Funding Circle have grown in stature in recent years as high street banks retreat from lending to small businesses.

A toxic cocktail of taxes and regulation – from higher National Insurance contributions to the cost of living crisis – has kept small companies such as Lumi on a knife-edge.

At the same time, British banks have pulled back from SME lending, with the likely rise in the bank tax on Wednesday set to force them to step even further back from business lending.

Alternative lenders offer fast decisions – Funding Circle says it can make a decision on a loan in less than five minutes – but this access to easy credit comes at a cost.

Interest rates on the loans can be high, and they often demand personal guarantees from customers.

Some of the most aggressive operators in the sector resemble the payday lenders that were once widespread but have since been regulated away. They offer cash in a pinch, at a price that can be extremely punitive.

Iwoca quotes a per-month interest rate for loans equivalent to an APR ranging between 20pc and 96pc. Funding Circle’s rates also come with an effective APR of between 14pc and 33pc on a representative loan of £100,000.

According to the Bank of England, the average effective interest rate on new loans to SMEs from major UK banks and building societies was 6.63pc in August.

“They are doing all the things that traditional SME lenders would have done years and years ago, where they know this family and the business, and they’re good guys and this, that and the other,” says Gary Greenwood, from Shore Capital.

The use of personal guarantees has long been criticised by the Federation of Small Businesses (FSB), as they turn a business loan into something that resembles a personal loan but remains unregulated by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), the City watchdog.

Tina McKenzie, the FSB national chairman, said they had a “chilling effect” on the economy. “A personal guarantee turns a business loan into a personal liability, yet it sits outside of the FCA’s regulatory perimeter,” she says.

Iwoca was founded in the UK in 2011 by James Dear and Christoph Rieche, two former bankers at Deutsche and Goldman Sachs.

Since then it has lent around £6bn to 150,000 SMEs, and it expects around 500,000 applications this year alone.

It is also one of the most prolific litigants when it comes to enforcing personal loans.

The company has brought more than 90 debt claims in the High Court alone this year, with Iwoca suing at least one individual who personally guaranteed the loan in almost every case.

Such is the scale of its legal actions that Iwoca’s claims account for more than half of all commercial disputes issued at the High Court in Leeds this year.

The total figure is likely higher because the High Court only hears claims worth £100,000 or more.

Businesses can often already be under significant financial stress when they turn to alternative lenders such as Iwoca.

The Telegraph was able to link 43 of Iwoca’s claims from this year to existing insolvency proceedings. In 30 of those, Iwoca was one of at least two short-term lenders the business had borrowed from.

Sources close to Iwoca said that it conducts credit checks on guarantors, and that guarantors are called to confirm that they understand what they are signing.

They added that using more than one lender was normal for a growing business and that research it had commissioned showed that businesses that had used the platform were more likely to be still active three years later than businesses overall.

However, for people like Vincent, the experience can be jarring.

Funding Circle cut a deal with Vincent to help him pay back most of the £250,000 loan.

He also offered Iwoca a settlement on its £250,000 loan that would pay back most of it, excluding interest, with the lender facing a net loss of £35,000, but the company refused to accept his proposal.

Instead, it claimed £184,000 — the value of the unpaid loan as well as the interest that had accrued on it, which Lumi had been unable to repay.

After no agreement was reached, Iwoca then went after Vincent personally.

Despite the fact that the business had collapsed, the interest on the loan continued to accrue right up until Iwoca’s lawyers had secured a county court judgment against him.

The company’s terms state that interest on any loan can accrue even after a judgment has been acquired.

Last month, Iwoca’s lawyers secured an interim charging order against his house, leaving Vincent worried about being forced to sell his home to pay off his debts.

An Iwoca spokesman said its lending had supported, over the past year, £3.5bn of UK GDP and 51,600 jobs.

“We are fully transparent about what we charge. Like almost all unsecured business lenders, we ask for a personal guarantee, which is what lets us lend without taking property or other assets as security.

“Around 70pc of customers who fall behind are back on track, or on an affordable repayment plan, within 60 days. Court is a last resort, and we have never applied to force the sale of a customer’s home.”

A personal guarantee is required on the vast majority of standard business loans that Funding Circle makes, many of which are back-stopped by the Government itself – including in Vincent’s case.

A Funding Circle spokesman said: “Accessing finance remains complex and slow for SMEs. Changing this is a role we take seriously, and in 2025 alone our lending supported 117,000 jobs and generated £8bn in GDP.”

However, for small businesses in desperate need of funding, with a government, bank sector and regulator that have largely abandoned them, there is often no one else to turn to.

“As a fairly young business, about three years old at that point, it was incredibly difficult for us to find any sort of lending. No banks would work with us, really,” Vincent says.

“I don’t know how anyone is supposed to start a business in the UK if you cannot get any sort of funding.”

data.title: Winter blackout risk rises for first time since 2022
data.description:
The risk of winter blackouts has risen for the first time in four years, amid warnings from Britain’s grid operator that net zero is making it harder to keep the lights on.

The National Energy System Operator (Neso) said on Friday that the forecast power buffer to protect the country from winter blackouts would be 5.9 gigawatts (GW), or 9.5pc of demand.

That compares with 6.1GW, or 10pc, last year.

It marks the first drop in the so-called de-rated margin, the projected amount of spare power during a cold spell, since the outbreak of the Ukraine war in 2022.

Neso said increased electricity demand had squeezed the margin. This may be coming from energy-hungry data centres, as well as rising household adoption of electric cars and heat pumps.

A damning independent report earlier this week warned that Neso control-room engineers were concerned that the switch to renewable energy was making it harder to manage the grid but felt pressure to “convey a positive message”.

The quango, responsible for the day-to-day management of Britain’s power system, stressed on Friday that supplies were still “sufficient for the forthcoming winter” and “expected to remain secure”.

However, the top civil servant in the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero admitted to MPs that the Government could not rule out blackouts.

Jonathan Brearley, the permanent secretary, told members of the public accounts committee: “We can never guarantee the lights won’t go out.

“As you know, there are always risks in any system.”

This winter’s safeguard figure was calculated using a different methodology to last year’s. The new methodology assigns wind farms a higher level of reliability.

Under the previous methodology, the margin would have been 5.2GW, or 8.4pc of demand.

Britain’s total power-generation capacity has grown from 127GW to 137GW in the past year. However, much of the increase comes from renewables, which are less reliable than other power sources such as gas and nuclear.

As a result, Neso cannot bank on the expanded capacity to provide a larger safety cushion.

‘There are always going to be risks’

The quango’s forecasts that Britain’s power will remain secure during the winter rest on the assumption it can call on European neighbours for help.

Without electricity imports from the Continent on the coldest winter days, the margin would be wiped out.

Mr Brearley said the Government may struggle to upgrade the grid sufficiently by 2030 to meet its pledge to power Britain with clean energy.

He told MPs: “We’ve got to recognise that there are always going to be risks around a programme this big.

“Some of those are within our control or the network company’s control, and some of those are outside of it.

“In this system, ultimately, the transmission companies are responsible for making sure these are delivered on time.”

Tim Jarvis, the chief executive of energy watchdog Ofgem, also said when pressed on the issue: “We accept there is risk there.”

Deborah Petterson, the director of resilience at Neso, said: “Despite continued geopolitical uncertainty and volatility in global energy markets, Britain enters this winter with a resilient and well-prepared electricity system.

“Our winter outlook shows we have sufficient margins and a diverse mix of generation sources to meet demand, even during periods of colder weather and higher system stress.

“While we never take resilience for granted, households and businesses can be confident that Great Britain’s electricity system remains secure, reliable and among the most resilient in the world.”

Separately, a winter outlook published by National Gas on Friday similarly predicted Britain’s supplies would be secure but cautioned that prices might surge.

data.title: Labour approves major solar farm in Robert Jenrick’s constituency
data.description:
Robert Jenrick has criticised the Energy Secretary for approving a major solar farm in his constituency, calling the plans a “disgrace”.

The Reform MP said the decision to grant approval for the Great North Road Solar scheme in his Newark constituency was a “hammer blow” and meant 10pc of the area would be carpeted with solar panels.

The controversial project, which will cover nearly 2,500 acres of prime farmland, has generated a significant local backlash from objectors increasingly furious at how the Nottinghamshire region is being targeted by solar developers.

On Tuesday, the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, led by Miatta Fahnbulleh, said consent had been granted for the scheme as well as a “biodiversity park” in the constituency.

Mr Jenrick, who is his party’s Treasury spokesman, said: “I am appalled and devastated that the Government has approved this vast solar scheme. This is a hammer blow to Newark and Nottinghamshire.

“The whole area will now be subjected to acre upon acre of solar panels. More than 10pc of my constituency will now be solar. Good farmland ruined. Years of mess and disruption. Views wrecked for generations. Labour clearly have a death wish against our county.

“I am disgusted that the views of local people have been utterly ignored. That was obvious from the beginning as Sherwood’s Labour MP even took a payment from the developer in the general election. The Energy Secretary has refused to meet local residents or answer basic questions. It’s a disgrace.”

Third scheme in Jenrick’s constituency

The scheme is one of the largest solar projects approved anywhere in the UK, generating 800 megawatts when the sun is shining.

It marks the third scheme in Mr Jenrick’s constituency to be approved, after the One Earth and Steeples solar plants.

Other mega-solar projects in the region include the Cottam, West Burton, and Gate Burton plants already slated for the Nottinghamshire and Lincolnshire borders.

The Campaign to Protect Rural England and numerous local parish councils highlighted that more than 60pc of the land is top quality farmland currently used for intensive arable crop production for wheat, barley, and oilseed rape.

The developer of the scheme is Elements Green, a private company based in Mayfair, London.

Rasmus Friis, its director, could not be reached for comment, but the project website said that the scheme “would continue the rich history of power generation in this area”.

This is a reference to the power stations that once operated nearby, whose legacy includes the substations providing the connections that now make the region so attractive for solar developers.

Announcing the decision, the Planning Inspectorate said it had considered thousands of local objections but rejected them:

“The Examining Authority listened and gave full consideration to all local views and the evidence gathered during the examination before making its recommendation to the Secretary of State.”

data.title: Lagarde steps down early at ECB to head off Le Pen threat
data.description:
Christine Lagarde is to step down as president of the European Central Bank (ECB) nine months early to head off the threat Marine Le Pen helps choose her successor.

The ECB confirmed on Thursday that Ms Lagarde would leave the organisation on Feb 7, well ahead of her scheduled departure date in October.

It will give existing European Union leaders time to pick ​her successor before France’s presidential election in April, which could result in victory by Ms Le Pen, who is leading in the polls.

Fears have grown among EU policymakers that if Ms Le Pen’s hard-Right National Rally swept to power it could push for a candidate who would undermine the ECB’s independence.

Ms Lagarde’s early exit means Emmanuel Macron, the current president, will help choose the new ECB leader.

ECB presidents are selected by EU member states but powerhouse economies like France enjoy significant sway over the process.

It comes amid turmoil in France, with financial markets rocked following widespread riots over the cost of living and poor conditions in schools.

Government borrowing costs in France soared to their highest level in 24 years last week following the violent protests and concerns about the spending promises of presidential frontrunners.

On Thursday, Ms Lagarde had appeared with two small plasters over her face in a video announcing her departure on Thursday, which she attributed to a “small surgery earlier this week” .

She later told ECB staff this was related to “a little skin cancer” and joked it had nothing to do with her recent attendance at International Monetary Fund meetings in Bangkok.

“I know I look funny. This is not kick-boxing in Thailand. It is just a little skin cancer that had to go,” she said in a video seen by Politico.

Ms Lagarde’s exit puts an end to long-running speculation about her future.

Frontrunners to replace Ms Lagarde include Klaas Knot and Pablo Hernandez de Cos, former central bank governors of the Netherlands and Spain respectively.

Europe’s central bank is navigating its way through a series of interest rate rises, seeking to prevent an oil price shock linked to the Iran war from feeding into ​other prices and ​wages.

This comes is alongside efforts to combat rising government bond yields, which have pushed up borrowing costs for households and ​businesses.

Ms Lagarde is widely expected to join the World Economic Forum (WEF) following her departure from the central bank.

António Costa, the president of the European Council, said the process to appoint Ms Lagarde’s successor would begin immediately with a view to making a “timely decision”.

Mr Costa said: “To ensure a smooth transition to the next leadership of the ECB, the process for the appointment of her successor will be initiated today and will proceed without delay, with a view to a timely decision by the European Council acting in its euro area composition.”

Ms Lagarde, 70, has led the ECB since November 2019, when she became its fourth leader.

She has since steered the central bank through the pandemic, the Russia-Ukraine war and most recently, the global energy crisis that has erupted in the wake of the war in Iran.

Ms Lagarde said in a video message on X: “I leave this institution with a sense of good work done, and an ECB that is fit for the future.”

Referring to her face plasters, she said: “Just to avoid any social media chatter: the plasters on my face are due to a small surgery earlier in the week. Follow doctor’s orders and get your skin checked regularly!”

Ms Lagarde would be taking the helm at the WEF after years of controversy.

It is currently co-chaired by BlackRock chief executive Larry Fink and Roche vice-chair André Hoffmann after the WEF’s founder Klaus Schwab departed in April 2025 over misconduct allegations. He was later cleared of material wrongdoing.

Børge Brende, its chief executive, also resigned earlier this year after an investigation into his links to Jeffrey Epstein. He was not accused of wrongdoing and the review found there no additional concerns beyond what was previously disclosed – that Mr Brende had communicated with Epstein but was unaware of his past criminal activity.

An ECB spokesman said: “President Lagarde’s successor will be appointed by the European Council following the nomination process outlined in Article 283 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union.

“The governing council thanked President Lagarde warmly and gave her a long-standing ovation.”
